1.synthesis:
Agni is asked to carry. Everything given into him rises, and the gods arrive through him — that is the premise the hymn opens on, and the reason the collection begins here rather than with sky or storm. Agni is the god who is actually present — burning on the hearth, visible — and so he is where contact begins.

*Agnim īḷe* — I praise Agni. The first verse gives him four titles, and each names work rather than glory. *Purohitam*, the one placed in front, who stands at the head of the rite. *Ṛtvijam*, the one who officiates when the season calls for it. *Hotāram*, the one who offers — and, in the older sense, the one who calls the gods by name. *Ratnadhātama*, the greatest holder of what is precious. The god is being described entirely through what he does for those who approach him.

The second verse makes a claim about time that is easy to read past. Agni is *īḍya* — worthy of praise — by the *pūrve ṛṣayaḥ*, the seers of long ago, and equally by the *nūtana*, those alive now. The same fire, the same address, across a distance nobody can measure. And the verse ends with the undertaking: *sa devāṁ eha vakṣati*, he shall convey the gods here. Anyone who recites the line steps into precisely what the line describes.

The third and fourth verses say what comes of it. Through Agni a person reaches *rayi* — wealth, but wealth as sustenance rather than hoard — and *poṣa*, nourishment that increases *dive-dive*, day upon day, along with *yaśas*, good standing, and strength in sons. Then the mechanism behind it: the *yajña* that Agni surrounds *viśvataḥ*, on every side, arrives among the gods. The word used for that offering is *adhvara* — the rite that suffers no injury, that nothing breaks into. Being encircled by fire is what keeps it whole.

The fifth verse turns from what Agni does to what he is: *hotā* again, and *kavikratu* — one in whom insight and effective action are the same faculty — and *satya*, true, and of the most brilliant renown. It closes *devo devebhir ā gamat*: the god comes, bringing the gods. The promise made in the second verse is fulfilled here, three verses later, and the hymn does not point this out.

The sixth verse states a law of the exchange. *Yad aṅga dāśuṣe tvaṃ agne bhadraṃ kariṣyasi, tavet tat satyam* — whatever good you do for the one who gives, that is your own truth. The generosity is not the worshipper's to claim; it belongs to Agni, and it returns. He is addressed here as *Aṅgiras*, a seer's name given to fire.

The seventh and eighth verses describe the approach itself, and they belong together. *Upa tvā... emasi* — we come near to you, *dive-dive*, day upon day, at the turning of dusk and dawn, *dhiyā*, with the mind engaged, *namo bharantaḥ*, bearing homage. And the one approached is: ruler of the rites, *gopām ṛtasya* — herdsman of ṛta, the one who keeps the order of things — shining, and *vardhamānaṃ sve dame*, growing in his own house. The Agni growing in your own house is the same Agni who guards the order of the world.

Then the ninth verse sets all of it down. After eight verses of office and function, of titles and powers, it asks for none of them: *sa naḥ piteva sūnave... sūpāyano bhava* — be easy to approach, as a father is to a son; stay near us, *svastaye*, for our wellbeing. The oldest prayer that survives in the tradition ends by asking the one who mediates everything to be, before anything else, approachable.
1.disagreements:
The tradition and the translators divide over *hotṛ*, the office named in verses 1 and 5. Sāyaṇa gives two derivations without choosing between them: from *hu*, to pour an offering, or from *hve*, to call — the one who sends the oblation up, or the one who summons the gods down. He identifies the hotā with the ṛtvij, citing the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa. Wilson follows the pouring sense throughout ("who presents the oblation"); Griffith leaves *hotar* untranslated in verse 1 and renders it "sapient-minded Priest" in verse 5.

On verse 6, Wilson has Agni's good "revert to you, Aṅgiras" — a circuit in which what is given comes back. Griffith reads a statement of reliability instead: "That, Angiras, is indeed thy truth." Sāyaṇa explains the vocative by deriving Aṅgiras from *aṅgāra*, a live coal, citing the Nirukta and the Brāhmaṇa tradition that the coals became the Aṅgirasas — which is why a fire can be addressed by a seer's name.

Verse 7's *doṣāvastar* splits them: Wilson takes it as dusk and dawn together, describing when the worshippers come; Griffith makes it an epithet of Agni, "dispeller of the night." Sāyaṇa reads verse 4's "on every side" concretely — the ritual fires standing at the four cardinal points of the enclosure — and glosses *adhvara* as the sacrifice free from injury or interruption.

1.practice:
This is the first hymn a student of the Ṛgveda receives, and Agni, whom it addresses, is not a historical object. Agni is still the witness before whom the saṃskāras are performed — the Agni circled at a wedding, kindled at the upanayana, lit at the last rite. Whatever else has changed, the addressee has not.

That Agni stands first is not an accident of shuffling. Eight of the ten maṇḍalas open with a sūkta to Agni — books one through seven and ten all begin with him; only the eighth opens with Indra, and the ninth is given over entirely to Soma. Across the collection some 236 of the 1,028 hymns name him, close to a quarter. Whoever arranged the Ṛgveda held a consistent principle: you begin with Agni, because Agni is where beginning is possible.

The sūkta also describes its own use. Verse 7 has the worshippers coming *dive-dive*, day upon day, at the turn of dusk and dawn, bearing homage *dhiyā* — with thought, not only with words. That is the sandhyā rhythm, stated in the text itself: not an occasional approach but a daily one, at the junctures, with attention. The hymn is not asking to be read once.

The second title given to Agni here is worth pausing on, because its root is in every saṅkalpa. *Ṛtvij* is *ṛtu* + √yaj — one who sacrifices at the proper season. Not the priest who knows the most, but the one who acts at the right time; the same *ṛtu* declared when the occasion of a rite is named. What that word is doing in the first verse of the collection is tying the whole enterprise to timeliness, an idea [[1.2]] takes up under a related word, *ṛta*.

What the hymn offers for reflection is the shape of its ninth verse. The relationship it finally asks for is not the awe due to power but the ease a son has with his father — *sūpāyano bhava*, be easy of approach. Everything preceding establishes Agni's authority; the last line asks him to set it aside. That order is deliberate, and it is the teaching.
1.title: Agni Given Every Title, Then Asked to Be a Father

2.synthesis:
The soma has been pressed and stands ready. What follows is not praise so much as hospitality — the drinkers are called in a fixed order, three verses each, and the order is itself the meaning. Wind first, then strength, and last the two who hold the world in its courses.

*Vāyav ā yāhi darśata* — Vāyu, come, you who are worth the sight. The somas are *araṃkṛtāḥ*, made ready, and the god is asked to do two things: drink, and hear. *Śrudhī havam* — listen to the call. Both halves matter, because the hymn is about to record that the call is answered.

The second verse names who is doing the calling. The *jaritāraḥ*, the singers, praise Vāyu with *ukthas* — recited verses, not chanted ones — and they are *sutasomāḥ*, having pressed the soma, and *aharvidaḥ*, knowers of the days. That last word is quiet but exact: these are people who know which day is the right day. The rite has a calendar, and they hold it.

Then the third verse turns the direction around. Vāyu's *dhenā* — his speech, his stream — goes out *dāśuṣe*, toward the one who gave, and it is *urūcī*, wide-reaching, and it comes *somapītaye*, for the drinking. The god is not merely summoned; something moves back down the line toward the worshipper.

The three Indra-and-Vāyu verses quicken. The pressed drops are set out, and the two are asked to come *upa prayobhiḥ*, with their pleasures — and then the hymn says something startling: *indavo vām uśanti hi*, the drops themselves desire you. The wanting is not only on the human side. The fifth verse calls the pair *vājinīvasū*, rich in the substance of strength, and asks them to come *dravat*, running. The sixth asks them to the *niṣkṛtam*, the appointed place — the spot prepared for the meeting — *makṣu*, quickly, and *itthā dhiyā*, thus with the mind's attention. Speed and attention together: the hurry is not carelessness.

The last three verses change register entirely. *Mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣaṃ varuṇaṃ ca riśādasam* — I call Mitra, whose *dakṣa*, whose effective power, is pure, and Varuṇa who destroys hostility. They are asked to perfect a *dhī* that is *ghṛtācī*, ghee-bearing: the thought itself is described as carrying an offering, as if the mind were a ladle.

The eighth verse is the hymn's centre of gravity, and it hammers one word. *Ṛtena mitrāvaruṇāv ṛtāvṛdhāv ṛtaspṛśā* — by ṛta, O Mitra and Varuṇa, growers of ṛta, touchers of ṛta. Three of the verse's words are built on the same root, and by it the two have attained *kratuṃ bṛhantam*, vast effective power. Ṛta is at once the truth of things, the working of the waters, and the sacrifice: to say the pair grow by it, increase it, and are in contact with it is to say they are what keeps the world running true.

The ninth closes by asking for something modest after all that height. The two are *kavī*, seers, *tuvijātā*, strong-born, *urukṣayā*, wide-dwelling — and what they are asked to bestow is *dakṣam apasam*, skill that works. Not visions. Competence.
2.practice:
These are the deities of the daily offering, and the order the hymn calls them in is the order of a rite still performed: the wind that carries, the strength that arrives, and last the pair who hold things in their courses.

Mitra and Varuṇa arrive here as a pair, and that is how they nearly always arrive. Across the whole Ṛgveda thirty-six sūktas are ascribed to *mitrāvaruṇau* — the two named as a single dual compound — and exactly one, [[3.59]], is addressed to Mitra by himself. Out of 1,028 hymns, Mitra stands alone once. Whatever these two are, the tradition treats them as one thing with two faces, which is why they can be asked in a single breath to perfect the thought and grant working skill.

The division between those faces is the one every Hindu who performs sandhyāvandana keeps. Mitra presides over the day and Varuṇa over the night, and *sandhyā* is exactly the observance of the junctures where one hands over to the other — the arghya offered as the day begins and again as it closes. The rite is built on the same division this hymn names. And the single Mitra sūkta supplies one of sandhyā's own verses: *mitrasya carṣaṇīdhṛto 'vo devasya sānasi*, the sustaining favour of Mitra who upholds the peoples ([[3.59]].6).

*Ṛta* is what to carry away. It is the word for the order that turns the seasons, moves the waters, and makes a promise hold — and the same word for the sacrifice. To act in accordance with ṛta and to perform the rite correctly are not two different things in this vocabulary. Mitra and Varuṇa are asked here not for favour but for that order to be maintained, and for *dakṣam apasam*, skill that actually works.

One caution about the word, because a near neighbour of it is in every pūjā. *Ṛta* is not *ṛtu*. *Ṛtu* is the season — the word named in the saṅkalpa when the time of the rite is declared, *ṛtau, māse, pakṣe*. *Ṛta* is the order itself. They are separate words that share the root √ṛ, to move or go, and the shared idea is regular recurrent motion: a season is what comes round again on time, and ṛta is the order by which anything comes round at all. The overlap is genuine — across the Ṛgveda *ṛta* appears in some 76 analysed forms and *ṛtu* in 20, and the glosses bleed into each other, "order" sitting inside ṛtu and "timely" inside ṛta.

The join between them is a word from the first hymn. *Ṛtvij*, the officiating priest — the title given to Agni in [[1.1]].1 — is *ṛtu* + √yaj, one who sacrifices at the proper season. The priest is named for the season, not for the truth. Doing the thing at its right time is itself how the order is kept.
2.disagreements:
*Ṛta* is where the readings part, and it is the most consequential divergence in the hymn. Wilson keeps the concrete range — Mitra and Varuṇa as "augmenters of water, dispensers of water" who connect the rite to its true reward — because Sāyaṇa allows the word to carry water and sacrifice alongside truth. Griffith goes to the abstraction: "through Law, lovers and cherishers of Law." One pair makes the rains work; the other upholds a principle.

Verse 3 divides the same way. Wilson's Vāyu answers with approving speech, and Sāyaṇa supplies the god's words outright — *I will drink the libation*. Griffith has "thy penetrating stream goes forth unto the worshipper," which makes it wind rather than reply.

Sāyaṇa identifies Mitra with the sun and Varuṇa with the regent of the waters, both among the twelve Ādityas, with Mitra presiding over the day and Varuṇa over the night.
2.title: Come and Drink — Vāyu, Indra, and the Keepers of Ṛta

3.synthesis:
Twelve verses, four sets of guests, three verses each — and beneath that tidy arrangement a single thread runs the whole length of the hymn and decides where it ends up.

The Aśvins are called first, and they are called by their hands. *Dravatpāṇī*, swift-handed; *śubhaspatī*, lords of brilliance; *purubhujā*, of ample enjoyment — and asked to take pleasure in the offerings set out. The second verse asks something more particular: it wants them to receive the songs *śavīrayā dhiyā*, with powerful thought, and calls them *dhiṣṇyā*, attentive. The praise is not just to be heard but to be met with mind. In the third they are *dasrā*, wondrous, and *nāsatyā*, and asked to come to where the *barhis* has been strewn and the soma stands mixed.

Indra follows, and here the hymn does something you can hear before you understand it. Verses 4, 5 and 6 all begin with the same two words — *indra ā yāhi*, Indra, come. Three times, unvaried, at the head of three consecutive verses. What changes is the reason each time. First: come, *citrabhāno*, of dazzling light, because the pressed drops are *tvāyavaḥ*, longing for you, purified through the fine strainer. Second: come *dhiyā iṣito viprajūtaḥ*, urged by thought and sped by the inspired — the summons is now the mind's, not the drink's. Third: come *tūtujānaḥ*, hurrying, *harivaḥ*, lord of the tawny horses, and place your pleasure in what has been pressed. The repetition is insistence, and the three grounds — the offering, the thought, the god's own speed — are the whole logic of invitation compressed.

The *Viśvedevāḥ* are asked next as *omāsaḥ*, helpers, and *carṣaṇīdhṛtaḥ*, upholders of the peoples — the same epithet the tradition gives Mitra in [[3.59]].6. They come *dāśvāṃsaḥ*, themselves giving, to the pressing of the one who gave. The eighth verse has one of the collection's homely images: come swiftly, *usrā iva svasarāṇi*, as cattle come to their pastures — gods hastening the way animals hurry toward familiar ground. In the ninth they are *asridhaḥ*, unfailing, *adruhaḥ*, without malice, and asked to enjoy the offering.

Then Sarasvatī, and the thread that has been running underneath comes to the surface. She is *pāvakā*, purifying, rich in *vāja*, and — the word that matters — *dhiyāvasuḥ*, wealthy through thought. The eleventh calls her *codayitrī sūnṛtānām*, the impeller of true and generous speech, and *cetantī sumatīnām*, the awakener of good thoughts. And the twelfth holds her two natures in one line without choosing: *maho arṇaḥ sarasvatī pra cetayati ketunā* — Sarasvatī makes the great flood known by her signal — *dhiyo viśvā vi rājati*, and she illumines all thoughts.

That last phrase is where the hymn has been going. *Dhī* — thought, insight, the mind at work — appears in the second verse as what the Aśvins should meet the praise with, in the fifth as what drives Indra to come, and finally in the tenth and twelfth as what Sarasvatī possesses and what she lights up. The hymn is not four unrelated invitations with a river goddess appended. It moves from thought as the worshipper's instrument to thought as something a power gives and illuminates, and Sarasvatī is where it arrives.
3.practice:
Sarasvatī is why this hymn still gets read outside a seminar. She is invoked here as a river you could stand beside and as the power that clarifies thinking, and the text refuses to make one a metaphor for the other. Everything the later tradition built — Sarasvatī as the patron of speech, learning, and music, worshipped at Vasant Pañcamī and at a child's *vidyārambha* — is already present in these three verses. *Codayitrī sūnṛtānām*, the impeller of true speech; *cetantī sumatīnām*, the awakener of good thoughts. The goddess before whom books and instruments are placed is being described in the third hymn of the Ṛgveda.

She is also rarer than her importance suggests. Across the collection sixteen sūktas name Sarasvatī, against sixty-nine for the Aśvins and eighty-six for the *Viśvedevāḥ*. What she receives is not volume but position — the closing movement of the third hymn, and the last word on what thought is.

The Aśvins are worth knowing here as healers. The tradition preserved them as *devānāṃ bhiṣajau*, the physicians of the gods, and this is the address it kept: twin riders, swift of hand, called to the offering with their hands already outstretched. Where the concern is illness or recovery, that is the door the Veda opens.

And *dhī* is the word to carry out of the hymn. It is not belief and it is not emotion — it is the mind actually working, and the hymn treats it as the thing that makes an offering land. Praise received *śavīrayā dhiyā*, with strong thought; Indra moved *dhiyā iṣitaḥ*, by thought; Sarasvatī *dhiyāvasuḥ*, wealthy through it. The same word stands behind *dhyāna*. Attention is not preparation for the rite — in this hymn it is the substance of it.
3.disagreements:
Sarasvatī's doubling is where the translators separate. Wilson keeps both aspects as genuinely two — she manifests a mighty river, and in her own form enlightens all understandings. Sāyaṇa states the position outright, citing the Nirukta that Sarasvatī is twofold, an embodied deity and a river, and that the hymns speak of her in both ways. Griffith compresses to "the mighty flood — she with her light illuminates, She brightens every pious thought," which reads the river as a figure for the mind.

Verse 9 turns on one epithet. Wilson's Viśvedevāḥ are "exempt from decay, omniscient, devoid of malice"; Griffith's are "changing shape like serpents, fearless, void of guile." Sāyaṇa offers two readings himself — those whose knowledge extends everywhere, or a name preserved from the legend in which the gods called after Agni in the waters, *ehi, mā yāsiḥ*, come, do not go.

On the Aśvins, Sāyaṇa records the tradition that they are the physicians of the gods, and takes *rudravartanī* as those who travel at the head of the warriors, deriving *rudra* from the root for weeping — those who make their enemies weep. He also notes *purubhuja* can be read as "great eaters" rather than long-armed.
3.title: Welcoming Four Guests — Aśvins, Indra, Viśvedevāḥ, Sarasvatī

4.title: Indra, Do Not Pass Us By; Let Rivals Call Us Blessed
4.synthesis:
Nothing in the first verse says who is being called. *Surūpakṛtnu*, the maker of fair forms, is invoked *ūtaye*, for help, *dyavi-dyavi*, day upon day — and the comparison is domestic to the point of bluntness: as a good milch cow is called at the milking. The god is approached the way a household approaches its own livelihood, at a fixed hour, expecting a yield.

The second verse brings him to the pressings. *Upa naḥ savanā ā gahi* — come near to our savanas — and drink, *somapā*, drinker of soma; the *mada*, the exhilaration, of the wealthy one is itself what gives cattle. The satisfaction and the gift are not two events.

The third verse is the most exposed moment in the sūkta. *Atha te antamānāṃ vidyāma sumatīnām* — then may we come to know the nearest of your good intentions — and then, without ornament: *mā naḥ ati khyaḥ, ā gahi*. Do not look past us. Come here. Everything the hymn wants sits in those four words, and they are said before Indra's name has been spoken once.

It is spoken in the fourth verse, and the address swings round: the singer stops speaking to the god and speaks to a man. *Parā ihi* — go across, ask Indra, *astṛta*, never overthrown, *vipaścit*, discerning, who gives his friends what is better. The hymn has put a second person in the room and sent him to make enquiries.

The fifth and sixth verses both open with *uta*, and together they form the strangest pair here, because both are about what other people will say. Let the *nidaḥ*, the fault-finders, say their piece and take themselves off elsewhere, while we set *duvaḥ* — reverent service — in Indra and nowhere else. And let the *ari* and the *kṛṣṭi*, the settled peoples, call us *subhaga*, well-portioned. *Syāma it indrasya śarmaṇi* — may we be inside Indra's *śarman*, his shelter. The petition is not only for goods; it is to be seen to be doing well.

The seventh verse returns to the cup. *Ā īm āśum āśave bhara* — bring the swift to the swift. The soma is *yajñaśrī*, the splendour of the yajña, *nṛmādana*, gladdener of men, and companion of the one who gladdens.

The eighth and ninth then lock onto a single word. Having drunk this, *śatakrato* — you of a hundred *kratus* — you became *ghanaḥ vṛtrāṇām*, the smasher of obstructions, and *prāvaḥ vājeṣu vājinam*, you helped the strong one in the trials of strength. The ninth picks that phrase straight off the end of the eighth and triples it: *taṃ tvā vājeṣu vājinaṃ vājayāmaḥ* — you, the strong one in the trials of strength, we make strong. Three forms of *vāja* in a row, the middle one carried over from the previous line, all for the winning of *dhana*, of what is at stake.

The tenth ends where the fourth began — with an instruction to men rather than to the god. *Tasmai indrāya gāyata*, sing to that Indra, the great riverbed of *rayi*, the good crossing, friend of the one who presses. A hymn that opened by withholding his name closes by telling other people to say it.
4.practice:
Indra is the deity a reader of the Ṛgveda meets more than any other. Of the 1,028 sūktas, 218 are ascribed to him alone and 276 name him somewhere in the ascription — a larger share than Agni's, and nothing else is close. This sūkta begins the longest unbroken stretch of Indra hymns in the first maṇḍala: [[1.4]] through [[1.11]], eight in a row, seven of them by one seer.

What the hymn is for is worth taking at face value. It asks not to be overlooked. *Mā naḥ ati khyaḥ* — do not look past us — is a small, unheroic sentence, and it is the centre of the sūkta. A reader who comes to the Veda expecting only cosmology finds instead the ordinary anxiety of anyone who has offered something and is waiting to see whether it registered.

The comparison in the first verse belongs to the same register. A good cow is called at milking time, every day, and she gives. The rite is placed inside the household economy, not above it, and the word for the request is *ūti* — help, the practical kind.

Two words here are worth carrying out. *Duvaḥ* is reverent service — not feeling, but attendance given to someone; the fifth verse's claim is that it is placed in Indra alone. And *śarman* is the shelter one asks to be inside, the noun a Hindu already meets as *śarma* and *śaraṇa* in later prayer. The sixth verse does not ask for victory over the *ari*; it asks that the *ari* should call the household fortunate. That is a request about standing among neighbours, and the Veda makes it without embarrassment.

*Vāja* — the strength that wins, and the prize won by it — runs through the eighth and ninth verses four times. It is the same word standing behind *vājapeya* and behind every later request for strength that is meant to be used, not admired.
4.disagreements:
The sixth verse turns on *ari*, and the translators take it in opposite directions. Wilson has "let our enemies say we are prosperous"; Griffith has "all our true people call us blest." The word appears ten times in the Ṛgveda and carries both a stranger-rival and a faithful-insider sense; nothing in the verse settles which is meant, and the difference decides whether the household is asking to be envied or to be praised at home.

On the third verse Sāyaṇa glosses *mā no ati khyaḥ* literally — "do not speak beyond us." Wilson expands that into a jealous reading, "pass us not by to reveal yourself to others"; Griffith flattens it to "Neglect us not."

The fifth verse divides the same way. Sāyaṇa turns the speakers round — *bruvantu*, "let them say," meaning let them praise Indra — and Wilson follows him, making the speakers "our ministers, earnestly performing his worship," who order the revilers away. Griffith keeps them as the mockers themselves.

Sāyaṇa reads the seventh verse's string of epithets as belonging to soma rather than to Indra, and glosses *patayat* as causing to fall and *mandayatsakham* as friend of the delighter. On *śatakratu* he offers two derivations without choosing: *kratu* as *karma*, act, so "of a hundred rites"; or *kratu* as *prajñā*, so "of great wisdom."

5.title: Sit Down and Sing — the Praise That Makes Indra Grow
5.synthesis:
The first words of this sūkta are not addressed to a god at all. *Ā tu ā ita, ni sīdata* — come now, come, sit down — and then *indram abhi pra gāyata*, sing out to Indra, *sakhāyaḥ*, companions, *stomavāhasaḥ*, bearers of the *stoma*. Before anything is asked, a company is assembled and seated. The hymn knows that what follows requires more than one voice.

The second verse gives them their subject: *purutamaṃ purūṇām*, the most-many of many, *īśānaṃ vāryāṇām*, master of things worth choosing — and it fixes the occasion, *some sacā sute*, alongside the pressed soma.

The third verse is a single word said four times. *Sa ghā no yoga ā bhuvat, sa rāye, sa puraṃdhyām gamad, vājebhir ā sa naḥ.* He, for our undertaking; he, for *rai*, wealth; he, for *puraṃdhi*; he, coming to us with *vājas*. Four different goods, and the same pronoun each time — the grammar itself insists there is one source.

The fourth verse gives the reason and then repeats the opening command: in whose engagement the enemies do not challenge his two *harī* — *tasmai indrāya gāyata*, sing to that Indra. The instruction from verse one has come round again, now with a ground attached.

The fifth verse is the most physical thing here. *Sutapāvne sutāḥ ime śucayaḥ yanti vītaye* — for the drinker of the pressed, these bright pressings go out; *somāsaḥ dadhyāśiraḥ*, the somas mixed with curds. The drink is described as it actually stood in the vessel.

The sixth verse states something surprising about Indra's beginning: *sadyaḥ vṛddhaḥ ajāyathāḥ* — you were born already grown, at once, for the drinking of the pressed, and for *jyaiṣṭhya*, eldership. He does not develop into greatness; he arrives at it.

The seventh asks the drink to go inside him. *Ā tvā viśantu āśavaḥ somāsaḥ indra girvaṇaḥ* — let the swift somas enter you, you who delight in songs — *śaṃ te santu pracetase*, may they be *śam*, weal, for you who are far-seeing. It is one of the few places where the worshipper asks that something be good *for the god*.

The eighth is the hymn's centre and its loudest line. *Tvāṃ stomā avīvṛdhan, tvām ukthā śatakrato, tvāṃ vardhantu naḥ giraḥ.* Three times *tvām*, you; three kinds of utterance — *stoma*, *uktha*, *gir*; and twice the root √vṛdh, the same root that stood in the sixth verse's *vṛddhaḥ*. Indra was born grown, and the seated company is growing him further. That is the claim the whole sūkta is built to make.

The ninth turns the growth outward: *akṣitotiḥ*, whose help is never used up, may Indra win this thousandfold *vāja*, in which all *pauṃsya*, all manly force, abides.

And the tenth ends without any grandeur whatever. *Mā no martā abhi druhan tanūnām* — let no mortals do harm to our bodies. *Indra girvaṇaḥ, īśāno yavaya vadham* — you are able; keep the blow away. Ten verses of magnification, and the last request is that nobody get hurt.
5.practice:
This is a hymn about what a group of people can do to a god by speaking. The verb is √vṛdh, to make grow — *avīvṛdhan* in the eighth verse, and *vardhantu* in the same line. The form *avīvṛdhan* occurs five times in the whole Ṛgveda, and two of those five are here and in [[1.11]].1, a sūkta ascribed to the son of the seer of this one. The idea is not decorative: praise is treated as something that adds to its object.

The eighth verse also names three kinds of speech in one breath — *stoma*, *uktha*, *gir*. A rite with three distinct sorts of trained utterance is already assumed in the fifth hymn of the collection, and the division of labour among *ṛtvijas* that later ritual formalises is visible in embryo here.

Two words repay attention. *Yoga* in the third verse is the getting of what one does not yet have — the effort word, later paired with *kṣema*, the keeping of what one has; the pair survives intact in the ordinary phrase *yoga-kṣema*. And *śam* in the seventh verse is weal, the word that opens the Ṛgvedic line every Hindu says at the head of a recitation, *śaṃ no mitraḥ śaṃ varuṇaḥ* ([[1.90]].9).

The instruction the hymn opens with is worth taking literally: sit down together, and sing. Not stand, not process — *ni sīdata*. Recitation here is a seated, collective act among *sakhāyaḥ*, companions, and the sūkta names that relationship before it names any benefit.

The last verse is the one to keep. After ten verses of enlargement, the request is that no mortal harm our bodies and that the weapon be turned aside. That is the register of the *śānti* formulae, and it is where a hymn of this kind honestly ends: not in vision, but in wanting the household intact tomorrow.
5.disagreements:
*Puraṃdhi* in the third verse is where the readings separate. Wilson takes it as understanding — "for the acquisition of knowledge" — following the sense of *dhī* inside the compound. Griffith takes it as plenty: "in abundance for our wealth." The word carries both fullness and insight, and this verse does not choose.

On the eighth verse Sāyaṇa draws a sharp line the translations partly lose: *stoma* is the praise accomplished by the Sāmaveda singers, *uktha* the *śastra* of the *bahvṛcas*, the unsung recitation. Wilson keeps the distinction visible ("the chants of the Soma... the hymns of the Ṛk"); Griffith renders both as English song — "chants of praise... lauds... the songs we sing" — and the three-way division of voice disappears.

Sāyaṇa reads *stomavāhasaḥ* in the first verse concretely, as those who bring the *trivṛt*, *pañcadaśa* and other *stomas* into this rite; Wilson gives simply "offering praises," Griffith "bringing hymns of praise."

On *jyaiṣṭhya* in the sixth verse Sāyaṇa derives from *jyeṣṭha*, eldest or best. Wilson makes the claim social — Indra grown "for maintaining seniority among the gods" — while Griffith keeps it abstract, "for preeminence." Whether the sixth verse asserts a rank among the gods or simply supremacy is not settled by the words.

6.title: Yoking Indra at Dawn — and the Maruts Alongside
6.synthesis:
*Yuñjanti* — they are harnessing. The sūkta begins in the middle of an action whose subject it does not name and whose object it describes only by colour and motion: the *bradhna*, the ruddy one, *aruṣa*, moving. *Pari tasthuṣaḥ* — those who stand around him; *rocante rocanā divi*, the lights are shining in the sky. Whoever is being yoked, the harnessing is happening at the hour when the sky first has light in it.

The second verse repeats the verb and makes the scene ordinary. *Yuñjanti asya kāmyā harī* — they yoke his two dear bays, one to each side of the chariot, *śoṇā*, crimson, *dhṛṣṇū*, bold, *nṛvāhasā*, carriers of men. A cosmic harnessing and a stable-yard harnessing are described in the same word.

The third verse is the finest line in the hymn and the hardest to render. *Ketuṃ kṛṇvann aketave, peśo maryā apeśase* — making a *ketu*, a visible sign, for what had no sign; making form for the formless, O men. Both *aketu* and *apeśas* occur nowhere else in the Ṛgveda; they were coined for this line. And then: *sam uṣadbhir ajāyathāḥ*, you were born together with the dawns. Not before them, not over them — with them.

The fourth verse turns to the Maruts and says something that resists paraphrase. *Ād aha svadhām anu punar garbhatvam erire, dadhānā nāma yajñiyam* — thereupon, following their own *svadhā*, their self-law, they moved again into the state of the unborn, taking on a name fit for sacrifice. A power puts itself back into the womb and comes out with a ritual name.

The fifth verse is a raid. With those who break even what is firm, with the *vahni*, the carriers, *guhā cid indra... avindaḥ usriyāḥ* — even in the hiding place you found the cows. This is the cattle-in-the-cave, which returns in [[1.11]].5 under the name of Vala.

The sixth has the singers doing what singers do: *devayantaḥ*, god-seeking, they sing according to their *mati* to the one who finds wealth, the great, the heard-of.

The seventh states the relation the hymn exists to state. *Indreṇa saṃ hi dṛkṣase* — may you be seen together with Indra, who does not flinch; *mandū samānavarcasā*, the two of you exhilarated, and of equal splendour. The Maruts are not Indra's retinue here. They are his match in brightness.

The eighth keeps them together: the offering sings out along with the blameless, heaven-bound *gaṇas* who are dear to Indra. The Marut troop is a *gaṇa*, a band, and the word is used of them plainly.

The ninth calls: *ataḥ parijman ā gahi* — come from there, you who go all round, or from the *rocana* of heaven — the same shining named in the first verse — for the songs reach out toward this.

And the tenth refuses to say where he is. *Itaḥ vā... divo vā pārthivāt adhi... maho vā rajasaḥ* — from here, or from above the earthly heaven, or from the great *rajas*, we seek the gift. A hymn that opened with an unnamed figure being harnessed ends by naming three whole regions and declining to choose.
6.practice:
The Anukramaṇī assigns this sūkta to Indra, and Indra's name stands in it four times — but most of what happens is done by the Maruts, and the seventh verse puts them beside him as *samānavarcasā*, of equal splendour. Across the collection the Maruts are the deity of 31 sūktas outright and are named in the ascription of 45. They never appear singly. They are a *gaṇa*, a troop, and the eighth verse uses that word of them; the phrase *mārutaṃ gaṇam* stands a few hymns later, in [[1.14]].3.

The third verse is why this hymn is worth returning to. *Ketuṃ kṛṇvann aketave* — making a sign where there was no sign. Whatever else Indra does in the Ṛgveda, this is the act named first in his own hymn: the giving of distinguishable form to what had none. It is said in the same breath as *sam uṣadbhir ajāyathāḥ*, born together with the dawns — which places the whole action at the hour of the morning *sandhyā*, the same juncture at which it is still recited.

*Ketu* is the word to carry. It means the mark by which a thing becomes recognisable — a banner, a signal — and it belongs to the family of *cit*, *cetana*, awareness. To make a *ketu* for what has none is to make something knowable, and the verse treats that as an act of creation.

The tenth verse names three places: here, the heaven above the earth, and the great *rajas* between. It is the same threefold division of the world a reciter names every morning in *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, and the hymn's use of it is practical rather than doctrinal — the point is that no one region can be specified, so all three are.

The cave of the cattle in the fifth verse is the first appearance in the collection of a story the Veda keeps returning to. A reader meeting it here should expect it again.
6.disagreements:
The first verse produces the widest divergence in the opening of the collection. Sāyaṇa reads its three descriptions as three deities, citing Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.9.4.1–2: *bradhna* is Āditya, *aruṣa* is Agni, *caran* is Vāyu — and their identification with Indra shows his supremacy, *paramaiśvaryayukta*. Wilson prints the result, a crowded line about "the mighty (Sun), the indestructive (fire), the moving (wind)." Griffith sees one animal: "the bright, the ruddy Steed."

The fourth verse divides them just as sharply, and in opposite directions. Wilson has the Maruts causing Indra to "resume his embryo condition (in the clouds)"; Griffith has the Maruts themselves "throw off the state of babes unborn." Entry and exit from the same words.

On the sixth verse Wilson makes the object the Maruts, "the mighty troop," while Griffith makes it Indra, "him who findeth wealth." Sāyaṇa reads the third verse as identifying Indra with the sun, and treats *ajāyathāḥ* as a second-person form used of him by Vedic licence, with *maryāḥ* an irregular plural.

For the fifth verse Sāyaṇa supplies the legend outright: the Paṇis stole the cows of the gods and hid them in a cave, and Indra found them with Saramā's help. Nothing in the verse names either. On the tenth he identifies the three regions as *pṛthivī-loka*, *dyu-loka* and the *antarikṣa* between.

7.title: Indra, Indra, Indra — and May He Be Ours Alone
7.synthesis:
No hymn in the opening of the Ṛgveda says a name as often as this one says Indra's. Twelve times in ten short verses; three times in the first line alone; and five verses in a row begin with it.

*Indram id gāthino bṛhat, indram arkebhir arkiṇaḥ, indraṃ vāṇīr anūṣata* — the *gāthin* sang Indra with the *bṛhat*, the *arkin* sang Indra with *arkas*, the *vāṇīs* roared to Indra. Three groups, three kinds of utterance, one accusative repeated. The verse is a picture of a rite in which several trained voices are doing different things at once.

The second verse shows him arriving. *Indra id haryoḥ sacā saṃmiślaḥ ā vacoyujā* — Indra mingled with his two bays, and those horses are *vacoyuj*, yoked by a word. The team that answers speech, harnessed by a hymn that is itself speech.

The third names two deeds, one for seeing and one for release. *Indro dīrghāya cakṣasa ā sūryaṃ rohayad divi* — he raised Sūrya in the sky so that there could be far seeing — *vi gobhir adrim airayat*, and he drove the rock apart. Light first, then what was shut in is let out.

The fourth asks for help in the plural: protect us in the *vājas*, and where the stake is a thousand, *ugra ugrābhir ūtibhiḥ* — the fierce one with fierce helps. The adjective is applied to the god and to what he sends, in the same breath.

The fifth halves the scale and keeps the request: *indraṃ vayaṃ mahādhane, indram arbhe havāmahe* — Indra in the great contest, Indra in the small one. The hymn refuses to reserve him for emergencies.

The sixth asks him to open something. *Sa no vṛṣann amuṃ caruṃ... apa vṛdhi* — bull, giver of everything at once, unclose that vessel for us, *apratiṣkutaḥ*, you who are never turned back.

The seventh stops and admits a failure. *Na vindhe asya suṣṭutim* — I do not attain his fitting praise. It stands exactly where the hymn has been most lavish, and it is the one honest verse in any hymn of this shape: the praises rise higher with each pressing, and none of them is adequate.

The eighth returns to force with an image from the herd: as a bull moves the cattle, so he moves the peoples by his *ojas*, *īśānaḥ apratiṣkutaḥ* — the same epithet as the sixth verse, master and unchecked.

The ninth makes the reach total. *Ya ekaś carṣaṇīnāṃ vasūnām irajyati, indraḥ pañca kṣitīnām* — who alone directs the peoples, the goods, the five settlements. The verb *irajyati* occurs twice in the whole Ṛgveda; the number five is given and never explained.

And the tenth turns all of it into a claim. *Indraṃ vaḥ viśvataḥ pari havāmahe janebhyaḥ* — we call Indra round to you from every side, away from other people — *asmākam astu kevalaḥ*, may he be ours alone. After twelve namings, the last word of the sūkta is a request for exclusive possession, and it is stated without apology.
7.practice:
A reader can hear what this hymn is doing before understanding a word of it. The name lands twelve times in ten verses, at the head of the first five and again at the head of the last. Sound is the argument.

The first verse is the most informative thing in the sūkta about how the rite actually worked. Three sets of performers are named — *gāthin*, *arkin*, and the *vāṇīs* — each with its own kind of utterance. *Gāthin* occurs nowhere else in the Ṛgveda, and *arkin* only twice, here and in [[1.10]].1, which is by the same seer. Whatever the exact assignment, the fifth hymn of the Indra run already assumes that a rite is performed by differently trained voices, not by one reciter.

Two verses bear directly on how to ask. The fifth calls Indra *mahādhane* and *arbhe* — in the great contest and the small — which is a licence to bring both to him; the Veda does not rank petitions by size. And the seventh says outright that no praise reaches its object: *na vindhe asya suṣṭutim*, I do not attain his fitting praise. That sentence, placed in the hymn that repeats his name more than any other, is the tradition supplying its own corrective to praise.

The last word is *kevala*, alone, only — the same *kevala* standing behind *kaivalya*. Here it means something a modern reader may find uncomfortable: may this god be ours and not other people's. It is worth reading as it stands rather than softening it. The identical half-line, *asmākam astu kevalaḥ*, occurs only once more in the Ṛgveda, at [[1.13]].10, where what is asked for exclusively is Tvaṣṭṛ.

The five *kṣitis* of the ninth verse are named and not identified. Who they were is unclear from this evidence.
7.disagreements:
The first verse's three groups are where the tradition commits and the translators do not. Sāyaṇa identifies them as offices: *gāthin* are the *udgātṛs* singing with the *bṛhat-sāman*, *arkin* are the reciters of the Ṛgveda, and *vāṇīḥ* he takes as the texts of the Yajus. Wilson prints the identification whole — "the chanters of the Soma... the reciters of the Ṛk... the priests of the Yajuṣ." Griffith declines it, giving only "the singers... reciters... the choirs."

The third verse splits on *gobhiḥ*. Wilson, following Sāyaṇa's frame in which Vṛtra had wrapped the world in darkness, reads it as water: Indra "charged the cloud with abundant waters." Griffith reads the cows: "He burst the mountain for the kine." The same word carries ray, water and cow, and the choice changes the deed from rainmaking to cattle-release.

On the seventh verse Sāyaṇa cites Nirukta 6.17–18, deriving *tuñj-* from a root of giving. Wilson turns the line into a comparison — praises given to other powers are Indra's due as well — while Griffith reads a rising scale: "Still higher, at each strain of mine, thunder-armed Indra's praises rise."

For the ninth, Sāyaṇa glosses the five *kṣitis* as classes of men fit for habitation, *nivāsārhānām*. Neither translator names them.

8.title: Indra: Wealth That Conquers, and a Branch in Fruit
8.synthesis:
The first verse asks for one thing and gives it four adjectives, every one of them a fighting word. *Ā indra sānasiṃ rayiṃ sajitvānaṃ sadāsaham varṣiṣṭham ūtaye bhara* — bring, Indra, for our help, *rayi* that wins, that conquers alongside, that always overpowers, that is highest. Wealth is not received here. It is taken.

The second and third verses say what it is for. *Ni yena muṣṭihatyayā ni vṛtrā ruṇadhāmahai* — by which we may shut out the obstructions, by the striking of fists and by horse, *tvotāsaḥ*, having you as our help. Then, in the third, something bolder: *indra tvotāsa ā vayaṃ vajraṃ ghanā dadīmahi* — helped by you, may we take up the *vajra* as a smiter and win the contest outright. The worshippers ask to hold the weapon themselves.

The fourth keeps them in the field: *vayaṃ śūrebhir astṛbhiḥ, indra tvayā yujā, vayaṃ sāsahyāma pṛtanyataḥ* — we, with heroes who shoot, with you as *yuj*, our yokefellow, may we overpower those who array against us. Twice *vayam*, we — the pronoun of a company that expects to fight.

Then the martial vocabulary stops. The fifth verse simply measures him: *mahān indraḥ paraḥ ca nu* — great, and beyond — and lets his *śavas*, his force, be as wide as *dyaus* by sheer extent.

The sixth verse is the quiet centre of the sūkta, and the most humane line in the Indra run. *Samohe vā ya āśata naras tokasya sanitau, viprāso vā dhiyāyavaḥ* — the men who press forward in the crush for the winning of *toka*, offspring; or the *vipras* who are *dhiyāyu*, hungry for *dhī*. The man who wants a son and the poet who wants thought are put in one line, in the same case, and the hymn ranks neither above the other. *Dhiyāyu* occurs nowhere else in the Ṛgveda.

The seventh swells. *Yaḥ kukṣiḥ somapātamaḥ samudra iva pinvate* — his belly, the greatest drinker of soma, fills like the sea, *urvīr āpo na kākudaḥ*.

The last three verses all begin the same way — *evā hi*, so indeed — and the shift is from petition to statement. The eighth: so his *sūnṛtā*, his true and generous speech, is abundant, rich in cattle, great, *pakvā śākhā na dāśuṣe*, like a ripe branch to the one who gives. It is the only image in the hymn taken from a garden rather than a field of battle, and it is the one the hymn chooses for what the giver receives.

The ninth: so your *vibhūtis*, your abundances, are *ūtis*, helps, and they are there *sadyaś cid*, immediately, for a giver like me — *māvate dāśuṣe*, the speaker putting himself in the general case.

The tenth: so his lovely things; and so let the *stoma* be sung and the *uktha* recited to Indra for the soma-drinking. After a hymn about weapons and stakes and a swelling belly, the last thing named is speech, and the two kinds of it.
8.practice:
This is a fighting people's prayer, and there is no use pretending otherwise. Its first request is for *rayi* described in four words that all mean overcoming, and its third verse asks that the worshippers themselves be able to lift the *vajra*. A reader who comes to the Veda expecting contemplation meets, in the eighth of 1,028 hymns, men asking for the strength to win.

But the sixth verse is why the sūkta is worth keeping. It names two kinds of person who come to Indra: those who push into the crush for the winning of *toka*, children, and the *vipras* who are *dhiyāyu* — desirous of *dhī*, the mind at work. The hymn puts them in one line and does not choose between them. The householder wanting descendants and the poet wanting insight are addressing the same power, on the same terms, in the same rite. Anyone who has wondered whether an ordinary domestic petition belongs alongside a contemplative one has an answer in this verse.

*Sūnṛtā* in the eighth verse is a word to carry. It is used of speech that is true and generous at the same time — not accuracy alone, and not kindness alone — and the Ṛgveda uses it eleven times. What comes to the giver is described as this speech, and then as a branch that has fruit on it and is within reach.

The threefold turn of the last verses is the shape of the hymn's teaching. *Evā hi* — so indeed — three times: this is how his bounty is, this is how his help is, and therefore this is what should be said to him. Petition first, then the recognition that the thing petitioned for is already the case, and only then praise. The order is not an accident.

Note also *dāśuṣe*, the one who gives, in verses eight and nine. In the Veda the worshipper is named by the act of giving, not by belief.
8.disagreements:
The eighth verse's *sūnṛtā* divides the two translators cleanly. Wilson takes it as speech — "the words of Indra to his worshipper are true, manifold, cow-conferring, and to be held in honour" — while Griffith takes it as a quality of the god: "So also is his excellence, great, vigorous, rich in cattle." One reading has Indra saying something; the other has him simply being something.

On the seventh verse Sāyaṇa offers an alternative that neither translator adopts wholesale: *kākud* may be the pinnacle of a mountain, giving "like the abundant waters from the mountain-tops." Wilson keeps the anatomy — "moist, like the ample fluids of the palate" — and Griffith goes to the sky, "like wide streams from the cope of heaven."

The second verse divides on *arvatā*. Wilson reads horse and takes the verse to contrast infantry with cavalry — hand-to-hand, or on horseback. Griffith reads the vehicle: "By thee assisted with the car."

On the tenth Sāyaṇa sets out the distinction the hymn's last line depends on: *stoma* is the sung praise accomplished by the Sāmaveda, *uktha* the *śastra*, the unsung recitation, and its repetition is the *hotā's* work. Wilson carries the distinction over as "chanted and recited praises"; Griffith gives "lauds and praises," and the difference between singing and saying is lost.

9.title: Indra, Impel Us — and Set Wide Fame in Us
9.synthesis:
Indra's name stands exactly once in each of the ten verses of this sūkta — not clustered, not withheld, but distributed evenly, one to a verse. The hymn keeps him present without ever raising its voice.

*Indra ā ihi matsi andhasaḥ* — come, and be gladdened by the *andhas*, the plant, at all the *somaparvans*, the joints of the soma-season; *mahān abhiṣṭir ojasā*, great, and superior by *ojas*. The occasion is not one evening but a recurring set of them.

The second verse pours, and it does so in mirrors. *Mandim indrāya mandine, cakriṃ viśvāni cakraye* — the gladdening one for the gladdener, the effective one for the doer of all things. The drink and the drinker are described with the same word twice over; what is offered is already of the same nature as who receives it.

The third asks him to enjoy it: *matsva suśipra mandibhiḥ stomebhiḥ*, be gladdened, fair-jawed one, by the gladdening *stomas* — praise now doing the work the drink did — *sacā eṣu savaneṣu ā*, here among these pressings.

The fourth turns to the songs and gives them a will of their own. *Asṛgram indra te giraḥ* — the songs have been released toward you; *prati tvām ud ahāsata*, they have sprung up to meet you, *ajoṣāḥ*, unsatisfied, to the bull, the lord. The praise is not content with having been uttered.

The fifth and sixth carry the hymn's hinge, and it is a single verb used twice with different objects. *Saṃ codaya citram arvāk rādha indra vareṇyam* — impel here the bright, choice *rādhas*, the bounty; may your abundance be *vibhu* and *prabhu*. Then the sixth: *asmān su tatra codaya, indra, rāye* — impel *us* there, toward wealth, us who are vehement and renowned. First the gift is asked to move; then the people are.

The seventh and eighth ask for the same thing twice in almost the same words. *Saṃ gomad indra vājavad asme pṛthu śravo bṛhad viśvāyur dhehi akṣitam* — set in us wide, great, unexhausted *śravas*, rich in cattle and in *vāja*, lasting our whole life. And again: *iti dhehi śravo bṛhad* — so set great *śravas*, and splendour won a thousandfold, and those cart-borne foods. *Śravas* is renown, what continues to be heard; the verb *dhehi*, set, place, is repeated so that there is no mistaking it as a request for something to be put *inside* the household rather than handed over to it.

The ninth gathers the callers: praising with songs, we call Indra, master of *vasu*, worthy of the *ṛc*, who comes — *gantāram ūtaye*, who comes for help.

And the tenth sets the whole thing on repeat. *Sute-sute nyokase* — at every pressing, to the one who has his fixed dwelling there — *bṛhad bṛhate*, greatly to the great one, the *ari* sings a strengthening song. The hymn ends by describing itself being sung again, and again, by whoever is there.
9.practice:
The verb at the centre of this sūkta is one every Hindu says daily without necessarily noticing. *Codaya* — impel, urge, set moving — appears in the fifth verse of the gift and in the sixth of the worshippers themselves. It is √cud, the root standing in *pracodayāt*, the last word of the Gāyatrī: *dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt* ([[3.62]].10), may he impel our *dhīs*. What the most-recited verse in the tradition asks Savitṛ for is what this hymn asks Indra for, in the same verb, two hymns before the end of the Madhucchandas set.

The order of the two requests is the teaching. First: send the bounty this way. Then: send *us* that way. A petition that begins by asking for a gift turns, within one verse, into asking to be moved oneself. Nothing in the hymn marks the turn; it simply happens, and it is the difference between wanting an outcome and wanting to be the kind of person who reaches it.

*Śravas* is the second word to carry. It is from √śru, to hear — the same root as *śravaṇa* — and it means what goes on being heard about a person. The seventh and eighth verses ask for it *akṣita*, unexhausted, and *viśvāyu*, lasting a whole lifetime. This is not fame as attention; it is the durability of a name.

Two small things are worth noticing about how the hymn is built. Indra is named once in every one of the ten verses — a discipline no other sūkta in this run keeps. And the last verse says *sute-sute*, at every pressing: the hymn locates itself not at a festival but in a repetition, which is what daily observance is.

The tenth verse's *ari* is the same disputed word that stands in [[1.4]].6.
9.disagreements:
The fourth verse is the sharpest divergence. *Ajoṣāḥ*, unsatisfied, is read by Griffith of the songs themselves — they "raised themselves unsatisfied," restless until answered. Wilson turns it around and makes the satisfaction Indra's: praises "which have reached you, and of which you have approved." Whether it is the god or the hymn that is left wanting changes the whole verse.

On *suśipra* in the third verse Sāyaṇa keeps two options open: *śipra* as the lower jaw, or as the nose. Wilson takes the jaw — "Indra with the handsome chin" — Griffith the cheek, "fair of cheek." Sāyaṇa also expands *viśvacarṣaṇe* as one to be worshipped by all who institute sacrifices.

The eighth verse's *rathinīr iṣaḥ* gets a concrete gloss from Sāyaṇa: foods conveyed in carts from where they are grown — rice, barley and other grains. Wilson prints the explanation; Griffith gives "Fair fruits of earth borne home in wains."

On the tenth Sāyaṇa derives *nyokas* from *ni*, fixed, and *okas*, dwelling. Wilson makes this an eternal mansion; Griffith relocates it to the rite — "dweller by each libation." And the *ari* who sings there is Wilson's "sacrificer" and Griffith's "pious man," neither of them the rival the word can also mean.

10.title: Indra, Sing Back to Us — and Be Called Kauśika
10.synthesis:
This is the last of the ten sūktas that open the Ṛgveda under one seer, and it is the first of them in *anuṣṭup* rather than *gāyatrī* — longer lines, more room. What it does with the room is ask Indra to answer.

*Gāyanti tvā gāyatriṇo, arcanty arkam arkiṇaḥ* — the singers sing you, the chanters chant the chant. Both halves double a word on its own root, and then: *brahmāṇas tvā śatakrato ud vaṃśam iva yemire*, the *brahmans* have raised you up like a bamboo pole. Three kinds of performer again, as in [[1.7]].1, and *arkin* occurs only in these two verses in the whole collection.

The second verse watches him work. When he had climbed from ridge to ridge and seen how much there was to be done, Indra takes note of the purpose, and the bull moves off with his herd.

The third summons the team. *Yukṣva hi keśinā harī vṛṣaṇā kakṣyaprā* — yoke the two long-maned bays, strong, filling out their girths — *atha naḥ indra somapāḥ girām upaśrutiṃ cara*, and then come to the hearing of our songs. Not to the songs: to the *upaśruti*, the act of listening to them.

The fourth is the verse the sūkta exists for. *Ā ihi stomān abhi svara, abhi gṛṇīhi, ā ruva* — come, sing back to the *stomas*, praise in return, roar out. Three imperatives of vocal response, addressed to a god. And then *brahma ca no vaso sacā indra yajñaṃ ca vardhaya*, strengthen our formulation and our yajña together.

The fifth explains what the recitation is for: an *uktha* is to be spoken to Indra, an increaser, that Śakra may take pleasure in our pressings and in our friendships.

The sixth asks for three things with the same pronoun: *tam it sakhitve īmahe, taṃ rāye, taṃ suvīrye* — him we seek for friendship, him for wealth, him for the strength of good men. Then *sa śakra uta naḥ śakad*: he, the able one, is able for us. The name and the verb are the same root, laid side by side.

The seventh asks him to open the *vraja*, the cattle-pen, and to make *rādhas*, bounty. The eighth says the two *rodasī* cannot contain him when he rages, and asks him to win the sunlit waters and shake the cattle down for us.

The ninth is the most intimate line in the Madhucchandas set. *Āśrutkarṇa śrudhī havam* — you whose ear hears, hear the call; *nū cid dadhiṣva me giraḥ*, take my songs to yourself now; *kṛṣvā yujaś cid antaram*, make this praise of mine nearer to you than even a yokefellow. The speaker is asking to be preferred.

The tenth grounds the claim in knowledge: *vidma hi tvā* — for we know you as the most bull-like, the one who hears the call in the *vājas*.

The eleventh calls him by a family name: *ā tū na indra kauśika mandasānaḥ sutaṃ piba* — come, Indra Kauśika, drink; *navyam āyuḥ pra sū tira*, extend our life anew; make the *ṛṣi* a winner of thousands.

And the twelfth closes by asking the songs to go all the way round him — *pari tvā girvaṇo gira imā bhavantu viśvataḥ* — and ends, as the first verse began, on doubled words: may increases follow the one increased in life, may the delights be delighted in.
10.practice:
The eleventh verse contains a word that occurs exactly once in the Ṛgveda. Indra is addressed as *Kauśika*, of the line of Kuśika — and Kuśika's line is the seer's own, since the Anukramaṇī names him Madhucchandas Vaiśvāmitra, of Viśvāmitra, who is Kuśika's son. The seer calls the god by his family's name. Whatever else that is, it is not distance.

This sūkta closes the opening block of the collection. Madhucchandas has eleven hymns in the entire Ṛgveda: [[1.1]] through [[1.10]], and then [[9.1]], which opens the Soma maṇḍala. One seer holds the first ten hymns a student ever meets, and the tenth of them is this.

What to take from it is the fourth verse. *Abhi svara, abhi gṛṇīhi, ā ruva* — sing back, praise in return, roar. It is easy to think of recitation as speech aimed at a silent recipient. This verse assumes the opposite: the rite is a conversation, and the god is asked to hold up his end of it audibly. The third verse has already asked him to come to the *upaśruti*, the listening, of the songs — as though attention were a place he could travel to.

The eleventh verse's *navyam āyuḥ pra sū tira*, extend life anew, is the *āyus* register a Hindu meets at every birthday observance and every rite that asks for long life. Here it sits between a drink and a request for a thousandfold gift, unembarrassed by the company.

And note the ninth: *kṛṣvā yujaś cid antaram*, make this praise nearer than a yokefellow. The relationship the hymn wants is not worship at a distance but preference — to be the one closest at hand. [[1.1]].9 asked Agni to be approachable as a father; ten hymns later the request has become a request to be preferred.
10.disagreements:
The bamboo of the first verse is Sāyaṇa's most vivid moment in this run, and he gives two readings without deciding. Either the priests raise Indra as acrobats raise a pole and balance on its top, or *vaṃśa* means family, and this is how ambitious men raise their line to consequence. Wilson prints "like a bamboo pole," Griffith "on high, like a pole," and both leave the acrobats out. Sāyaṇa also assigns the verse's three groups to offices — *gāyatrin* to the *udgātṛ*, *arkin* to the *hotā*, *brāhmaṇāḥ* to the *brahman* priest and other brāhmaṇas.

The second verse divides on who is climbing. Sāyaṇa refers the ridge-to-ridge ascent to the *yajamāna*, going up the mountain to gather soma or fuel; Wilson follows him. Griffith makes Indra himself the climber, looking down on the toilsome task.

On the seventh verse Sāyaṇa reads the cow-pen through rain: Indra should fertilise the fields and provide pasture so the cattle yield milk. Wilson turns this into food "rendered everywhere abundant"; Griffith keeps it as spoil, "easy to turn and drive away."

*Dadhiṣva* in the ninth verse is from √dhā, to place — Wilson renders "hold in your heart my praises," Griffith "take to thee readily my songs." Sāyaṇa supplies the Kuśika legend behind the eleventh verse: Kuśika did penance desiring a son equal to Indra, and Indra was born as Gāthin's son.

11.title: Indra Against Vala and Śuṣṇa — Guile Met by Guile
11.synthesis:
Eight verses, the shortest sūkta in the opening run, and the only one by this seer. It is built on a claim that is easy to miss: the deeds it recounts are not asserted, they are attested. Twice it says that people know.

*Indraṃ viśvā avīvṛdhan giraḥ* — all the songs have made Indra grow. The verb is the same one that stood at the centre of [[1.5]].8, in the neighbouring hymn by the seer's father; it occurs five times in the whole Ṛgveda. He is *samudravyacasam*, of the ocean's extent — a compound found nowhere else — *rathītamaṃ rathīnām*, most charioteer of charioteers, and *vājānāṃ satpatiṃ patim*, lord of the *vājas*.

The second verse names fear in order to dismiss it. *Sakhye te indra vājino mā bhema śavasaḥ pate* — in your friendship, lord of force, let us not be afraid — *tvām abhi pra nonumaḥ jetāram aparājitam*, we shout out to you, the conqueror unconquered. The Anukramaṇī gives the seer's name as Jetā, and *jetāram* stands here in his one hymn; whether the name comes from the word or the word from the name is not something this evidence settles.

The third verse makes a claim about reliability rather than power. *Pūrvīr indrasya rātayo na vi dasyanty ūtayaḥ* — Indra's gifts are many and his helps do not run dry — when he bestows *magha*, bounty, on those who praise him.

The fourth compresses a biography into four words and then piles on titles. *Purāṃ bhindur yuvā kavir amitaujā ajāyata* — the breaker of strongholds, young, a *kavi*, of unmeasured *ojas*, was born; upholder of every act, wielder of the *vajra*, much praised. Young and a *kavi* in the same line: strength and seer-knowledge are not opposed here.

The fifth is the first of the two deeds. *Tvaṃ valasya gomato 'pāvar adrivo bilam* — you opened the hole of Vala, who was rich in cattle; and the gods, no longer afraid, urged forward, came to your side. The fear denied in the second verse is the fear the gods actually had.

The sixth places the speaker in the scene. *Tavāhaṃ śūra rātibhiḥ praty āyaṃ sindhum āvadan* — through your gifts, hero, I have come, speaking toward the *sindhu*; the *kārus*, the makers of song, stood by. And then the phrase the hymn turns on: *vidus te tasya kāravaḥ*, the singers know this of you.

The seventh gives the second deed and repeats that phrase exactly. *Māyābhir indra māyinaṃ tvaṃ śuṣṇam avātiraḥ* — by *māyās* you brought down the *māyin* Śuṣṇa, the contriver undone by contrivance. *Vidus te tasya medhirāḥ*, the wise know this of you; *teṣāṃ śravāṃsy ut tira*, raise their renown. The witnesses are to be rewarded for having witnessed.

The eighth closes where the first opened, on the songs and on the gifts. *Indram īśānam ojasābhi stomā anūṣata* — the *stomas* have roared to Indra who rules by *ojas* — whose gifts are a thousand, *uta vā santi bhūyasīḥ*, or more than that. The hymn will not put a ceiling on the number, and it does not need to: it has already said who counted.
11.practice:
*Māyā* is the word to take from this hymn, because a Hindu reader arrives at it carrying a much later meaning. In the seventh verse Śuṣṇa is a *māyin*, a possessor of *māyā*, and Indra defeats him *māyābhiḥ*, by *māyās*. Both sides have it. Here the word means craft, contrivance, the power to produce an effect — not illusion, and certainly not the cosmic delusion of the Vedāntic vocabulary. That sense is a later development. In the Ṛgveda *māyin* occurs nine times and *māyābhiḥ* thirteen, and in this verse the same instrument is used by the antagonist and by the god.

The second thing to notice is the hymn's method. Twice it says *vidus te tasya* — they know this of you: the *kārus* in the sixth verse, the *medhiras* in the seventh. This is not praise claiming to be true; it is praise pointing at witnesses. And the seventh verse asks that the witnesses be repaid in *śravas*, renown — the same thing [[1.9]] asked for the household. The people who preserve the account are to benefit from having preserved it, which is as close as the Ṛgveda comes to describing why a tradition of transmission exists at all.

The Anukramaṇī ascribes this sūkta to Jetā, son of Madhucchandas, and it is the only hymn in the entire Ṛgveda under his name — against his father's eleven. The collection is not made only of prolific seers; it keeps single hymns by people who left nothing else.

The opened cave of the fifth verse is the same event as [[1.6]].5, where the finding of the cattle is told without Vala's name. A reader who follows this story will meet it many more times.

And the second verse says the plainest thing in the run: *mā bhema* — let us not be afraid. It is said in the context of *sakhya*, friendship, not of power.
11.disagreements:
The sixth verse is genuinely unresolved. Wilson makes the speaker return to Indra "celebrating your liberality while offering this libation," reading *sindhum* as the flowing juice; Griffith keeps the geography — "I am come to the flood addressing thee." River or pressed soma, the two readings put the seer in different places.

The seventh's closing half-line divides them too. *Teṣāṃ śravāṃsy ut tira*: Wilson takes *śravas* as sustenance and reads "bestow upon them abundant food"; Griffith takes it as renown and turns the imperative on Indra himself — "now go beyond their eulogies." Sāyaṇa glosses Śuṣṇa as the drier-up, *bhūtānāṃ śoṣaṇa-hetum*, the cause of the withering of beings, citing Nirukta 3.11, so that the deed becomes rain ending a drought.

For the fifth verse Sāyaṇa supplies the fuller legend from the Anukramaṇikā: Vala was an *asura* who stole the cattle of the gods and hid them, with the Paṇis as his soldiers, and Indra recovered them after surrounding the cave.

On the fourth, *purāṃ bhinduḥ*, breaker of strongholds, Sāyaṇa supplies whose strongholds — the *asuras'*. The text itself does not say. And *samudravyacasam* in the first verse Sāyaṇa explains as pervading like the ocean, identifying Indra with the firmament.

12.title: Agni Chosen as Messenger — and Kindled by Agni
12.synthesis:
After eight sūktas to Indra the collection returns to Agni, and it returns with a different word in front. *Agniṃ dūtaṃ vṛṇīmahe* — we *choose* Agni as messenger. [[1.1]] opened with *īḷe*, I praise; this one opens with an act of selection. Three more titles follow: *hotā*; *viśvavedas*, knower and holder of all; and *sukratu*, of good *kratu*, effective in this yajña. But the first of the four is *dūta*, and that governs everything after it.

The second verse doubles the name. *Agnim-agnim havīmabhiḥ sadā havanta viśpatim* — Agni, Agni, they call always with their callings, the *viśpati*, lord of the settled people, *havyavāha*, carrier of the offering, *purupriya*, dear to many. Three words in the line come from the roots of calling and offering; the verse is made of the act it describes.

The third sends him. *Agne devān iha ā vaha jajñānaḥ vṛktabarhiṣe* — being born, bring the gods here for the one whose *barhis* has been stripped and strewn; *asi hotā naḥ īḍyaḥ*, you are our *hotā*, and to be praised.

The fourth follows him out and back. *Tān uśato vi bodhaya* — wake them, the willing ones — *yad agne yāsi dūtyam*, when you go on your embassy; *devair ā satsi barhiṣi*, and sit down with the gods on the *barhis*. The messenger travels and then returns to sit among the guests he fetched.

The fifth is the only hostile verse. *Ghṛtāhavana dīdivaḥ prati sma riṣato daha* — you into whom ghee is poured, shining one, burn back those who would injure, the ones attended by *rakṣas*.

The sixth is the centre. *Agninā agniḥ sam idhyate* — Agni is kindled by Agni — *kavir gṛhapatir yuvā havyavāḍ juhvāsyaḥ*: seer, master of the house, young, carrier of the offering, whose mouth is the ladle. Everything else in the rite is brought from outside; this one thing is lit from itself.

The seventh asks for praise to be directed at a particular quality: *kavim agnim upa stuhi satyadharmāṇam adhvare* — praise the *kavi* Agni whose *dharman* is *satya*, whose ordinance holds true — *devam amīvacātanam*, the god who drives out *amīva*, sickness.

The eighth and ninth are a matched pair about the one who serves. Whoever, as *haviṣpati*, honours you as *dūta* — be his protector. Whoever, bearing the offering, seeks to win Agni for the gods' feast — *tasmai pāvaka mṛḷaya*, to him, purifier, be merciful. Two conditional sentences, both beginning *yaḥ*, both ending in a request for kindness rather than for goods.

The tenth repeats the third's own words: *agne devān iha ā vaha* — bring the gods here, to our yajña and our offering — with *pāvaka* and *dīdivaḥ* now standing as his names.

The eleventh is the one verse of the twelve that does not say Agni. Being praised, bring us *rayi* and *iṣ*, nourishment, rich in men — *gāyatreṇa navīyasā*, by the newest *gāyatra*. The hymn names its own metre and calls itself new.

And the twelfth asks only to be liked: with bright flame and with all the callings of the gods, *imaṃ stomaṃ juṣasva naḥ*, take pleasure in this praise of ours.
12.practice:
The first word of this hymn is a choice. *Vṛṇīmahe* is from √vṛ — the root behind *vara*, a boon, and *varaṇa*, the choosing of a priest — and it makes the rite begin with an election rather than an emotion. A reader who wants to know what the Veda thinks worship is could do worse than start here: someone selects an intermediary, and states the qualifications.

The sixth verse is the one to hold onto. *Agninā agniḥ sam idhyate* — Agni is kindled by Agni. Every other component of a rite is fetched: the grass is cut, the ghee is churned, the soma is pressed. Fire alone is taken from fire. What the verse states as a physical fact is also the plainest available statement of how a tradition continues at all — nothing is generated from nothing; a flame is handed on.

In the same verse Agni is *gṛhapati*, master of the house. The word is still current, and it names exactly what it names: the Agni of this hymn is not an abstraction but the one a household keeps burning. The seventh verse adds *amīvacātana*, driver-away of sickness — the epithet a reader turns to when the concern is illness in the house rather than prosperity.

*Pāvaka*, purifier, stands twice here (verses nine and ten) and again at the opening of the next sūkta, [[1.13]].1. It occurs twenty times in the Ṛgveda, and three of those twenty are in these two adjacent hymns by the same seer.

This sūkta also marks a change of hands. Sūktas [[1.1]]–[[1.10]] belong to Madhucchandas and [[1.11]] to his son; from here through [[1.23]] the collection is Medhātithi Kāṇva's, who has fifteen sūktas in the Ṛgveda — twelve of them consecutive, here at the start.

And the eleventh verse is worth a moment for its confidence: *gāyatreṇa navīyasā*, with the newest *gāyatra*. The oldest surviving hymns of the tradition describe themselves as new.
12.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa opens with a detail neither translator carries: citing Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.8.5, he notes that Agni was the *dūta* of the *devas* and Uśanas Kāvya the *dūta* of the *asuras*. The office named in the first verse had a counterpart on the other side.

On *viśpati* in the second verse Sāyaṇa derives *viś* as *prajāḥ*, people, and Wilson gives "lord of men." Griffith reads the household instead — "Lord of the House" — which anticipates the *gṛhapati* of the sixth verse but is not what the word says here.

*Jajñānaḥ* in the third verse Sāyaṇa explains as born by the friction of two fire-sticks, and Wilson prints the gloss ("generated by attrition"); Griffith attaches the birth to the worshipper instead, "born for him who strews the sacred grass."

For the sixth verse Sāyaṇa supplies the ritual mechanics behind Agni kindled by Agni: the oblation goes into the *āhavanīya*, which may be taken from the household fire or produced afresh by churning. He also glosses *gṛhapati* as *pālaka*, protector of the *yajamāna's* house.

One caution about the witness itself: in the Wilson text as transmitted here, the rendering of verse 7 duplicates verse 8 and loses the Sanskrit's *satyadharman* and *amīvacātana*. Griffith's verse 7 — "the Sage whose ways are ever true, The God who driveth grief away" — is the reliable one at that point.

13.title: Agni, the Doors, the Three Goddesses — First Āprī
13.synthesis:
This sūkta is not composed the way the eleven before it were. It follows a fixed order that recurs nine more times in the Ṛgveda, in six different seer-families, and the order is the point: the powers are called in sequence, and each verse hands on to the next. Five times the same phrase is used — *upa hvaye*, I call near — and what the hymn amounts to is a guest-list read aloud.

*Susamiddho na ā vaha devān agne haviṣmate* — thoroughly kindled, bring the gods for the one who has the offering; *hotaḥ pāvaka yakṣi ca*, and sacrifice, O *hotā*, O purifier. *Susamiddha*, well-kindled, stands nowhere else in the Ṛgveda.

The second calls Tanūnapāt. *Madhumantaṃ tanūnapād yajñaṃ deveṣu naḥ kave adya kṛṇuhi vītaye* — make our yajña honeyed among the gods today, O *kavi*, for their feasting. The name occurs six times in the collection, all of them in hymns of this form.

The third calls Narāśaṃsa, *priya*, dear, *madhujihva*, honey-tongued, *haviṣkṛta*, maker of the offering.

The fourth returns to Agni by name and gives him a vehicle: *agne sukhatame rathe devān īḷita ā vaha* — on the easiest-running chariot, being praised, bring the gods — *asi hotā manurhitaḥ*, you are the *hotā* set in place by Manu. That last phrase returns verbatim in the next sūkta, [[1.14]].11.

The fifth turns to the seat. *Stṛṇīta barhir ānuṣag ghṛtapṛṣṭhaṃ manīṣiṇaḥ* — strew the *barhis* in due order, ghee-backed, you of *manīṣā* — *yatrāmṛtasya cakṣaṇam*, where there is the appearing of the deathless.

The sixth opens the way in. *Vi śrayantām ṛtāvṛdho dvāro devīr asaścataḥ* — let the divine doors, increasers of *ṛta*, unfailing, swing wide, *adya nūnaṃ ca yaṣṭave*, today and now, for sacrificing. Doors described as growing *ṛta*: the furniture of the rite is not inert.

The seventh calls Night and Uṣas together, *supeśasā*, beautifully formed, to sit on this *barhis*. The eighth calls the two divine *hotās*, *sujihvau*, sweet-tongued, *kavī*, to perform this yajña for us — the honeyed tongue of the third verse now belonging to a pair.

The ninth is the verse most readers will recognise. *Iḷā sarasvatī mahī tisro devīr mayobhuvaḥ* — Iḷā, Sarasvatī, Mahī, three goddesses who bring *mayas*, delight — *barhiḥ sīdantv asridhaḥ*, let them sit on the grass, unerring. Sarasvatī, who closed [[1.3]] alone and at length, appears here as one of three, in a single line.

The tenth calls Tvaṣṭṛ, *agriya*, foremost, *viśvarūpa*, of every form — and ends *asmākam astu kevalaḥ*, may he be ours alone. That half-line occurs only twice in the Ṛgveda; the other is [[1.7]].10, where the exclusive claim was on Indra.

The eleventh addresses Vanaspati: *ava sṛja... devebhyo haviḥ* — release the offering to the gods — *pra dātur astu cetanam*, and let the giver's *cetana*, his being known, go forth.

The twelfth ends the sequence and locates it. *Svāhā yajñaṃ kṛṇotana indrāya yajvano gṛhe* — with *svāhā* make the sacrifice for Indra in the house of the one who sacrifices — *tatra devān upa hvaye*, there I call the gods. Everything in the hymn has been leading not to heaven but to a house.
13.practice:
This is the first *āprī* sūkta in the Ṛgveda, and there are exactly ten. They stand at [[1.13]], [[1.142]], [[1.188]], [[2.3]], [[3.4]], [[5.5]], [[7.2]], [[9.5]], [[10.70]] and [[10.110]] — one to a seer-family, each running the same sequence of invocations in the same order. That a form this rigid is repeated ten times across six families is itself the evidence that it is a form, and not a composition somebody happened to make twice.

This one is the odd member in two respects, both checkable. Where the other nine name Bhāratī as the third goddess, [[1.13]] alone names **Mahī** — the word stands in the ninth verse, and *bhāratī* appears in the ascriptions of nine sūktas but never in this one. And the Anukramaṇī does not give *barhis* a verse of its own here, as it does in the others; the fifth verse is counted to Agni.

The twelfth verse carries something every Hindu says. *Svāhā* — the word spoken at the moment the offering is released — makes its first appearance in the Ṛgveda, in textual order, right here. It occurs seventeen times in the collection.

What an *āprī* invokes is worth stating plainly, because it is unusual. Not only gods: the kindled fire, the strewn grass, the doors of the enclosure, night and dawn, the two officiants, three goddesses, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vanaspati, and the call itself. The apparatus of the rite is addressed as though it were animate — the doors are *ṛtāvṛdh*, increasers of *ṛta*. For a reader who has only ever seen ritual objects treated as equipment, that is the shift this hymn asks for.

Sarasvatī appears here in a triad. A reader who met her in [[1.3]] as the one who illumines all thoughts meets her in this hymn as one of three seated on the grass, and the difference is instructive: the same goddess is not always given the same room.
13.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa holds a single position across the whole sūkta, and it decides how one reads it: these are not eleven deities but Agni under eleven names. The doors are *agniviśeṣamūrtayaḥ*, particular forms of Agni; Night and Uṣas are two fire-forms presiding over their times; the two *hotās* are two Agnis; Iḷā, Sarasvatī and Bhāratī are *agnimūrtayaḥ*, and also three personified flames; Tvaṣṭṛ here is *tvaṣṭṛ-nāmakam agnim*, the Agni called Tvaṣṭṛ; and *svāhā* too is identified with Agni. Wilson prints the identification verse by verse, giving Agni the names Susamiddha, Tanūnapāt, Īḷita. Griffith does not follow: each power stands as itself — "Son of Thyself," "Dear Narasamsa," "the Doors Divine."

The fifth verse's *amṛtasya cakṣaṇam* gets two readings from Sāyaṇa without a decision: the ghee sprinkled on the grass has the appearance of *amṛta*, or Agni himself is the deathless one. Wilson takes the first — "the semblance of ambrosia" — Griffith the second, "Where the Immortal is beheld."

On *tanūnapāt* Sāyaṇa offers three derivations: devourer of clarified butter; consumer of its own substance, *tanū* as fuel; or *napāt* read as one who does not preserve, who destroys. And on the ninth verse he equates Mahī with Bhāratī, adding the later identifications of the three as earth, eloquence and speech.

14.title: Agni Fetches Them All — First Viśvedevāḥ Sūkta
