14.synthesis:
The Anukramaṇī ascribes this sūkta to the Viśvedevāḥ, and every command in it is addressed to Agni. They are the guests; he is the only one spoken to. That arrangement is the hymn.

*Ā ebhir agne duvo giro viśvebhiḥ somapītaye devebhir yāhi yakṣi ca* — come, Agni, with all these gods, to our *duvaḥ*, our reverent service, and our songs, for the soma-drinking; and sacrifice. The last two words, *yakṣi ca*, are the same that ended the first verse of [[1.13]].

The second names the singers and leaves a genuine ambiguity standing. *Ā tvā kaṇvā ahūṣata, gṛṇanti vipra te dhiyaḥ* — the Kaṇvas have called you; the *dhīs* sing, and they are called *te*, yours. Whether the thoughts belong to Agni or are merely directed at him, the line does not say.

The third verse has no verb at all. *Indravāyū bṛhaspatiṃ mitrāgniṃ pūṣaṇaṃ bhagam, ādityān mārutaṃ gaṇam* — Indra and Vāyu, Bṛhaspati, Mitra and Agni, Pūṣan, Bhaga, the Ādityas, the Marut troop. Eight accusatives and nothing done to them. The naming is the whole verse.

The fourth pours. *Pra vo bhriyanta indavo matsarā mādayiṣṇavaḥ* — for you the drops are carried forward, exhilarating, gladdening, *drapsā madhvaś camūṣadaḥ*, drops of honey sitting in the bowl.

The fifth describes the people doing it. *Īḷate tvām avasyavaḥ kaṇvāso vṛktabarhiṣaḥ, haviṣmanto araṃkṛtaḥ* — the Kaṇvas praise you, wanting help, their *barhis* strewn, with offerings, made ready. In [[1.2]].1 it was the *somas* that were *araṃkṛtāḥ*, made ready; here the word is used of the men.

The sixth yokes. *Ghṛtapṛṣṭhā manoyujo ye tvā vahanti vahnayaḥ* — the ghee-backed, *manoyuj*, yoked by thought, who carry you: let them bring the gods for the soma-drinking. Indra's team in [[1.7]].2 was *vacoyuj*, yoked by a word; Agni's is yoked by mind.

The seventh asks for a particular kind of company. *Tān yajatrān ṛtavṛdho agne patnīvataḥ kṛdhi* — make those worthy of worship, those increasers of *ṛta*, accompanied by their wives — *madhvaḥ sujihva pāyaya*, and give them the honey to drink, O sweet-tongued.

The eighth says how they will drink it, and it is the boldest line here. *Ye yajatrā ye īḍyās te te pibantu jihvayā, madhor agne vaṣaṭkṛti* — let those worshipful and praiseworthy ones drink with *your* tongue, at the *vaṣaṭ*-call. Not beside Agni: through him.

The ninth restates the promise the collection made at its start. *Ākīṃ sūryasya rocanād viśvān devān uṣarbudhaḥ, vipro hoteha vakṣati* — the inspired *hotā* shall convey here all the gods who wake at dawn. *Vakṣati* occurs four times in the whole Ṛgveda, and the first is [[1.1]].2, *sa devāṁ eha vakṣati*.

The tenth asks him to drink alongside: with all of them, with Indra, with Vāyu, by the *dhāmans* of Mitra — the three powers [[1.2]] called, in that order.

The eleventh names his office. *Tvaṃ hotā manurhitaḥ, agne, yajñeṣu sīdasi* — you are the *hotā* set in place by Manu; you sit at the sacrifices; *sa imaṃ no adhvaraṃ yaja*, so perform this *adhvara* of ours.

And the twelfth ends with a harnessing: yoke the ruddy mares, the bays, the red ones — *tābhir devān ihā vaha*, with them bring the gods here.
14.practice:
The Viśvedevāḥ are not an afterthought category. Sixty-three sūktas of the Ṛgveda are ascribed to them outright and eighty-six name them somewhere — after Indra, Agni and Soma, the largest ascription in the collection. This is the first of them, and it establishes the form: rather than address a company directly, the hymn addresses Agni and asks him to bring the company.

The reason is stated in the eighth verse, and it is the plainest answer the opening of the Ṛgveda gives to the question of why anything at all is poured into fire. *Te te pibantu jihvayā* — let them drink with your tongue. The gods do not come to the offering; the offering reaches them because Agni consumes it. *Vaṣaṭkṛti* in that line — at the *vaṣaṭ*-call — occurs nowhere else in the Ṛgveda, and it is the moment of release a reciter still marks.

The ninth verse closes a circle. *Vakṣati*, he shall convey, appears four times in the entire collection, and its first occurrence is the second verse of the first hymn: *sa devāṁ eha vakṣati*. Fourteen hymns later the same rare form is used again for the same undertaking, now with the *hotā* as its subject. A reader who has come this far in order has already met the promise being kept.

The seventh verse asks for the gods *patnīvataḥ* — accompanied by their wives. The invitation is issued to households, not to individuals, and that assumption runs through domestic observance to this day.

Two more words worth carrying. *Duvaḥ* in the first verse is reverent attendance rather than feeling — the same word that stood in [[1.4]].5. And *manoyuj* in the sixth: horses yoked by thought. Whatever conveys the god moves at the speed of the mind, which is also the speed at which a recitation travels.
14.disagreements:
The ninth verse's first word defeats everyone. *Ākīm* has no assignable lemma in the grammatical apparatus, and the two translators send the gods in opposite directions: Wilson brings them "hither from the shining sphere of the sun," Griffith takes them "Away, from the Sun's realm of light." The verse is unclear from this evidence and should be read as unclear.

The third verse is a bare string of names in the accusative with no verb, and Sāyaṇa says so, then supplies one — "sacrifice, Agni, to" — which Wilson prints. Griffith leaves the list bare. Sāyaṇa additionally classes Mitra, Pūṣan and Bhaga together as Ādityas, forms of the sun, and derives *bṛhaspati* as *bṛhat*, great or divine, plus *pati*, master, the preceptor of the gods.

On the second verse's *te dhiyaḥ* Wilson reads action — the Kaṇvas "extol your deeds" — while Griffith keeps it as utterance, "sing thee songs of praise." Neither settles whose the *dhīs* are.

*Araṃkṛtaḥ* in the fifth verse Wilson takes as ornament ("offering ornaments"), Griffith as readiness ("with all things prepared"). Sāyaṇa explains *ghṛtapṛṣṭhāḥ* in the sixth as backs shining from the ghee that is the horses' feed, and notes on the twelfth that Rohita is the name of Agni's horse — where Wilson makes the team mares and Griffith "the Red Mares."

15.note: padapāṭha reads grāvaḥ at v3; the accented saṃhitā and the morphology both give gnāvaḥ, which is followed here
15.title: Drink with the Ṛtu — Indra, Maruts, Agni, Aśvins
15.synthesis:
One word governs this hymn, and it is a word every Hindu still says aloud before a rite. *Ṛtunā* — in the turn, at the season, when it is this one's moment — stands in ten of the twelve verses; only 7 and 8 are without it. Nothing here is asked out of order. Each power is called, given a vessel, and told to drink when its turn comes round.

*Indra somaṃ piba ṛtunā* — Indra, drink the soma in your turn. The *indavaḥ*, the drops, are *matsarāsaḥ*, exhilarating, and *tadokasaḥ*, having their dwelling there: they are asked not merely to enter him but to stay and make their home in him.

The second verse gives the Maruts their vessel — *potrāt*, from the cup of the Potṛ, the priest whose office is purifying — and the request matches the vessel exactly: *yajñaṃ pūnītana*, purify the yajña. They can be asked to purify because they are *sudānavaḥ*, of good giving.

The third addresses the Neṣṭṛ as *gnāvaḥ*, accompanied by the *gnās*, the wives of the gods. *Abhi yajñaṃ gṛṇīhi naḥ* — speak our yajña forward, commend it upward. And the ground given is the word that closed the first verse of the whole collection: *tvaṃ hi ratnadhā asi*, you are a holder of what is precious.

Agni, in the fourth, is the only one in the hymn asked to bring anyone else. Bring the gods here, seat them in the three *yonis*, attend on every side, and drink in your turn.

The fifth returns to Indra and quietly changes the case of the governing word: *ṛtūn anu*, following the seasons, plural, one after another. He drinks from the brāhmaṇa's *rādhas*, and the reason offered is not power but relationship — *tavet hi sakhyam astṛtam*, your friendship is not to be overthrown.

The sixth gives Mitrāvaruṇau their epithet *dhṛtavratā*, holders of the vow, and states how they reached what they hold: *ṛtunā yajñam āśāthe*, by the turn you two attained the yajña. Their *dakṣa*, effective competence, is *dūḷabham*, hard to deceive.

Four verses then go to Draviṇodas, the giver of *draviṇa*. In the seventh, men with the pressing stones in their hands praise him in the *adhvara* and in the *yajñas*. In the eighth he is asked for *vasūni* — goods *yāni śṛṇvire*, whose report travels, goods that get heard of. In the ninth he wants to drink, so: pour, and step forward, and from the Neṣṭṛ's vessel be sped on by the *ṛtus*. And the tenth counts itself — *yat tvā turīyam ṛtubhir yajāmahe*, since we worship you a fourth time along with the ṛtus, then be one who gives to us. The hymn is keeping its own tally out loud.

The eleventh gives the Aśvins the *madhu*. They are *śucivratā*, of clean observance, and *yajñavāhasā*, conveyers of the yajña — the pair whose work is carrying.

The twelfth ends at the hearth. *Gārhapatyena santya ṛtunā yajñanīr asi* — by the gārhapatya, O generous one, in your turn, you are the leader of the yajña; and then *devān devayate yaja*, worship the gods on behalf of the man who is turned toward them. After eleven verses of divine guests and priestly vessels, the last verse comes to rest on a household's own fire, and the last act in the hymn is not the worshipper's at all. It is done for him.
15.practice:
*Ṛtu* is the word declared in every saṅkalpa, when the time of a rite is named — *ṛtau, māse, pakṣe*. This sūkta is where a reciter can see what the word is carrying. It does not mean only *when*. It means that an observance has an internal order of turns, and that each power in it has a moment that is properly its own. Ten of the twelve verses say so.

The hymn is organised by whose vessel the drink comes from: the Potṛ's in verse 2, the Neṣṭṛ's in verses 3 and 9, the brāhmaṇa's in verse 5, and the gārhapatya at the close. A second sūkta in the collection is built the same way — [[2.36]] moves through *hotrāt*, *potrāt*, *āgnīdhrāt*, *brāhmaṇāt*, *praśāstrāt* — and the Anukramaṇī gives that hymn precisely the deity sequence of these first six verses: Indra, Maruts, Tvaṣṭā, Agni, Indra, Mitrāvaruṇau. Two hymns in different maṇḍalas holding one shape.

For a householder the last verse is the one that lands. The *gārhapatya* is Agni a married man keeps and from which the others are taken; it is Agni that does not go out. The hymn spends eleven verses among vessels most people will never handle and then puts the whole business into Agni that stands in the house — and asks that the worship be performed *devayate*, for the one who is godward, by someone else's hands.

Two words here are worth carrying. *Ratnadhā*, holder of the precious, is given to the Neṣṭṛ in verse 3 and is the same title given to Agni in [[1.1]].1. And *dhṛtavrata*, the vow held firm, is given to Mitrāvaruṇau in verse 6 — the epithet that [[1.25]] will hand, startlingly, to a human being.
15.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa treats Ṛtu as both an abstraction and a person — Wilson prints the double gloss at verse 1, "proper duty, also personified divinity of a season" — while Griffith simply leaves *Rtu* untranslated throughout and lets the reader decide.

Verse 3 is a text-critical point rather than an interpretive one. The padapāṭha in this apparatus prints *grāvaḥ*, which would be the pressing stone; the accented saṃhitā reads ग्नावो and the morphology gives *gnāvat*, accompanied by the *gnās*. Wilson has "with your spouse" and Griffith "with thy Dame" — both translators read the *gnās*, and the padapāṭha here appears to be corrupt.

On verse 5 Sāyaṇa glosses *brāhmaṇād rādhasaḥ* as a costly vessel, *dhanabhūtāt pātrāt*, and further identifies the *brāhmaṇa* with the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, one of the sixteen officiants; Wilson follows him into that detail. Griffith reads it plainly as "from the Brahmana's bounty."

On verse 7 Sāyaṇa identifies Draviṇodas as an appellative of Agni — *das*, giver, of *draviṇa* — and takes *adhvara* and *yajña* in that verse as a technical pair, the root rite (*prakṛti-rūpa*, agniṣṭoma) against the modified ones (*vikṛti-rūpa*, ukthya). Griffith renders the name flatly as "Wealth-giver" and lets the identification go unstated.

16.note: Sāyaṇa's bhāṣya for 1.16 is not present in this apparatus
16.title: Indra's Bays, and a Hymn That Touches the Heart
16.synthesis:
Nine gāyatrī verses to Indra, and for eight of them nothing is asked. The hymn's whole labour is getting him here and getting the drink into him; the request waits until the last line.

*Ā tvā vahantu harayo vṛṣaṇaṃ somapītaye* — let the *harī*, the tawny pair, carry you here, the *vṛṣan*, the bull, for the soma-drinking. The verse ends with *sūracakṣasaḥ*, sun-eyed, standing in the plural without a settled owner: it may describe the horses, or the men who are calling.

The second verse puts the food down first. Here are the *dhānāḥ*, the parched grains, *ghṛtasnuvaḥ*, dripping with ghee; let the two bays bring Indra in the *sukhatame rathe*, the easiest-running chariot. Hospitality, arranged before the guest arrives.

The third fixes the hymn to a timetable, and does it by repeating the name. *Indraṃ prātar havāmahe, indraṃ prayaty adhvare, indraṃ somasya pītaye* — Indra we call at dawn, Indra as the adhvara moves forward, Indra for the drinking of soma. Three pādas, three occasions, the accusative unchanged at the head of each.

In the fourth the horses are *keśin*, maned: come near to our pressing with them, *sute hi tvā havāmahe*, for it is at the pressing that we call you. The invitation is tied to a moment that has already arrived.

The fifth carries the hymn's only image, and it is an image of thirst rather than of power: come to this *stoma* of ours, to this *savana* that has been pressed, and drink *gauro na tṛṣitaḥ*, like a thirsty *gaura*. The sixth keeps the imperative going — these *somāsaḥ indavaḥ* are on the *barhis*; drink them, *sahase*, for strength.

The seventh is where the hymn turns and looks at itself. *Ayaṃ te stomo agriyo hṛdispṛg astu śaṃtamaḥ* — let this praise of ours, put first, be *hṛdispṛk*, heart-touching, and *śaṃtama*, most bringing of peace; *atha somaṃ sutaṃ piba*, and then drink the pressed soma. The order is stated in so many words: the word first, the drink after it. Three consecutive verses — 5, 6 and 7 — end in the imperative *piba*, and only this one puts a condition in front of it.

The eighth widens out and functions as reassurance. *Viśvam it savanaṃ sutam indro madāya gacchati* — to every pressing that has been pressed Indra goes, for *mada*, for the exhilaration; and he is *vṛtrahā*. Placed here, the general statement does a particular job: he comes to all of them, therefore he will come to this one.

Only then, in the ninth, the ask. *Sa imaṃ naḥ kāmam ā pṛṇa gobhir aśvaiḥ śatakrato* — fill up this desire of ours with cattle and with horses, O *śatakratu*, of a hundred *kratus*; *stavāma tvā svādhyaḥ*, and we would praise you, well-attentive. Even the closing line does not end on the wanting. It ends on the praising, and on the quality of mind brought to it.
16.practice:
Indra holds more of the Ṛgveda than anyone else: of the 1,027 sūktas, 218 are given to him alone, against 186 for Agni. A reader who wants to know what the Ṛgveda mostly *is* has to sit with hymns like this one, which are not dramatic and are not about Vṛtra.

Verse 3 states this sūkta's own occasion — *prātar*, at dawn — and it is the morning pressing that the hymn is set in. Verse 4 makes the same point differently: *sute hi tvā havāmahe*, it is at the pressing that we call you. The invitation is not general. It belongs to a moment that has already come, which is the same discipline [[1.15]] states as *ṛtunā*.

What a reciter can take from here is verse 7. *Hṛdispṛk* — heart-touching — is a criterion for a stotra, stated inside the Veda itself, and it is applied by the singer to his own composition as a hope rather than a boast: *astu*, let it be. Words are offered before the drink, and they are offered on the understanding that they might not land. The last word of the hymn, *svādhyaḥ*, says the same thing from the other end: well-minded, with the attention in good order.

*Śatakratu*, of a hundred *kratus*, is the epithet in verse 9 and it is the one name for Indra that has stayed in ordinary use. *Kratu* is not strength; it is the capacity to conceive a thing and carry it through. To call him that in the verse where you finally ask for cattle and horses is to say what you think the giving actually depends on.

This sūkta belongs to a long single-author run: Medhātithi Kāṇva is the ṛṣi of twelve consecutive hymns, [[1.12]] through [[1.23]], and of four more elsewhere — 8.1, 8.2, 8.32 and 9.2. Sixteen in all.
16.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's bhāṣya for this sūkta is not present in the apparatus used here, so the two English versions stand without him, and where they diverge there is nothing to adjudicate between them.

They diverge at once. In verse 1 Wilson attaches *sūracakṣasaḥ* to the priests — "may (the priests), radiant as the Sun, (make you manifest)" — supplying a whole verb to do it. Griffith attaches it to the horses: "Those, Indra, who are bright as suns." The word is a nominative plural and the hymn does not say whose eyes are meant.

In verse 5 both render *gaura* as "stag" — Wilson "like a thirsty stag (gaura)", Griffith "like a stag athirst" — where the word is properly the wild bovine, the gaur, not a deer. The Victorian English quietly changes the animal.

In verse 9 *svādhyaḥ* separates them by register rather than by sense: Wilson has "profoundly meditating," Griffith "with holy thoughts." The apparatus reads the compound as *su* + *ādhī*, and the difference between a meditation and a longing is not decided by the form.

17.note: Sāyaṇa's bhāṣya for 1.17 is not present in this apparatus; 17.6 dhīmahi is verified as √dhā, not √dhī
17.title: Indra and Varuṇa Named Together — Help and Shelter
17.synthesis:
The hymn's method is its first word. *Indrāvaruṇayoḥ* — a dual compound binding two very unlike powers into one addressee, so that neither can be asked for anything without the other. Force and the keeping of vows are not argued into partnership here. They are simply spoken to as one.

The first verse chooses rather than begs: *avaḥ ā vṛṇe*, I choose *avas*, help, from the two *samrāj*s, the over-kings — *tā naḥ mṛḷātaḥ īdṛśe*, may the two be gracious in a case such as this.

The second gives the reason it is worth asking. *Gantārā hi sthaḥ avase* — you two are goers, ones who actually come, when a *vipra* like me calls; and you are *dhartārā carṣaṇīnām*, upholders of the peoples. That last epithet is not theirs alone; the collection gives it to Mitra at [[3.59]].6 and to the Viśvedevāḥ at [[1.3]].7. It marks the office of holding a people up, whoever is doing it.

The third asks for *rāyaḥ*, wealth, *anukāmam*, according to desire — and then asks for something else entirely: *tā vāṃ nediṣṭham īmahe*, we approach you two at the very nearest range. Nearness, not reach.

The fourth repeats one word twice in a single line. *Yuvāku hi śacīnāṃ yuvāku sumatīnām* — yours in respect of *śacī*, capacity, yours in respect of *sumati*, good favour; may we be so, among givers of *vāja*.

The fifth is the one verse that distinguishes them, and it does it in half a line each. *Indraḥ sahasradāvnām* — Indra among the givers of thousands; *varuṇaḥ śaṃsyānām* — Varuṇa among those who are to be praised. One is measured by what he hands over, the other by what is said of him. And their shared *kratu* is *ukthya*, fit to be recited over.

The sixth asks for more than sufficiency. Through their *avas* we would win and set down — *ni ca dhīmahi*, from √dhā, to place, not from *dhī* — and then a rare and homely closing: *syād uta prarecanam*, and let there be an overflow. Not enough. More than enough.

The seventh calls them *citrāya rādhase*, for bright and various bounty, and asks *asmān su jigyuṣaḥ kṛtam*, make us thoroughly victorious — the only martial line in the hymn, and it asks for the condition rather than for a battle.

The eighth carries the hymn's one *dhī*, and puts it to work: *siṣāsantīṣu dhīṣu ā asmabhyaṃ śarma yacchatam* — in our thoughts, which are trying to win you, extend *śarma* to us. The thought is not described as pure or as still. It is described as making an attempt.

The ninth ends by asking about the hymn rather than about the reward. *Pra vām aśnotu suṣṭutiḥ* — may the good praise reach you, *yāṃ huve yām ṛdhāthe sadhastutim*, the joint praise which I call out and which you two cause to prosper. Five of the nine verses carry the dual compound itself; the last thing asked for is that the words arrive.
17.practice:
Seven sūktas in the whole collection are addressed to *indrāvaruṇau*, and this is the first of them — [[1.17]], 4.41, 6.68, 7.82, 7.83, 7.84, 8.59. Set that against the thirty-six places where Varuṇa is named with Mitra instead. Varuṇa's ordinary partner is Mitra; being yoked to Indra is the rarer arrangement, and it changes what a person can ask for in one breath. From Mitrāvaruṇau one asks that the order hold. From Indrāvaruṇau one asks to win *and* to be forgiven.

That combination is worth sitting with, because it is the shape of most real petitions. Verse 7 wants victory; verse 8 wants *śarma*, shelter; verse 5 has already said that one of the two is praised for giving and the other for being praiseworthy. The hymn does not resolve the tension between conquering and being sheltered. It addresses both to the same pair and moves on.

The word to carry away is *prarecanam* in verse 6 — the overflow, the remainder past what was needed. Vedic petitions are usually for sufficiency: food, cattle, sons, a long life. This one asks that after the winning and the storing there be something left over. It is an unembarrassed verse, and there are not many like it.

One caution for a reader tracking *dhī* through these hymns. Verse 6's *dhīmahi* looks like the word and is not: the morphology gives √dhā, to place or set down, so the line means "may we lay it up," not "may we meditate." The genuine *dhī* in this sūkta is in verse 8, in the locative plural, and there it is described as *siṣāsantī* — striving to win. The Veda's word for thought is a word for effort.
17.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's bhāṣya for 1.17 is absent from this apparatus, but his hand is visible through Wilson, and verse 4 is where it shows. Wilson takes *yuvāku* as a mixture — printing "the mingled (libations)" with the glosses "mixture of curds and ghee" and "mixture of butter milk, water and meal" — producing an English sentence about prepared offerings. Griffith reads the plain pronominal sense: "May we be sharers of the powers, sharers of the benevolence of you who give strength bounteously." The apparatus lemma is *yuvāku*, "your," which is on Griffith's side.

Verse 5 divides them over whether the two are distinguished at all. Wilson distributes the halves — "Indra is a giver among the givers of thousands; Varuṇa is to be praised among those who are deserving of laudation." Griffith merges them: "Indra and Varuna, among givers of thousands, meet for praise."

Verse 7 is worth noting as an editorial matter rather than an interpretive one: Wilson prints the same English sentence for verses 7 and 8, which loses verse 7's *citrāya rādhase*, for bright bounty, and its *jigyuṣaḥ*, victorious. Griffith keeps them distinct.

18.title: Brahmaṇaspati, Without Whom No Yajña Succeeds
18.synthesis:
Nine verses to the lord of *brahman* — of the formulated, effective word — and the claim at the centre of them is a negative: without him, nothing done with words comes out right.

The first verse asks for a man to be made resounding, and gives a precedent by name. *Somānaṃ svaraṇaṃ kṛṇuhi brahmaṇas pate, kakṣīvantaṃ yaḥ auśijaḥ* — make the presser of soma ring out, as you did Kakṣīvat the son of Uśij. A hymn that will spend its length on an abstract power opens by pointing at a person to whom this actually happened.

The second stacks his offices: *revān*, rich; *amīvahā*, striker of sickness; *vasuvid*, finder of goods; *puṣṭivardhana*, increaser of thriving; *turaḥ*, quick. And then the request, which is not for any of those things — *sa naḥ sisaktu*, may he attach himself to us.

The third names the danger, and the danger is also speech. *Mā naḥ śaṃsaḥ araruṣaḥ dhūrtiḥ martyasya praṇak* — let no *śaṃsa* of the ungiving one, no malice of a mortal, reach us; *rakṣa naḥ brahmaṇas pate*. Word against word: what is said about a man is what threatens him, and the lord of the word is the shelter.

The fourth widens the guard to three. *Sa gha vīro na riṣyati yam indro brahmaṇas patiḥ somo hinoti martyam* — that man does not come to harm whom Indra, Brahmaṇaspati and Soma urge on. The verb is *hinoti*, impels: the safety is not a wall around him but a push behind him.

The fifth adds a fourth guardian and it is a surprising one. *Tvaṃ taṃ brahmaṇas pate somaḥ indraś ca martyam dakṣiṇā pātu aṃhasaḥ* — may Dakṣiṇā guard that man from *aṃhas*, from narrowness, from the pinch. The fee handed to the officiants is set beside three gods as a protecting power in its own right.

With the sixth the address changes and the hymn's one personal request arrives. *Sadasas patim adbhutam priyam indrasya kāmyam sanim medhām ayāsiṣam* — I have gone to Sadasaspati, lord of the seat, wondrous, dear, desired of Indra, for *sani*, gain, and for *medhā*, mental grasp. Out of nine verses, what is asked for oneself is intelligence.

The seventh says why that is the thing to ask for. *Yasmād ṛte na sidhyati yajño vipaścitaś cana* — without whom the yajña does not succeed, not even the yajña of the *vipaścit*, the one who knows; *sa dhīnāṃ yogam invati*, he drives the *yoga*, the yoking, of the *dhī*s. Knowing the procedure is not enough. The thoughts have to be harnessed together, and that harnessing is his work, not the expert's.

The eighth follows the offering out of the hand: *āt ṛdhnoti haviṣkṛtim*, he makes the making-of-the-oblation prosper; *prāñcaṃ kṛṇoti adhvaram*, he makes the adhvara go forward; *hotrā deveṣu gacchati*, the invocation reaches among the gods. Three stages, three verbs, one agent.

The ninth ends in the past tense and in the first person. *Narāśaṃsaṃ sudhṛṣṭamam apaśyam saprathastamam divo na sadmamakhasam* — I have seen Narāśaṃsa, most resolute, most far-extended. *Apaśyam*: not a petition, a report. Three names have been used for one power across the hymn — Brahmaṇaspati in verses 1, 3, 4 and 5, Sadasaspati in 6, Narāśaṃsa in 9 — and the last of them is reached not by asking but by looking.
18.practice:
Four sūktas in the whole Ṛgveda are addressed to Brahmaṇaspati alone — this one, 1.40, 2.25 and 2.26 — and eight name him somewhere. Bṛhaspati, the name the later tradition mostly uses, is named in thirteen. The tradition reads the two as one power; the counts are worth having separately, because they show how small a footprint the lord of the word has in a collection that is made entirely of words.

Verse 6 is where this hymn earns its place in a working life. *Medhā* — the retentive, composing intelligence behind *medhāvin* — is the one thing the singer asks for himself, and he asks it of the deity of formulated speech. Verse 7 explains the request: the yajña of even the *vipaścit* does not succeed without him, because what he supplies is *dhīnāṃ yogam*, the yoking of the thoughts. *Dhī* and *yoga* stand together in one Ṛgvedic phrase, and the sense is mechanical rather than mystical — several thoughts pulling in one direction, like animals in harness. Competence is not the same as being collected. Anyone who has performed a rite while distracted knows the difference this verse is naming.

Verse 5 is the other one to keep. *Dakṣiṇā*, the gift made to the officiants, is placed among the guardians alongside Indra, Soma and Brahmaṇaspati, and asked to protect a man from *aṃhas* — a word for constriction, the state of having no room. What is given away is counted as protection, not as expense. That is a Vedic position on generosity, stated without any moralising around it.

And verse 3 names the threat this hymn was built against: not an enemy's weapon but his *śaṃsa*, his saying. Where speech can wound, the answer sought is the lord of speech.
18.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa identifies all three names in this hymn with Agni — Brahmaṇaspati as Agni in connection with prayer, Sadasaspati as Agni the protector of the assembly, Narāśaṃsa as Agni or as the personified yajña at which men praise the gods — and Wilson carries each identification into his English as a parenthesis. Griffith leaves all three untranslated and makes no identification at all. A reader comparing them is comparing a commentary with a translation, not two translations.

On verse 9 Sāyaṇa cites Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 6.27 for the equation directly: "I beheld that divinity Sadasaspati, who is to be praised by men, who is also called Narāśaṃsa." On verse 1 he supplies the Kakṣīvat legend at length — Dīrghatamas, the Kaliṅga queen, and her maid Uśij — and quotes Nirukta 6.10, *aham kakṣīvān ṛṣir asmi*.

Verse 7 is where the translators part. Wilson glosses *dhī* twice over as *buddhi*, understanding, or *karma*, act, and renders "he pervades the association of our thoughts"; Griffith has "he stirs up the series of thoughts." Both feel the strangeness of *yoga* here and neither translates it as yoking.

19.title: Agni, Come with the Maruts — Asked Nine Times
19.synthesis:
The refrain governs everything. *Marudbhir agna ā gahi* — Agni, come with the Maruts — closes all nine verses without a single variation. What changes is only what stands in front of it, and each verse adds one more thing to the account of the company he is being asked to bring.

The first verse states the occasion. *Prati tyaṃ cārum adhvaraṃ gopīthāya pra hūyase* — you are called forward to this lovely adhvara, for the *gopītha*, the drinking. Then the refrain.

The second, before any description of the Maruts begins, protects Agni's standing. *Nahi devo na martyo mahas tava kratuṃ paraḥ* — neither god nor mortal is beyond the *kratu* of you, the great one. Placed second, it settles a question the rest of the hymn might otherwise raise: the escort does not diminish the one escorted.

From the third the Maruts are described, and only described — they are never once addressed. They *mahaḥ rajasaḥ viduḥ*, know the great *rajas*, the middle region; they are *viśve devāsaḥ adruhaḥ*, all shining, without treachery.

The fourth: *ye ugrāḥ arkam ānṛcuḥ anādhṛṣṭāsaḥ ojasā* — the fierce ones who have sung the *arka*, unassailable in *ojas*. The word *arka* is both the chant and, in an old ritual identification, the water; the verse can be read either way and the hymn does not choose.

The fifth holds beauty and terror in one line, which is the standing Vedic description of them: *śubhrāḥ*, bright; *ghoravarpasaḥ*, of dreadful form; *sukṣatrāsaḥ*, of good rule; *riśādasaḥ*, consumers of the hostile.

The sixth puts them at rest: *ye nākasya adhi rocane divi devāsaḥ āsate* — who sit in heaven, above the shining vault. It is the only still verse in the hymn.

The seventh and eighth belong together and should be read as a pair, because the same three words stand in both. *Ye īṅkhayanti parvatān tiraḥ samudram arṇavam* — who set the mountains swaying, across the surging sea. And then *ā ye tanvanti raśmibhis tiraḥ samudram ojasā* — who stretch themselves out with their beams, across the sea, by their strength. *Tiraḥ samudram* twice: the same water crossed once in the shaking and once in the stretching, so that the crossing is what the two verses have in common and the manner of it is what distinguishes them.

Only in the ninth does the offering appear. *Abhi tvā pūrvapītaye sṛjāmi somyaṃ madhu* — for your first drink I pour out the soma-sweet. Eight verses of summoning, and the drink arrives last, followed by the refrain one final time.

What the hymn does, structurally, is unusual. Every vocative in it is *agne*. The Maruts occupy seven of the nine verses and are spoken of throughout in the third person, as *ye*, those who. Agni is the one who can be addressed — he is present, on the hearth, being spoken to — and the Maruts are reached only through him. The refrain is not decoration. It is the hymn's entire argument, repeated until it is unmistakable: the way to the ones who cannot be approached is the one who can.
19.practice:
This is the only sūkta in the entire Ṛgveda whose deity the Anukramaṇī assigns, for the hymn as a whole, to *agniḥ-marutaḥ* — Agni together with the Maruts as a single addressee. Other hymns name the two, but always in separate verse-blocks: [[1.15]], [[1.23]], 2.36, 6.48, 8.103. Only here are they one thing for nine verses running. The Maruts on their own hold thirty-one sūktas.

The form is what a reciter meets first, and it is worth naming for what it does. A refrain in every verse means that a third of what you say is already known before you say it. The mind is not asked to track new material at the end of each verse; it is released, at a fixed point, to attend. This is the same principle behind every *japa* a Hindu performs — the repeated portion is not filler, it is where attention is allowed to rest — and here it is built into a sūkta of the Ṛgveda itself.

The theology in it is worth stating plainly. The Maruts are storm — mountains swaying, the sea crossed, thunder — and they are not spoken to. Agni is on the hearth, in front of the person reciting, and he is spoken to nine times. Where a power is too large or too far to be addressed directly, the tradition's answer is not to shout louder but to address the one who is present and ask him to bring the rest. That is Agni's whole office, stated in [[1.1]].2 as *sa devāṁ eha vakṣati*, and this hymn is that office applied to a single storm-band, over and over.

*Ojas* in verses 4 and 8, *kratu* in verse 2 — the vocabulary here is of raw force held in check by an intermediary. Nothing is asked for in the whole hymn except presence.
19.disagreements:
Verse 4 carries the most consequential split, and it is old rather than modern. Sāyaṇa cites Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.6.5.1–2, *āpo vā arkaḥ* — the waters are the *arka* — and so Wilson prints "who are fierce, and send down rain," with a note deriving *arka* from √arc, to worship, by way of the Brāhmaṇa's identification of worship with water. Griffith takes the ordinary sense: "The terrible, who sing their song." The same word gives a rain-band or a choir.

Verse 3 divides the same way. Sāyaṇa quotes Nirukta 4.19 that *rajas* means water, light or the world, and adduces RV [[5.55]].5, the Maruts rising from the ocean and sending down rain; Wilson accordingly writes "who know (how to cause the descent) of great waters." Griffith keeps space: "who know the mighty region of mid-air."

On verse 1 Wilson takes *gopītha* as the soma-drinking, Griffith as "the milky draught." On verse 6 Sāyaṇa glosses *nākasya adhi* as *sūryasya upari*, above the sun, which Wilson follows; Griffith has "above the sky-vault's luminous sphere." At verse 8 Sāyaṇa adds only a plain observation, that the verse notices the influence of winds upon the sea.

20.title: The Ṛbhus — Craftsmen Who Won a Share Among Gods
20.synthesis:
Eight verses about makers, and the hymn opens by declaring how it was itself made. *Ayaṃ devāya janmane stomo viprebhir āsayā akāri ratnadhātamaḥ* — this *stoma*, greatest holder of what is precious, was made by the *vipra*s *āsayā*, with the mouth, for the divine birth. The Ṛbhus made things with their hands; the singers make this with their mouths; and the same root, √kṛ, will run through the hymn from here — *akāri* in verse 1, *akrata* in verse 4, *akarta* in verse 6.

The second verse gives their first commission. *Ye indrāya vacoyujā tatakṣur manasā harī* — who fashioned for Indra the two bays that are yoked by a word, and fashioned them *manasā*, with the mind; *śamībhir yajñam āśata*, by their labours they reached the yajña. The craft is mental, the tool is effort, and the destination is a place at the rite.

The third uses the carpenter's verb twice in one verse, and the second use is startling. *Takṣan nāsatyābhyāṃ parijmānaṃ sukhaṃ ratham* — they carved for the Nāsatyas a chariot that goes everywhere and runs easy; *takṣan dhenuṃ sabardughām* — they carved a milch cow, ever-yielding. A living animal, made the way a chariot is made.

The fourth is the deed the tradition kept. *Yuvānā pitarā punaḥ satyamantrāḥ ṛjūyavaḥ ṛbhavo viṣṭy akrata* — the Ṛbhus, of true *mantra*s and straight in their seeking, made their parents young again. The hymn states it flatly, in the same list as chariots and cups, without a word of wonder.

The fifth shows the result. *Saṃ vo madāsaḥ agmata indreṇa ca marutvatā ādityebhiś ca rājabhiḥ* — your exhilarating draughts have come together with Indra attended by the Maruts, and with the Ādityas, the kings. They are now drinking in company that was not theirs by birth.

The sixth is the hymn's boldest verse. *Uta tyaṃ camasaṃ navaṃ tvaṣṭur devasya niṣkṛtam akarta caturaḥ punaḥ* — and that new *camasa*, the cup finished by Tvaṣṭā, you made fourfold again. They took the work of the gods' own artisan, already complete, and improved on it by dividing it — which is the act that gets them their place, and also the act that could have destroyed them.

The seventh asks. *Te no ratnāni dhattana trir ā sāptāni sunvate ekam-ekaṃ suśastibhiḥ* — set treasures for us, thrice seven, for the one who presses, one by one, moved by our good praises. *Ekam-ekam*, one and one: even the request is itemised, in the manner of people who count parts.

The eighth states what they got, and the wording matters. *Adhārayanta vahnayaḥ abhajanta sukṛtyayā bhāgaṃ deveṣu yajñiyam* — as *vahni*s, bearers of the offering, they held; and *by sukṛtyā*, by good workmanship, they took for themselves a share among the gods, a share in the yajña. Not *were given* — *abhajanta*, they apportioned to themselves. The last word of the hymn is a claim about how a share is come by.
20.practice:
Ten sūktas in the collection are addressed to the Ṛbhus alone — this one, [[1.110]], 1.111, 1.161, 3.60, and five running in the fourth maṇḍala, [[4.33]] to 4.37 — and thirteen name them somewhere. This is the first of them, and the shortest.

What the tradition preserved them for is stated in the last verse. The Ṛbhus were men. They did not obtain their place by descent, by revelation or by austerity — what the hymn names is *sukṛtyā*, good work, work done well. Everything they are praised for is manufacture: a chariot, a cow, two horses, a cup divided into four, and their own parents made young again. For a householder whose days are spent making and mending things, this is the sūkta in the Ṛgveda that says the work itself is a road.

Verse 5 has them drinking with Indra and the Ādityas, and Sāyaṇa connects it to a real place in the rite: he cites Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.3 for the third, evening pressing being offered to Indra with the Ādityas together with Ṛbhu, Vibhu and Vāja. The verse is describing the company at a particular hour of a particular day.

Verse 4 is the one to keep for a family. Of all the Ṛbhus' works, making their parents young again is the one that survived into every later retelling, and the hymn spends no rhetoric on it at all. It sits between a milch cow and a set of cups. A tradition that puts caring for the old on the same list as competent carpentry is saying something about both.

And verse 1 deserves a moment from anyone who recites. *Viprebhir āsayā akāri* — made by the singers with the mouth. The hymn knows it is itself a manufactured object, made by an instrument, offered to makers.
20.disagreements:
Verse 1 sets the terms. Sāyaṇa reads *devāya janmane* as the class of divinities who came to be — three sons of Sudhanvan, of Aṅgiras's line, *manuṣyāḥ santas tapasā devatvam prāptāḥ*, men who reached godhood by tapas — and Wilson prints that whole reading. Griffith flattens it to "the Celestial Race," which loses the entire point: that this birth was into divinity, not from it.

Verse 4's *viṣṭī* splits them. Sāyaṇa glosses it *vyāptiyuktaḥ*, meeting no obstruction, so Wilson has "succeeding (in all pious acts)"; Griffith reads the noun *viṣṭi*, labour — "with constant labour." The apparatus lemma here is *viṣṭi*, "labor," which supports Griffith and, incidentally, the hymn's own theme.

Verse 7's *trir ā sāptāni* has no settled reading. Sāyaṇa offers seven rites in each of three classes — agnyādheya, pākayajña, agniṣṭoma — and also notes that *triḥ* may attach to the treasures rather than to the sevens; Wilson takes the sacrifices, Griffith the libations.

On verse 8 Sāyaṇa gathers the corroborating tradition rather than arguing: RV [[1.110]].4, *martāsaḥ santo amṛtatvam ānaśuḥ*, being mortals they attained immortality; and Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 3.30, that the Ṛbhus won the soma-drinking among the gods by devotion.

21.note: Sāyaṇa's bhāṣya for 1.21 is not present in this apparatus; hvaye at v1 verified as 1sg present
21.title: Indra and Agni, Awake Over the Assembly
21.synthesis:
Six verses, and the dual compound *indrāgnī* stands in every one of them. Nothing else in the hymn repeats. The name is the whole armature, and the pairing is the point: the god of force joined to the god who is physically present at the rite, so that reach and nearness are asked for together and never separately.

*Iha indrāgnī upa hvaye* — here I call Indra-and-Agni; *tayor it stomam uśmasi*, it is their praise, theirs and no one else's, that we want; and they are *somapātamā*, the greatest of soma-drinkers. The verb is first person singular: one man calling.

The second verse turns away from the gods and speaks to the people in the room. *Tā yajñeṣu pra śaṃsata indrāgnī śumbhata naraḥ, tā gāyatreṣu gāyata* — praise the two in the yajñas, make them beautiful, sing them in the gāyatras. Three imperatives, all addressed to *naraḥ*, men. It is a rare kind of verse, and its effect is to make the reciters aware that they are the ones doing this.

The third gives a reason outside the pair: *tā mitrasya praśastaye indrāgnī tā havāmahe* — we call them for the *praśasti* of Mitra. The word can be the god or the friend and patron who has commissioned the rite; the hymn does not say which, and both readings leave the same structure — the two are called on someone else's behalf.

The fourth brings them to a specific moment. *Ugrā santā havāmahe upedaṃ savanaṃ sutam* — being fierce, they are summoned to this pressing, this one, already pressed; *indrāgnī ā iha gacchatām*, let the two come here.

The fifth is the hymn's business, and everything before it has been preparation. *Tā mahāntā sadaspatī indrāgnī rakṣa ubjatam, aprajāḥ santu atriṇaḥ* — great ones, lords of the *sadas*, the seat where the rite is held, press the *rakṣas* down; and let the *atrin*s, the devourers, be *aprajāḥ*, without offspring. The curse is precise and it is not a curse of destruction: what is asked is that what consumes should not continue past this generation.

The sixth asks for wakefulness rather than for action. *Tena satyena jāgṛtam adhi pracetune pade, indrāgnī śarma yacchatam* — by that truth, stay awake; in the station of discernment, extend *śarma*, shelter. The hymn ends on *jāgṛ*, to keep watch, and makes the shelter follow from the watching rather than from a blow.

What is not in these six verses is as telling as what is. There is no *rayi*, no *vāja*, no cattle, no horses, no sons, no long life — none of the standing objects of Vedic petition appears anywhere in the sūkta. In six verses a man asks for exactly two things: that what devours be stopped from breeding, and that the two great powers stay awake over the place where his people are gathered. It is the shortest hymn in this stretch of the collection and the one with the least self-interest in it.
21.practice:
Twelve sūktas across the Ṛgveda are addressed to *indrāgnī*, and this is the first — [[1.21]], 1.108, 1.109, 3.12, 5.86, 6.59, 6.60, 7.93, 7.94, 8.38, 8.40 and 10.161. The pairing puts together the two most-invoked gods in the collection, Indra with 218 sūktas to himself and Agni with 186, and asks them as one.

The title given them in verse 5, *sadaspatī*, lords of the *sadas*, is worth following, because the same ṛṣi used it three hymns earlier. At [[1.18]].6 *sadasas pati* is the lord of the word, from whom *medhā* is asked; here it is a dual, and what is asked is protection of the gathering itself. Medhātithi Kāṇva is the ṛṣi of both, and of the twelve consecutive sūktas [[1.12]] through [[1.23]] — a single hand working the same vocabulary across a long stretch, which is one of the reasons this block of the first maṇḍala reads as continuous.

*Jāgṛ*, the closing verb, runs on into his next hymn: at [[1.22]].21 it is the *viprā*s who are *jāgṛvāṃsaḥ*, wakeful, kindling Viṣṇu's highest station. Here the wakefulness is asked of the gods; there it is claimed by the men. Between the two verses the whole burden shifts, and it shifts inside one ṛṣi's own work.

For a household, the practical content of this sūkta is verse 5 read alongside verse 6. What is asked for the place where people assemble is not that it be defended but that it be watched over — and the shelter is granted from *pracetune pade*, the station of discernment. Protection here is a function of attention, not of force.
21.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's bhāṣya for 1.21 is not present in this apparatus, so the two English versions must be weighed against the Sanskrit directly, and on one point the Sanskrit decides. In verse 1 *hvaye* is a first-person singular present. Wilson prints an imperative addressed to someone else — "Invoke hither Indra and Agni" — where Griffith's "Indra and Agni I invoke" follows the form. The hymn begins with one man speaking, and verse 2 then turns and instructs the others; Wilson's rendering loses that movement.

Verse 3 divides them over *mitrasya*. Wilson takes it as the human patron — "for the benefit of our friend (the instructor of the rite)" — while Griffith takes the god: "for the fame of Mitra." Nothing in the verse settles it, and the two readings put the hymn at the service of different people.

Verse 6's *pracetune pade* comes out as a place of knowledge in Wilson, "the station which affords knowledge (of the consequence of acts)," and as a place of seeing in Griffith, "the place of spacious view." The root allows both; the difference is whether the two gods keep watch from somewhere high or from somewhere wise.

22.note: the pada-thread (vv 5, 14, 17, 20, 21) is verified from the padapāṭha
22.title: Aśvins, Savitṛ, Pṛthivī, and Viṣṇu's Three Strides
22.synthesis:
Twenty-one verses moving through seven addressees, and one word threads them from the fifth verse to the last: *pada* — a step, a footprint, a station, the place where something stands.

The Aśvins take the first four. *Prātaryujā vi bodhaya* — wake the two who yoke at dawn. The hymn's first act is waking somebody. They are *surathā*, of good chariot, *rathitamā*, best of charioteers, *ubhā devā divispṛśā*, both gods who touch heaven. The third verse turns their whip into something else entirely: *yā vāṃ kaśā madhumaty aśvinā sūnṛtāvatī, tayā yajñaṃ mimikṣatam* — your whip is honeyed, full of *sūnṛtā*, true and generous speech; with that, season our yajña. The instrument of driving is asked to sweeten. And the fourth denies distance rather than crossing it: *nahi vām asti dūrake... sominaḥ gṛham*, the soma-presser's house is not far off for you two.

Savitṛ takes verses 5 to 8. He is *hiraṇyapāṇi*, golden-handed, called *ūtaye*, for help — and *sa cettā devatā padam*, he discerns the *pada*, the station, of the deity. In the sixth he is *apāṃ napāt*, and it is his *vratas* that are wanted. In the seventh he is *vibhaktā*, the apportioner of bright wealth, and *nṛcakṣas*, one who looks on men — his work here is division, not creation. And the eighth stops addressing gods altogether: *sakhāyaḥ ā ni ṣīdata*, friends, sit down. One instruction to the human company in twenty-one verses, and it is to be seated.

Verses 9 to 12 bring the wives. Agni is told to convey the *patnī*s of the gods, willing, and Tvaṣṭā with them; then the *gnā*s by name — Hotrā, Bhāratī, Varūtrī, Dhiṣaṇā. In the eleventh they are *nṛpatnīḥ acchinnapatrāḥ*, their wings uncut, asked to attend with *avas* and with great *śarma*. In the twelfth three more are called by their own names: Indrāṇī, Varuṇānī, Agnāyī, *svastaye*, for wellbeing.

Verses 13 to 15 come down to the ground. Dyaus and Pṛthivī are asked to season this yajña with the same verb the Aśvins' whip was given, *mimikṣatām*, and to fill us *bharīmabhiḥ*, with sustenance. In the fourteenth the *viprā*s lick the ghee-rich milk of those two, *dhītibhiḥ*, with their thoughts, *gandharvasya dhruve pade* — in the Gandharva's firm station. And the fifteenth is the verse that anyone who has ever put a hand on the ground will recognise: *syonā pṛthivi bhava anṛkṣarā niveśanī, yacchā naḥ śarma saprathaḥ* — be kind, Pṛthivī, be thornless, be a place to settle into; extend to us wide shelter.

The last six go to Viṣṇu, and it is his first appearance in the collection. The sixteenth asks the gods to help us *ato*, from where Viṣṇu strode, by the seven *dhāman*s of the earth. The seventeenth: *idaṃ viṣṇur vi cakrame tredhā ni dadhe padam* — this whole thing Viṣṇu strode across; three times he set his foot down; *samūḷham asya pāṃsure*, and it was all gathered in the dust of it. The eighteenth says what the strides are for: *trīṇi padā vi cakrame viṣṇur gopā adābhyaḥ, ato dharmāṇi dhārayan* — three steps taken by the undeceivable herdsman, and from that he holds up the *dharman*s. Not display; load-bearing. The nineteenth turns to the onlookers — *viṣṇoḥ karmāṇi paśyata*, look at his works — and names him *indrasya yujyaḥ sakhā*, Indra's yoked friend.

The last two verses are the ones the tradition kept. *Tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padaṃ sadā paśyanti sūrayaḥ, divīva cakṣur ātatam* — that highest *pada* of Viṣṇu the *sūri*s always see, stretched out like an eye in the sky. And then, at the very end, the verb changes: *tad viprāso vipanyavo jāgṛvāṃsaḥ sam indhate viṣṇor yat paramaṃ padam* — that highest station of Viṣṇu, the singers, praising, staying awake, *kindle*. The hymn's last word for what men do with the highest thing there is is the word for lighting a fire.
22.practice:
Six sūktas in the entire Ṛgveda name Viṣṇu, and three are addressed to him alone — [[1.154]], 1.156 and [[7.100]]. These six verses are his first appearance in the collection. For a tradition in which Viṣṇu later becomes central, that is the exact size of the Ṛgvedic footprint, and it is worth knowing rather than assuming.

What is here is the three strides, and nothing else. There is no dwarf, no Bali, no boon, no request for three paces of ground. The Vāmana narrative is later. What the Ṛgveda gives is the bare act — *tredhā ni dadhe padam* — and one reason for it: *ato dharmāṇi dhārayan*, from that he holds the ordinances up. The strides are structural before they are ever a story.

*Tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam* (verse 20) is among the most widely recited lines the Ṛgveda has, and it is worth noticing what verse 21 does to it. Verse 20 says the highest station is *seen*. Verse 21 says it is *kindled* — *sam indhate*, the verb of lighting Agni — by those who are *jāgṛvāṃsaḥ*, awake. Between the two verses the reciter stops being a spectator.

Verse 15 is the household's verse. *Syonā pṛthivi bhava* — be kind, be thornless, be a place to settle in. It asks the ground for exactly what anyone asks of the ground they are going to live on. Sāyaṇa records that the verse is used at the *mahānāmnī* observance at the moment of touching the earth.

And verse 12 is where a reader looking for the goddesses in the Ṛgveda should be sent. Indrāṇī, Varuṇānī, Agnāyī, called by their own names alongside Hotrā, Bhāratī, Varūtrī and Dhiṣaṇā in verse 10 — seven named divine women in three verses, which is more than most of the collection manages.
22.disagreements:
Verse 20's *sūrayaḥ* is the most consequential divergence. Wilson has "the wise ever contemplate that supreme station"; Griffith has "the princes evermore behold." The apparatus lemma is *sūri*. Whether seeing Viṣṇu's highest station belongs to the learned or to the patrons who commission rites is not a small difference, and the word supports both.

Verse 17 preserves an ancient disagreement intact. Sāyaṇa records two named opinions on *tredhā nidadhe padam*: Śākapūṇi's, that the three steps are earth, firmament and heaven — with Viṣṇu present in them as Agni, Vāyu and Sūrya — and Aurṇavābha's, that they are the eastern mountain, the meridian sky and the western mountain, which makes Viṣṇu the Sun and the strides sunrise, noon and setting. He chooses neither.

Verse 6's *apāṃ napāt* is doubled too. Sāyaṇa allows the Sun who is the parent of the waters, citing Manu 3.76, or a reading from *na pālayati* — one who does not cherish the waters but dries them by his heat. Wilson prints the strange "who is no friend to water" beside the literal "son of the waters"; Griffith simply has "the Waters' Offspring."

On verse 11 Sāyaṇa explains *acchinnapatrāḥ* by saying the wives of the gods take the form of birds and no one had cut their wings; Wilson and Griffith both keep the wings but neither supplies the birds.

23.note: ubhā devā divispṛśā verified as occurring twice in maṇḍala 1: 1.22.2 and 1.23.2
23.title: Vāyu, Indra, Pūṣan, and the Healing Waters
23.synthesis:
Twenty-four verses, and the first six retrace a hymn already in the book. Vāyu alone, then Indravāyū, then Mitrāvaruṇau — the whole architecture of [[1.2]], compressed so this sūkta can keep going past it: through Indra with the Maruts, the Viśvedevāḥ, Pūṣan, and then eight verses to the *āpaḥ*, where it arrives.

*Tīvrāḥ somāsaḥ ā gahi* — the somas are sharp, *āśīrvantaḥ*, mixed with milk; come, Vāyu, and drink them *prasthitān*, as set out. The second calls Indravāyū with a half-line occurring exactly twice in this maṇḍala: *ubhā devā divispṛśā... havāmahe*, both gods who touch heaven. Its other occurrence is [[1.22]].2, where it belongs to the Aśvins — one formula handed from pair to pair across consecutive hymns by a single ṛṣi. In the third the two are *manojuvā*, swift as thought, *sahasrākṣā*, thousand-eyed, and *dhiyaḥ patī*, lords of the *dhī*s.

Mitrāvaruṇau hold 4 to 6, *pūtadakṣasā*, of purified *dakṣa*. Then the line that repeats one word until it cannot be missed: *ṛtena yau ṛtavṛdhau ṛtasya jyotiṣaḥ patī* — by ṛta the two who increase ṛta, lords of the light of ṛta. Three occurrences in one verse, exactly as at [[1.2]].8. The sixth divides their offices: let Varuṇa be *prāvitā*, the one who helps in advance, and Mitra help with all helps.

Verses 7 to 9 bring Indra *marutvantam*, accompanied — *sajūr gaṇena tṛmpatu*, may he be satisfied together with the troop; the eighth asks the whole band to hear; the ninth sets them to work, *hata vṛtraṃ sudānavaḥ indreṇa sahasā yujā*, strike Vṛtra with Indra as yoke-fellow.

The Viśvedevāḥ with the Maruts take 10 to 12: *pṛśnimātaraḥ*, having Pṛśni for mother; their thunder going out *dhṛṣṇuyā*, boldly, like the shout of conquerors; and *haskārād vidyutaḥ pari jātāḥ*, born out of the laughter of the lightning — the one flash of image in a long hymn.

Pūṣan takes 13 to 15, and his office is recovery. *Ā aja naṣṭaṃ yathā paśum* — drive him to us as one drives home a lost animal. Then *pūṣā rājānam apagūḷhaṃ guhā hitam avindat*: he found the king, concealed, set in a hiding place. And in the fifteenth he brings *ṣaṭ yuktān*, six yoked things, into line, *gobhir yavaṃ na carkṛṣat*, as one ploughs barley with oxen — the six read as the seasons, the *ṛtu* of [[1.15]] returning as something recovered rather than commanded.

Then the waters, for eight verses. *Ambayo yanty adhvabhiḥ* — the mothers go along their roads, *jāmayaḥ*, sisters of those performing the adhvara, mixing sweetness into milk. The seventeenth calls those gathered near Sūrya; the eighteenth calls them *devīḥ*, divine, and puts them where the cattle drink. The nineteenth states the claim — *apsv antar amṛtam apsu bheṣajam*, in the waters is *amṛta*, in the waters is *bheṣaja*, medicine. The twentieth attributes it rather than asserting it: *apsu me somo abravīt*, Soma told me — within the waters are all the medicines, and Agni who is good to all. The twenty-first turns it on a body: *bheṣajaṃ varūthaṃ tanve mama, jyok ca sūryaṃ dṛśe*, medicine as armour for my body, and that I may long see Sūrya. The twenty-second turns it on a life: carry off *yat kiṃ ca duritaṃ mayi*, whatever hardship is in me, whatever I have betrayed, whatever I cursed, and the *anṛta* — the exact negation of the word said three times in verse 5. The twenty-third puts the man in the river: *āpo adya anu acāriṣam, rasena sam agasmahi*, today I have gone after the waters, we have joined with their essence.

The last verse asks to be filled and to be known. *Saṃ mā agne varcasā sṛja, saṃ prajayā saṃ āyuṣā* — pour me together with splendour, offspring, lifespan; and let the gods know this of me, and Indra with the ṛṣis. A hymn that opened with a drink for Vāyu closes with a bath, a body, and a request to be recognised.
23.practice:
Four sūktas in the collection are addressed to the *āpaḥ* alone — 7.47, 7.49, [[10.9]] and 10.30 — and eight name them somewhere. Here they get eight consecutive verses, and those verses carry the Veda's plainest statement about why a Hindu touches water before doing anything else: *apsv antar amṛtam apsu bheṣajam*. Deathlessness is in the waters; medicine is in the waters. Not as metaphor — verse 18 places the same divine waters where the household's cattle drink.

Verse 23 describes its own use and needs no reconstruction: *āpo adya anu acāriṣam*, today I have gone after the waters; *rasena sam agasmahi*, we have joined with their essence. This is spoken while bathing, by someone standing in it. Verse 22 is spoken in the same posture and asks the water to carry off *durita*, and specifies what it means — betrayal, a curse spoken, *anṛta*. The Vedic account of wrongdoing here is not stain but load, and water is what carries a load away.

Verse 21's closing phrase is the Veda's ordinary way of asking for a long life: *jyok ca sūryaṃ dṛśe*, that I may long see Sūrya. Nothing beyond that is requested. A reader who wants to know what the Ṛgveda hopes for should note how often the answer is simply more days, and daylight in them.

Pūṣan's three verses are worth marking for what they name. His work is finding: the hidden king in verse 14, the lost animal in verse 13, and in verse 15 the six brought back into line. Where a tradition needs an address for what has gone missing, this is the one the Ṛgveda supplies.

And *ṛta* and *anṛta* both stand in this single hymn — three times in verse 5, once in verse 22. The order of things and the failure of it are named eighteen verses apart, by one voice, in one sitting.
23.disagreements:
The Pūṣan verses are where Wilson and Griffith diverge most sharply, because Sāyaṇa supplies an object that the Sanskrit leaves open. Wilson, following him, makes what Pūṣan finds the soma — "the resplendent Pūṣan has found the royal (Soma juice), although concealed, hidden in a secret place" — while Griffith leaves it unnamed: "Pusan the Bright has found the King, concealed and hidden in a cave." On verse 15's *ṣaṭ*, Sāyaṇa reads *vasantādīn ṛtūn*, spring and the rest of the seasons; Wilson prints "the six (seasons)" and Griffith declines to identify them.

Verse 19's vocative *devāḥ* is the other real split. Sāyaṇa takes it as the officiants and other brāhmaṇas, citing Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.7.3.1, *ete vai devāḥ pratyakṣaṃ yad brāhmaṇāḥ* — these deities who are visibly present are the brāhmaṇas; Wilson accordingly addresses "divine (priest)." Griffith addresses the gods: "Be swift, ye Gods, to give them praise."

On verse 20 Sāyaṇa notes the entry of Agni into the waters (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.6.6.1) and the legend of Agni hiding there in fear, which is why Agni can be named among what the waters contain. On verse 3 he assigns *sahasrākṣa* to Indra as the sky studded with constellations, and *manojavā* to Vāyu, distributing a dual epithet between the two.

24.note: Griffith's verse numbering in this apparatus runs one behind the Sanskrit from v4 onward and stops at 14; compared by content, not by number
24.title: Whose Name to Call — Śunaḥśepa Reaches Varuṇa
24.synthesis:
The hymn opens with a question, and the collection holds few like it. *Kasya nūnaṃ katamasya amṛtānāṃ manāmahe cāru devasya nāma* — of whom now, of which of the immortals, shall we call to mind the dear name? *Ko no mahyai aditaye punar dāt, pitaraṃ ca dṛśeyaṃ mātaraṃ ca* — who will give us back to great Aditi, that I may see my father and my mother? The speaker does not know whom to address. He knows only what he wants.

The second answers in the first verse's own words. *Agner vayaṃ prathamasya amṛtānāṃ manāmahe cāru devasya nāma, sa no mahyai aditaye punar dāt* — of Agni, first of the immortals, we call to mind the dear name; he shall give us back. Every word returns with the interrogatives filled in: *kasya* becomes *agneḥ*, *kaḥ* becomes *saḥ*. The doubt is answered by substitution.

The metre shortens to gāyatrī for three verses to Savitṛ, and what they ask for is a *bhāga*, a portion. He is *īśāna vāryāṇām*, master of desirable things; the fourth names the portion set in his hands *purā nidaḥ*, before reproach, *adveṣaḥ*, free of hatred; the fifth would rise by his *avas* to take hold of *mūrdhānaṃ rāyaḥ*, the head of wealth. Three verses asking for a share, from a man about to be given as one.

With the sixth the metre returns to triṣṭubh and the hymn reaches Varuṇa, who holds the remaining ten. *Nahi te kṣatraṃ na sahaḥ na manyum vayaś cana amī patayantaḥ āpuḥ* — not the birds in flight have reached your *kṣatra*, your force, your *manyu*; nor these waters going without pause; nor those that overcome the raging of *vāta*.

The seventh is the strangest verse in the maṇḍala. *Abudhne rājā varuṇo vanasya ūrdhvaṃ stūpaṃ dadate pūtadakṣaḥ, nīcīnāḥ sthur upari budhnaḥ eṣām, asme antar nihitāḥ ketavaḥ syuḥ* — in the bottomless he holds up the high crest of the wood; these stand downward, their base above; may their signals be set within us. What is described stands upside down, and the singer asks for it inside him. The eighth makes a road where there was none: a wide path for Sūrya, *apade pādā pratidhātave*, a place to set feet where there was no footing.

The ninth says, of guilt, the word that will end both this hymn and the next. *Śataṃ te rājan bhiṣajaḥ sahasram* — a hundred healers are yours, a thousand; *bādhasva dūre nirṛtim*, drive Nirṛti far off; *kṛtaṃ cid enaḥ pra mumugdhi asmat*, release from us even the *enas* already done. The tenth looks up: those set on high, seen at night, gone somewhere by day — *adabdhāni varuṇasya vratāni*, his *vrata*s cannot be cheated, and the moon goes shining by night. The stars vanishing at dawn is not disorder; it is the rule being kept.

The eleventh sets singer and patron side by side — *tat tvā yāmi brahmaṇā vandamānaḥ, tad ā śāste yajamāno havirbhiḥ* — then *mā naḥ āyuḥ pra moṣīḥ*, do not steal our life away. The twelfth names the man: what is told him night and day, and what the *keta* out of the heart declares, is that the king whom the seized Śunaḥśepa called should release *us*. The thirteenth gives his position — *triṣu ādityaṃ drupadeṣu baddhaḥ*, bound at three posts. The fourteenth is all *namas*: with homage, yajñas and oblations we ask the anger down, *enāṃsi śiśrathaḥ kṛtāni*, slacken the guilts committed.

And the fifteenth loosens the rope. *Ud uttamaṃ varuṇa pāśam asmat, ava adhamaṃ vi madhyamaṃ śrathaya* — the topmost bond up, the lowest down, the middle apart; *atha vayam āditya vrate tava anāgaso aditaye syāma*, and then, inside your own *vrata*, may we be faultless and belong to Aditi. The hymn ends on the word it began with — and the condition it names is not escape from Varuṇa but standing inside his observance.
24.practice:
Śunaḥśepa Ājīgarti is named as the ṛṣi of seven consecutive sūktas, [[1.24]] through [[1.30]], and of 9.3 — eight in all. This is the first, and it is where the tradition's most famous rescue is anchored.

What is worth knowing is how little of that story is in the hymn. The Ṛgveda gives three things: *gṛbhītaḥ*, seized; *triṣu drupadeṣu baddhaḥ*, bound at three posts; and a name. Everything else — the sonless king, the son who fled to the forest, the father who sold his second son, the price — comes from the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, and the Rāmāyaṇa tells it differently again. The two accounts do not agree, and the hymn adjudicates between them not at all. What the Ṛgveda preserves is a man tied up, working through the gods one at a time until he reaches one who unties.

That search is the hymn's usable shape. Verse 1 does not know whom to call. Verse 2 tries Agni, who is nearest. Verses 3 to 5 try Savitṛ and ask him only for a share. Verse 6 arrives at Varuṇa and does not leave him for ten verses. A person who does not know where to direct a prayer is being shown a procedure, not shamed for not knowing.

The second thing to carry is the Vedic account of guilt, which is not a doctrine of stain. In verse 9 *enas* is asked to be *released* — *pra mumugdhi* — six verses before any rope is mentioned. In verse 14 the *enāṃsi* are to be *slackened*. In verse 15 the *pāśa* is loosened at three points. Guilt and cord take the same verbs, and the loosening is asked of the one who tied them.

Verse 9 also gives Varuṇa a hundred healers and a thousand — set that beside [[1.23]].19, four hymns earlier, where the *bheṣaja* is in the waters. In this stretch of the collection the powers that bind and the powers that heal are the same powers.
24.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa supplies the occasion, and supplies it twice over. He gives the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa account — Hariścandra, who promised Varuṇa his firstborn; Rohita, who fled; Ājīgarta, who sold his second son as a substitute; Viśvāmitra advising from among the officiants — and separately records the Rāmāyaṇa I.61 version, in which Śunaḥśepa is sold for a hundred cows to Ambarīṣa of Ayodhyā and learns his prayer from Viśvāmitra at Puṣkara. He does not reconcile them. On verse 1 he also allows that *kasya* may be read as a name — of Ka, that is Prajāpati — citing *ko ha vai nāma prajāpatiḥ*.

Verse 7 is where the translators separate completely. Wilson, with Sāyaṇa's *vanasya stūpam* as a mass of radiance and *abudhne* as the baseless firmament, has Varuṇa "sustaining on high a heap of light, the rays of which are pointed downwards, while their base is above." Griffith reads a tree: "sustaineth erect the Tree's stem in the baseless region. Its rays, whose root is high above, stream downward." The lemma is *vana*, wood or forest, which does not settle it — an inverted tree or an inverted radiance.

One editorial caution. In this apparatus Griffith's numbering runs one verse behind the Sanskrit from verse 4 onward and ends at fourteen, so the two English versions here must be compared by content and never by verse number.

25.note: veda six times across vv 7-9 and the vrata thread (vv 1, 6, 8, 10) verified from the padapāṭha
25.title: Varuṇa Knows the Path of the Birds, and Loosens
25.synthesis:
The longest hymn the collection gives to Varuṇa alone is built on one word. *Vrata* — an observance, a rule held to — is broken in verse 1, kept by a man in verse 6, kept by Varuṇa in 8 and 10.

*Yac cid hi te viśo yathā pra deva varuṇa vratam minīmasi dyavi-dyavi* — whatever *vrata* of yours we damage, day after day, as people do. The fault is admitted and dated: *dyavi-dyavi*, the phrase [[1.1]] uses for approaching Agni. Nothing exceptional is confessed; it is the ordinary daily failure. The second asks not to be handed to the killing weapon of his displeasure, nor to the *manyu* of his being offended.

The third is exact and startling. *Vi mṛḷīkāya te manaḥ rathīr aśvaṃ na sanditaṃ gīrbhir varuṇa sīmahi* — with our songs we would bind your mind toward mercy, as a charioteer binds a tethered horse. A hymn that ends by asking to be untied begins by tying.

The fourth sends the mind out: *parā hi me vimanyavaḥ patanti vasyaïṣṭaye, vayo na vasatīr upa* — they fly from me toward the seeking of good, as birds to their nests. The fifth asks the one dated question: *kadā*, when shall we bring Varuṇa here, the *urucakṣas*, wide-seeing, for mercy?

The sixth does what the collection rarely does. *Tad it samānaṃ āśāte venantā na pra yucchataḥ, dhṛtavratāya dāśuṣe* — the two attain that in common; loving, they do not neglect the *dāśvān* who is *dhṛtavrata*, whose vow is held firm. The epithet that will belong to Varuṇa two verses later goes first to a human being.

Verses 7 to 9 are the centre, and the most insistent thing in the hymn: *veda*, he knows, six times, twice in each verse. *Veda yo vīnāṃ padam antarikṣeṇa patatām, veda nāvaḥ samudriyaḥ* — he knows the track of birds flying through mid-air; belonging to the ocean, he knows the ships. He knows the twelve months with their offspring, *veda ya upajāyate*, and the one born in addition. He knows the turning of *vāta*, and those who dwell above. Three kinds of knowledge: what leaves no track, what must be counted, what is out of sight.

The tenth seats him — *ni sasāda dhṛtavrato varuṇaḥ pastyāsu ā sāmrājyāya*, he has sat down among the dwellings, for over-kingship. He is not remote; he has taken a place. From there, in the eleventh, he looks over *kṛtāni yā ca kartvā*, what is done and what is yet to do. In the twelfth what is asked of all that seeing is small: good roads, and *pra na āyūṃṣi tāriṣat*, that he carry our lifespans across.

The thirteenth dresses him in a golden *drāpi* and seats his *spaś*, his watchers, all around. In the fourteenth no deceiver deceives him, no injurer among men, no hostile design. The fifteenth gives what he gives — *yaśas* made among men *asāmi*, not by halves, and made into our own bellies.

The sixteenth answers the fourth. *Parā me yanti dhītayaḥ gāvo na gavyūtīr anu, icchantīr urucakṣasam* — my *dhīti*s go out, as cattle to pasture, seeking the wide-seeing one. Earlier the mind flew off like birds; here it goes out like cattle, and what it seeks is named.

The seventeenth opens a conversation: let the two of us speak together again, since my sweet has been brought. The eighteenth claims sight rather than asking for it — *darśaṃ nu viśvadarśatam*, I have seen him whom all can see. The nineteenth and twentieth ask only to be heard: *imaṃ me varuṇa śrudhi havam*.

And the twenty-first: *ud uttamaṃ mumugdhi no vi pāśaṃ madhyamaṃ cṛta, ava adhamāni jīvase* — loosen the topmost from us, untie the middle bond, undo the lowest — *jīvase*, in order to live. The same threefold loosening ends [[1.24]] — two hymns by one ṛṣi arriving at one request, and here the reason given is the plainest available.
25.practice:
Nine sūktas of the 1,027 are addressed to Varuṇa alone. This is the longest of them at twenty-one verses; the next longest, 2.28, has eleven, and the rest run to five, seven, eight or ten. Set that against 218 sūktas to Indra and 186 to Agni. For a god the tradition treats as this weighty — the keeper of oaths, the one before whom perjury matters — nine is a small number, and knowing it changes how a reader holds him.

What this hymn gives is the Vedic account of doing wrong, and it is not an account of pollution. The first verse says *vratam minīmasi dyavi-dyavi*, we damage your observance day after day — a rule not kept, admitted as routine. The last verse asks for the *pāśa* to be loosened at three points. Between them there is no washing, no burning off, no substitution. What is bound is untied, and it is untied by the one who holds the cord. A reader who was taught that the Veda's concern is ritual purity should sit with those two verses.

Verse 6 is the one to memorise. *Dhṛtavrata*, whose vow is held firm — the epithet the hymn will spend on Varuṇa in verses 8 and 10 — is given first to a human *dāśvān*, a giver. Keeping your word is not a divine monopoly; it is the quality that makes a man someone the gods do not neglect. That the same word covers the god and the householder is the whole of Varuṇa's ethics in one adjective.

Verse 8 names the intercalary month — the twelve, and then *ya upajāyate*, the one that is born in addition — and names it as something Varuṇa knows. The pañcāṅga a household still consults, with its *adhika māsa* inserted to keep the lunar count against the solar year, is keeping the same reckoning this verse credits to him.

And verses 4 and 16 together are worth a reciter's attention. The mind is compared to birds going to their nests and to cattle going to pasture — twice, at a distance of twelve verses, and both times it is described as going *away*. The Veda's picture of a wandering mind is not a failure. It is an animal heading for what feeds it, and the work is to name what that is.
25.disagreements:
Verse 4 is where the two translators produce opposite hymns. Wilson, following Sāyaṇa's sense of *vimanyu* as free from anger, supplies the subject: "My tranquil (meditations) revert to the desire of life, as birds hover around their nests." Griffith reads a desertion: "They flee from me dispirited, bent only on obtaining wealth, as to their nests the birds of air." In one the thoughts turn toward the god; in the other they abandon the singer. Verse 16 repeats the figure with cattle, and there both agree that the thoughts are seeking Varuṇa — which tells against Griffith's verse 4.

Verse 15 divides them over *yaśas*. Wilson, with Sāyaṇa, takes it as food — "who has distributed unlimited food to mankind, and especially to us" — pushed there by *udareṣu*, in the bellies. Griffith keeps it glory: "He who gives glory to mankind, not glory that is incomplete, to our own bodies giving it."

On verse 6 Wilson supplies Mitra as the second of the pair, though the Anukramaṇī gives the whole hymn to Varuṇa; Griffith leaves the dual unfilled, "this with joy they both accept in common."

Sāyaṇa reads verses 13 and 18 together as pointing to an image — the golden *drāpi* is *suvarṇamayaṃ kavacam*, and the chariot is seen *adhi kṣami*, on the earth. On verse 8 he identifies the extra month plainly as the *adhikamāsa* of the luni-solar year.

26.title: Agni Robed to Offer — Every Gift Falls in Him
26.synthesis:
The hymn opens by reversing the direction we expect a prayer to run. *Vasiṣva hi miyedhya vastrāṇy ūrjāṃ pate* — put on your garments, you who are fit for the offering, lord of *ūrj*, of nourishing strength — and then *sa imaṃ no adhvaraṃ yaja*: perform this rite of ours. Not "accept what we offer" but "offer it". Agni is asked to dress and officiate. The men who kindled him become, for the length of ten verses, the household that has engaged a priest.

The second verse seats him. *Ni no hotā vareṇyaḥ sadā yaviṣṭha* — sit as our *hotā*, the one who pours and calls, the chosen one, ever-youngest — drawn by our *manman*, our formed thoughts, and by speech that carries light. The third says what kind of officiant this is: *ā hi ṣmā sūnave pitāpir yajaty āpaye sakhā sakhye vareṇyaḥ*, as a father for a son, as a kinsman for a kinsman, as a friend for a friend, the chosen one performs. Three relations in a single line, and every one of them is symmetric. The priest engaged is not a stranger hired but a relative already in the house.

The fourth verse brings the guests. Let Varuṇa, Mitra and Aryaman, *riśādasaḥ*, wearers-down of hostility, sit upon our strewn *barhis* — *manuṣo yathā*, as they did for Manu. The rite claims descent rather than novelty. The fifth turns back to Agni as *pūrvya hotā*, the officiant who was there before us, and asks him to take pleasure in this *sakhya*, this friendship, and to hear the songs. What was requested in verse one as office is requested here as relationship.

The sixth verse makes the hymn's largest claim, and makes it in passing. *Yac cid dhi śaśvatā tanā devaṃ-devaṃ yajāmahe tve id dhūyate haviḥ* — whatever we offer, in unbroken succession, to god after god, that oblation is poured into you. It settles the question a reader of any long liturgy eventually asks. The many addresses do not divide the offering among themselves; they all enter at one place.

Verses seven and eight then turn on a single word about the worshippers rather than the god. Let him be our dear *viśpati*, lord of the settlement, gladdening, chosen — and may we be *svagnayaḥ*, possessed of good fires, and dear to him. The eighth uses the word twice more: it was as *svagnayaḥ* that the gods took hold of what is desirable for us, and it is as *svagnayaḥ* that we direct our minds to you. Three occurrences in two verses. The condition of being heard is stated as a property of the household — whether its fires are well kept — and not as a property of the prayer.

The ninth verse asks for something the collection rarely asks. *Atha no ubhayeṣām amṛta martyānāṃ mithaḥ santu praśastayaḥ* — then, O immortal, let the praises of both of us, of mortals and of you, run mutually. Praise going in both directions, the god commending the men as the men commend him.

The tenth closes by widening the addressee. *Viśvebhir agne agnibhiḥ* — with all your fires — take pleasure in this *yajña* and in this speech, *sahaso yaho*, offspring of strength. The one Agni asked in verse one to robe himself is here a plurality, and the single hearth this household tends is enrolled among all of them.
26.practice:
The ṛṣi named for this hymn, Śunaḥśepa Ājīgarti, holds seven of the first thirty sūktas of the Ṛgveda — 1.24 through 1.30 — and one more at 9.3, eight in the whole collection. This is the third of that run, and the two before it are addressed to Varuṇa. A reader working through the beginning of the Ṛgveda in order meets, in these seven hymns, one voice sustained longer than almost anywhere else so early.

The word this sūkta repeats about Agni is one every Hindu says daily without meeting it as vocabulary. *Vareṇyaḥ* — choiceworthy, the one to be preferred — falls in verses 2, 3 and 7. It is the same word as *vareṇyaṃ* in *tat savitur vareṇyaṃ* ([[3.62]].10), the verse of the sandhyā. There it describes the light of Savitṛ; here it describes the fire on the hearth, three times, each time attached to the work of officiating rather than to splendour. What is *vareṇya* is what you would choose if the choosing were yours.

The sixth verse is the one to carry away, and it is why Agni stands where he stands in every household observance. Whatever is offered, to whichever god, is poured into him. A tradition that names hundreds of deities is saying that the offerings do not therefore go to hundreds of places. That is the same claim implied when Agni is the witness at the wedding, the upanayana and the last rite: not that he is the most important addressee, but that he is the way anything reaches an addressee at all.

*Svagnayaḥ* — "having good fires" — is worth sitting with for what it does not say. It is not "having good thoughts" or "having offered much".
