Verses 7 and 8 put the qualification on the state of the household's fires: kept, tended, not let out. The men who can be heard are the men whose hearth is in order. It is a domestic test, and it is the one the hymn names three times.

And the ninth verse asks for mutual praise between mortals and the immortal — *mithaḥ*, reciprocally. Not protection, not wealth. A relationship in which both parties speak well of the other.
26.disagreements:
The first word divides the readings. Sāyaṇa glosses *vastrāṇi* as *ācchādakāni tejāṃsi*, investing radiances, so Wilson has Agni "assume your vestments (of light)" and drops *miyedhya* into "Lord of sustenance"; Griffith keeps the plain sense — "O worthy of oblation... assume thy robes" — and the padapāṭha's *vastrāṇi* supports him. The same split runs through verse 2, where Wilson supplies "(invested) with radiance" for *divitmatā* and Griffith renders "through our heavenly word".

Verse 8 is where the two translators actually disagree about who acts. Wilson makes the subject the priests: "as the brilliant (priests), possessed of holy fires, have taken charge of our oblations". Griffith has "The Gods, adored with brilliant fires, have granted precious wealth to us". The padapāṭha reads *svagnayaḥ hi vāryaṃ devāsaḥ dadhire ca naḥ* — *devāsaḥ* is nominative plural, so the gods are the ones who took hold, and Griffith is closer.

Sāyaṇa's other notes here are identifications rather than arguments: Aryaman is an Āditya presiding over the twilight; the *manuṣaḥ* of verse 4 is Manu the Prajāpati; *pūrvya hotā* is the officiant born before us; and *sahaso yaho* in the last verse is *balasya putra*, offspring of strength.
26.note: vareṇya (vv 2,3,7) and svagnayaḥ (vv 7,8×2) counted from the padapāṭha; miyedhya verified as a 3-occurrence word corpus-wide (1.26.1, 1.36.9, 1.44.5)

27.title: Agni Who Shares Out — a Last Verse of Namas
27.synthesis:
Twelve verses to Agni in gāyatrī, and then one verse in triṣṭubh addressed to nobody in particular and to everybody — the change of metre is the hymn changing its mind about who is listening.

It begins with a comparison that has puzzled every reader: *aśvaṃ na tvā vāravantaṃ vandadhyai agniṃ namobhiḥ samrājantam adhvarāṇām* — to praise you with *namas*, Agni, like a horse with a full tail, you who rule over the rites. The second verse asks that this *sūnuḥ śavasā*, this offspring of power, wide-striding, kindly, generous, be ours. The third widens the range of the protection: *dūrāc ca āsāc ca*, from far off and from near, guard us always from the mortal who intends harm. Near and far will return at the end of the hymn in a different currency.

The fourth verse states the transaction plainly — carry this our *sani*, our gift, and this newest *gāyatra*, our song, forward to the gods. What the household has is a thing and a poem, and both need a courier. The fifth then asks for a share, and the way it asks is the hymn's most exact moment: *ā no bhaja parameṣu ā vājeṣu madhyameṣu śikṣā vasvo antamasya* — give us a portion in the highest *vājas*, in the middle ones, and let us have of the wealth that is nearest to hand. Highest, middle, nearest: the request is graded, and the last term is the modest one.

The sixth explains why sharing out is Agni's particular office. *Vibhaktāsi citrabhāno* — you are the divider, the apportioner, you of dazzling light — and near, as in the wave of the Sindhu, you flow at once to the one who gives. Then three verses of what a share amounts to. The seventh: the mortal you help in the *pṛts*, the clashes, whom you urge on in the *vājas*, holds unfailing nourishment. The eighth: no one at all overtakes such a man, O overpowering one; his *vāja* is worth hearing about. The ninth: may he, present among all peoples, be the one who carries across with horses, and with the inspired be the winner. Five of these verses turn on *vāja*, and the word is doing double duty throughout — the contest and the strength that wins it.

The tenth verse names Agni in an unexpected register: *jarābodha*, awakened by praise, take up this *stoma* for Rudra, worth seeing, for the one who is worshipful clan by clan. The eleventh restores the familiar: may he, great, unmeasured, *dhūmaketu*, smoke-bannered, abounding in light, urge us to *dhī* and to *vāja* — thought and strength named in one breath, in that order. The twelfth asks him to hear the *ukthas* like a wealthy lord of the settlement, the divine beacon, of vast radiance.

Then the metre changes and the addressee opens out. *Namo mahadbhyo namo arbhakebhyo namo yuvabhyo nama āśinebhyaḥ* — homage to the great, homage to the small, homage to the young, homage to the aged. Four *namas* in one line, to gods sorted by size and by age and by nothing else. *Yajāma devān yadi śaknavāma* — let us worship the gods if we are able, which concedes that we may not be. And the last request is for the reciter's own tongue: let me not injure the praise due to a greater one. After twelve verses of asking for a portion, the hymn ends by worrying about a portion it might fail to give.
27.practice:
The single word *namas* frames this hymn. It appears once in the first verse, as the instrument of praise, and then four times in the last, as the whole of it — five occurrences, four of them in the closing line. Between them lies everything the household wants: protection near and far, a share in the contest, food that does not run out. The hymn spends twelve verses on what it needs and one verse on bowing, and it is the bowing verse that changed metre.

That last verse is the reason this sūkta stays in use. *Namo mahadbhyo namo arbhakebhyaḥ* — to the great and to the small. Any observance names some deities and passes over others, and the Ṛgveda's own arrangement is frankly unequal: the Anukramaṇī assigns 218 of the 1,028 sūktas to Indra alone and 186 to Agni alone, while Rudra alone has three. The final verse of this hymn is where that inequality is acknowledged from inside — homage to the small ones too, and a fear of slighting a greater one by omission. It is the same instinct that puts a general *namas* at the end of a pūjā after the named invocations are done, and the same instinct behind *yajāma devān yadi śaknavāma*: we will worship as far as we are able, and we know that is not all the way.

The graded request of verse 5 is worth keeping too. Highest *vājas*, middle ones, and *vasu* that is *antama*, nearest — the wealth within reach. A reader who has heard petitionary prayer described as greed can look at the order here: the hymn asks for the far things first and then, without embarrassment, for the near ones.

One curiosity for the collector. *Jarābodha* in verse 10 — the one whom praise wakes — occurs exactly once in the entire Ṛgveda, here. And *citrabhānu*, of dazzling light, in verse 6, occurs eight times corpus-wide; three of those eight fall in maṇḍala 1, and they are given to three different gods: to Indra at [[1.3]].4, to Agni here, and to Savitṛ at [[1.35]].4. The epithet is not a possession of any one of them.
27.disagreements:
Verse 10 is where the readings separate hardest. Sāyaṇa treats *jarābodha* as a description — awakened (*bodha*) by praise (*jarā*) — and equates the *rudra* of the same line with Agni in his fierce aspect, *krūrāya agnaye*. Wilson follows in substance but keeps Jarābodha as a name and renders the rest as "the worshipper offers agreeable laudation to the terrible (Agni)". Griffith keeps neither, giving "Help, thou who knowest lauds, this work, this eulogy to Rudra, him Adorable in every house" — which leaves Rudra standing as Rudra.

The opening simile divides them as well. Wilson expands it into a gloss — Agni scatters our foes "like a horse (who brushes off flies with) his tail" — where Griffith says only "like a long-tailed steed" and leaves the point of comparison alone.

The final verse produces two different endings. Wilson: "may I not omit the praise of the elder divinities", a fear of leaving someone out. Griffith: "no better prayer than this, ye Gods, acknowledge", which turns the line into a claim for the prayer just made. The padapāṭha has *mā jyāyasaḥ śaṃsam ā vṛkṣi devāḥ*, and Wilson's reading follows the words more closely.

Sāyaṇa adds that *navyāṃsaṃ gāyatram* in verse 4 means the newest gāyatrī verses — the hymn describing itself.

28.title: Indra at the Mortar — the Ulūkhala's Only Hymn
28.synthesis:
Nine verses, and for the first four the hymn does not describe Indra at all. It describes a kitchen.

*Yatra grāvā pṛthubudhna ūrdhvo bhavati sotave* — where the broad-based stone stands up for the pressing — *ulūkhalasutānām aved u indra jalgulaḥ*: there, Indra, gulp down what the mortar has pressed. The second verse: where the two pressing-boards are made like two haunches. The third: where the woman practises the down-stroke and the up-stroke. The fourth: where they bind the churning-staff with cords as though to rein in a horse. Four times *yatra*, four times the same refrain, and each *yatra* points at one more piece of equipment or one more pair of hands. The god is being told where to come by being shown the working parts.

The third of those four is the one to notice. *Yatra nārī apacyavam upacyavaṃ ca śikṣate* — where the woman learns, or masters, the going-down and the coming-up. Whatever the motion is, a woman is doing it, and the verb is one of trained skill rather than mere labour. The Ṛgveda does not often let us watch a rite being made rather than performed.

At the fifth verse the addressee changes without warning. The hymn stops speaking to Indra and speaks to the mortar. *Yac cid dhi tvaṃ gṛhe-gṛhe ulūkhalaka yujyase* — if indeed you are yoked in house after house, little mortar, then sound out here as brightly as you can, loud as the drum of men who are winning. The vocative is a diminutive, and it is affectionate. The scale of the claim is domestic: *gṛhe-gṛhe*, in every house. Whatever the great rites do with soma, this instrument is in ordinary kitchens, and the hymn asks it to make the noise of a victory.

The sixth keeps talking to it, and raises its title: *uta sma te vanaspate vāto vi vāty agram* — and over your top, lord of the forest, the wind blows. The mortar is addressed by the name of the standing tree it was cut from, as though the wind still moved in its crown. Then: press out soma for Indra to drink, O mortar.

The seventh and eighth take the pair of them, mortar and pestle, together. *Āyajī vājasātamā* — the two that draw the offering, the best winners of *vāja* — up there they gape wide like two bay horses champing at fodder. And in the eighth they are *vanaspatī*, two lords of the forest, lofty, asked to press with lofty pressers a sweet draught for Indra today. Wooden implements have become a team of horses, then a pair of gods, then a pair of colleagues working beside the human pressers.

The ninth verse ends the hymn by putting things away. Bring up what remains in the cups; pour the soma onto the *pavitra*, the filter; set the residue down on the ox-hide. No praise, no petition, no closing benediction — a set of instructions for what to do with the leftovers. The hymn began at the moment the stone was raised and ends at the moment the vessels are cleared, and the god was called in the middle of the work rather than before or after it.
28.practice:
This is the only sūkta in the Ṛgveda addressed to the ulūkhala. The Anukramaṇī assigns verses 5–6 to *ulūkhalam* and 7–8 to *ulūkhalamusale*, the mortar and pestle as a pair, and those four verses are the whole of it — the word occurs six times in the collection, all six in this hymn. The stone pressers, the *grāvāṇaḥ*, do better: three whole sūktas belong to them ([[10.76]], [[10.94]], [[10.175]]) and one verse more at 7.104.17. The wooden mortar of an ordinary house gets these four verses and nothing else in the collection.

That matters for what a Hindu is being shown here. The instruments of the rite are not props. They are addressed in the vocative, given the title *vanaspati* that belongs to the standing tree, and asked to do something — to sound, to press. The same instinct is alive in every household that does āyudha-pūjā, that will not step over a book or a tool, that treats the implements of work as receiving honour rather than merely bearing it. This hymn is the oldest surviving instance of that instinct in the tradition, and it is directed at a kitchen mortar.

The domestic register is stated by the text itself. *Gṛhe-gṛhe*, house by house, in verse 5 — the mortar is not a temple object. And verse 3 puts a woman at the centre of the pressing, learning the stroke. Whatever the elaborate soma rite later became, this hymn locates its sound in a place where food is made.

There is one more thing here worth keeping. The last verse does not end in praise. It ends in cleaning up: what is left goes on the filter, and the residue on the ox-hide. A rite that has a correct way of finishing, down to the disposal of remnants, is a rite that treats its own conclusion as part of itself. Anyone who has been taught not to leave the lamp burning untended, or how the tīrtha is to be given and taken, recognises the instruction.
28.disagreements:
Verse 3 is the sharpest division in the hymn, and it decides what the reader sees. Sāyaṇa reads *apacyavam upacyavam* as going out of and into the hall (*śālā*), so Wilson has "the housewife repeats egress from and ingress into (the sacrificial chamber)". Griffith reads the same words as the motion of the implement: "There where the woman marks and leans the pestle's constant rise and fall." One gives a woman walking in and out; the other gives a woman pounding.

Sāyaṇa is careful to say that it is not the wooden objects that are addressed but the divinities presiding over the mortar and pestle. He also glosses *vanaspati* as a large tree used by metonymy for the mortar, and identifies the *adhiṣavaṇya* of verse 2 as two shallow vessels for receiving the juice. On the closing verse he supplies a whole procedure — the remnants in the vessels are placed on a cart, carried off, and cast upon the *pavitra*, two or three blades of kuśa serving as a filter, or else strained through goat's hair — and he attaches the verse to a Hariścandra, a priest or a divinity of that name. Neither translation follows him on that last identification.

Wilson and Griffith agree closely on verse 5's *dundubhi*, the drum of conquerors, and on verse 7's two bay horses champing.

29.title: Indra Asked Seven Times to Make Us Spoken Of
29.synthesis:
Seven verses, and five lines of every one of them are the same five lines. *Ā tū na indra śaṃsaya goṣv aśveṣu śubhriṣu sahasreṣu tuvīmagha* — bring us, Indra, to be well spoken of in cattle, in horses, in shining things, in thousands, O richly bountiful. Whatever the individual verse has just said, it lands in that. The hymn is in paṅkti, one of only twelve sūktas in the whole Ṛgveda set in that metre alone, and the shape of the metre is what makes the refrain possible: two fresh lines and then the fixed five.

What the first verse says before falling into the refrain sets the whole tone. *Yac cid dhi satya somapā anāśastā iva smasi* — even though, O true one, O soma-drinker, we are as if *anāśasta*, unpraised, of no account. And then the refrain asks him to *śaṃsaya*, to make us spoken of. The two words are built on the same root, √śaṃs, to speak, to declare. The hymn opens by admitting it has no standing and then, seven times, asks for exactly the thing it has just said it lacks. Nothing in the English shows this; it is visible only when the words are separated.

The second verse gives the god the epithets that answer the admission: *śiprin*, of the strong jaws, *vājānāṃ pate*, lord of the strengths, *śacīvaḥ*, of effective power — yours is the wondrous doing. If we are nothing, you are the one who is something.

Then the hymn turns, and the remaining five verses are all removals. The third asks him to put two watchers to sleep: *ni ṣvāpaya mithudṛśā sastām abudhyamāne*, lull to sleep the two who look at each other, let them lie unwaking. The fourth generalises it into a single clean opposition — *sasantu tyā arātayo bodhantu śūra rātayaḥ*, let those ungenerosities sleep, let the generosities wake, O hero. The same verb pair, sleep and wake, applied first to a particular menace and then to a whole class of them. It is the hymn's one piece of architecture and it takes two verses.

The fifth turns to noise. Crush the braying ass, Indra, that brays with that ugly sound. The sixth asks that the wind fly far away from the wood on its crooked, whirling course. The seventh: strike down every one who shouts around us, and destroy the *kṛkadāśu* — a word nobody has securely identified. Three verses in a row against things that make a bad noise, and after each of them the refrain asks to be well spoken of.

That is the hymn's real subject, and it is not cattle. Somebody is talking, and the talk is bad — an ass braying, a crowd shouting around, two figures watching who should be made to sleep. The refrain's request is for the opposite kind of speech. The wealth named in it, cattle and horses and thousands, is the form the good report would take, not the thing wanted. What the household wants is to stop being *anāśasta* and to be *śaṃsita* instead: to have its name said well, where it can hear it.
29.practice:
The refrain is the whole method here, and it is the method a Hindu already uses. Five lines repeated seven times, with only two lines changing — that is how a *japa* works, how a stotra with a fixed *pada* works, how the *svāhā* falls at the end of every offering in a homa. The variable part carries the occasion; the fixed part carries the intention. This sūkta is the shape in its earliest surviving form, and it is worth noticing that the fixed part is the request and the variable part is the complaint. The complaint changes each time. What is asked for does not.

*Anāśasta* in the first verse is the honest thing in this hymn. It means unpraised, uncelebrated, of no reputation. A household says, before it says anything else, that it currently counts for nothing — and then asks the god not for goods but for standing. Cattle, horses, bright things, thousands: these appear in the refrain as the *medium* of the good report, the visible form reputation takes in that society. Anyone who has watched a family measure itself against its neighbours by what is visible at a wedding will recognise the anxiety exactly.

The third and fourth verses are also where a reader should be careful with themselves. Asking that enemies be put to sleep, that an ass be crushed, that a shouter be struck down — this is a hymn of hostility, and the tradition has not hidden it. The Ṛgveda contains prayer of this kind and does not apologise for it. What the fourth verse does, though, is turn the personal grudge into a general principle: let *arāti*, ungenerosity, sleep, and let *rāti*, giving, wake. The enemy has become a quality rather than a person, and that shift, inside one verse of the same hymn, is the part worth carrying.

Among the Ṛgveda's 1,028 sūktas, only twelve are set in paṅkti alone, and three of those twelve are in maṇḍala 1 — this hymn, [[1.80]] and [[1.81]]. If the five-line refrain here feels unusual, that is because it is.
29.disagreements:
Verse 3 has no agreed referent. Sāyaṇa supplies one: the two who look at each other are the *yamadūtyau*, the two female messengers of Yama, and *mithudṛśā* means looking at one another after the manner of twins. Wilson prints that identification in brackets; Griffith declines it entirely — "Lull thou asleep, to wake no more, the pair who on each other look" — and leaves the pair unnamed. The padapāṭha gives only *mithudṛśā sastām abudhyamāne*, a dual, with no clue to who they are.

Verse 5 turns on why an ass. Sāyaṇa explains that the enemy praises with speech that is really abuse, *nindārūpayā vācā*, and is therefore called an ass, because an ass makes a harsh sound one cannot bear to hear. Both translators keep the ass and the discordant braying.

Verses 6 and 7 defeat both translators in the same way. Wilson's *kuṇḍṛṇācī* is an "adverse breeze with crooked course"; Griffith's is "the tempest in a circling course". Wilson's *kṛkadāśu* becomes "every one that does us injury"; Griffith's, "him who in secret injures us". Neither is translating a known word, and the readings should be taken as guesses honestly made.
29.note: refrain verified identical in all 7 verses of the padapāṭha; anāśastāḥ / śaṃsaya both √śaṃs; the count of paṅkti-only sūktas (12) taken from all ten Anukramaṇī files

30.title: Indra Called Friend, Then the Aśvins and Uṣas
30.synthesis:
Twenty-two verses: sixteen to Indra, three to the Aśvins, three to Uṣas. The long first movement is not a catalogue of exploits but an argument about what kind of relation a man may have with a god, and the word it settles on is *sakhi*, friend.

It starts with drinking. The pressed drops are poured into Indra as into a well (v1); a hundred pure draughts or a thousand mixed with milk run down to him as water runs to low ground (v2); and when room has been made in his belly for the exhilaration, it is like the sea (v3). Three verses of pure capacity. Then the fourth softens the whole thing with a domestic image — you come near to this as a pigeon comes to his mate on the nest — and adds that he attends to our speech. The fifth asks that the man who praises have *vibhūti* and *sūnṛtā*, abundance and true generous speech.

The sixth is a command: *ūrdhvas tiṣṭha na ūtaye*, stand up for our help in this contest, *śatakrato* — and then, remarkably, "about other matters we shall confer together". The seventh states the principle: *yoge-yoge tavastaraṃ vāje-vāje havāmahe sakhāyo indram ūtaye* — at every yoking, in every contest, we, as friends, call the stronger Indra for help. *Yoga* here is the yoking of animals to work, and it is the ordinary word for undertaking something. The eighth admits the condition — *if* he hears our call, let him come with a thousand helps.

The ninth and tenth reach backwards and outwards: I call him from the ancient dwelling, the one whom your father called before me; we ask you, desired by all, much-invoked, friend, good one, on behalf of the singers. Then verses 10, 11 and 12 all carry the vocative *sakhe*. Friend of us your friends, soma-drinker, thunder-armed (v11). So let it be, friend — do as we wish (v12). Three consecutive verses in which the god is addressed by no title higher than friend, immediately after being told to stand up and fight. The thirteenth wants the shared feast, *sadhamāda*, with him, rich and food-full.

Verses 14 and 15 use one image twice: one like you, self-obtained, sets things moving for the singers *akṣaṃ na cakryoḥ*, like the axle in two wheels — and again, you set going the singers' desire *akṣaṃ na śacībhiḥ*, like the axle by its workings. The god as the part that makes the rest turn. The sixteenth, in triṣṭubh where all around it is gāyatrī, breaks the pattern to record a gift: Indra has always won riches with snorting, neighing horses, and a chariot of gold has come.

Then the Aśvins, in three verses that stay with wheels. Come with strength that is horse-rich, cow-rich, gold-rich (v17). Your chariot is yoked for both of you alike, immortal, and it travels in the *samudra* (v18). And the nineteenth: you hold one wheel on the head of the *aghnya* while the other goes round the sky. The axle that turned for Indra has become a vehicle with one wheel down here and one wheel up there.

Uṣas closes the hymn, and she is addressed as a question. *Kas te uṣaḥ kadhapriye bhuje marto amartye* — which mortal enjoys you, O immortal, O lover of praise; whom do you approach? The twenty-first answers on the household's behalf: we have thought of you, from near and from far, ruddy and dappled like a mare. The twenty-second asks her to come with those strengths and settle wealth here — *duhitar divaḥ*, daughter of heaven. The hymn that began with a god's capacity to absorb ends by asking a goddess who she visits, and saying: we were thinking of you.
30.practice:
This is where Uṣas first receives verses of her own in the Ṛgveda. Before 1.30.20 she appears only as half of a pair — *uṣāsānaktā*, Dawn-and-Night, in the Āprī hymn [[1.13]].7. Here she is addressed alone for the first time, and the first thing said to her is a question about whom she goes to. Twenty sūktas in the collection belong to her alone, seven of them running consecutively in maṇḍala 7 (7.75 to 7.81); she is named in twenty-three altogether. For a deity whose arrival every practising Hindu still marks at *prātaḥ sandhyā*, that is a small share, and its position here — the closing movement of a long Indra hymn — is the tradition's first word about her.

The word to carry out of the Indra section is *sakhi*. Verses 7, 10, 11 and 12 call Indra friend, and verse 7 makes it structural: *yoge-yoge... sakhāyo indram ūtaye*, at every undertaking we call him as friends. This is not the register of a subject before a king. The tradition has never had only one posture toward the divine, and the friend-posture is the oldest attested one; what the Bhagavad-gītā later has Arjuna say about having addressed Kṛṣṇa carelessly as *sakhā* has its root here, in a hymn where the household tells a god to stand up and fight and then says, about the rest, we will talk it over.

*Yoga* in verse 7 deserves a note because the word later travels so far. Here it is a yoking — of animals, of effort, the joining that begins a task — set beside *vāja*, the contest. *Yoge-yoge, vāje-vāje*: at each joining, at each contest. The discipline that later takes the name is named for this: the act of harnessing.

And the last three verses are a model for how to address what arrives on its own schedule. Uṣas is not asked to come earlier or to stay. She is told that she was thought of, from near and from far, and asked to leave something behind.
30.disagreements:
Verse 11 produces two entirely different beneficiaries. *Śipriṇīnām* is a feminine genitive plural. Sāyaṇa supplies *gavām*, cows, so Wilson has Indra bestow "(abundance of cows) with projecting jaws" and prints his reasoning in a bracket. Griffith takes the feminines as women: "Friend of our lovely-featured dames". A herd, or the household's wives.

Verse 16 reverses the direction of a gift. Wilson: Indra "has given us as a gift a golden chariot". Griffith: "A car of gold hath he whose deeds are wondrous received from us, and let us too receive it." One has the god giving, the other the god accepting.

Verse 19's *aghnya* is the same word that returns at [[1.37]].5, and the translators are consistent in disagreeing about it. Griffith reads a bull — "High on the forehead of the Bull one chariot wheel ye ever keep" — while Wilson, following Sāyaṇa's sense, gives "on the top of the solid (mountain)".

Sāyaṇa identifies Uṣas as *dyudevatāyāḥ duhitṛ*, daughter of the personified heaven, which is what verse 22 says outright. On verses 14 and 15 he explains the axle simile mechanically — *akṣaṃ na cakryoḥ*, of the two wheels of a car, with the turning supplied — and Wilson follows him into a rather laboured English.

31.title: You, Agni: the First Aṅgiras, and Our Forethought
31.synthesis:
Fifteen of these eighteen verses open with *tvam*, you; in eleven of them the second word is *agne*. Nothing else is repeated, so this is not a refrain — it is a finger held on one point while everything else moves. What moves is the scale of the claim, from the beginning of the world down to a household that has lost its way.

The first verse puts Agni at the origin: you were the first Aṅgiras, a ṛṣi, a god and the auspicious *sakhā* of the gods; in your *vrata* were born the Maruts, *kavis* whose work is knowledge, with gleaming spears. The second holds the same position and adds a puzzle — *dvimātā*, of two mothers, wise, spread through all existence, lying in many places for man. In the third, heaven and earth trembled at the choosing of the *hotā*; you bore the burden and offered to the great ones. The fourth brings him to human hands: you made heaven roar for Manu, and did more for the good-doing Purūravas; when the rubbing of your two parents releases you, they carry you first east and then west.

Then the office. The fifth: you are the bull who increases nourishment, to be called on when the ladle is lifted, and you know the *āhuti* together with the *vaṣaṭ*-cry. The sixth: you carry across the man whose ways are crooked, and in the fight for heroes you strike down the many by means of the few. The seventh: day by day you set the mortal in the highest immortality, and make ease for both kinds of birth. The eighth turns to the singer — make our *kāru* renowned so that he wins wealth; may we better the rite with new work — and asks Heaven and Earth, with the gods, to favour us.

From the ninth the hymn finds its second word and will not let it go. *Pramati* — forethought, the mind that looks ahead on someone's behalf. Be wakeful, a god among gods, *tanūkṛt*, body-maker, and *pramati* for the singer (v9). *Tvam agne pramatis tvaṃ pitāsi naḥ* — you are our forethought, you are our father, you are the maker of vitality, and we are your kin (v10). You are called the *pramati* even of the weak, a father, and you teach the simple man and point out the directions (v14). And in the sixteenth, *āpiḥ pitā pramatiḥ somyānām* — the kinsman, the father, the forethought of those who press soma. Four occurrences, each time paired with fatherhood.

Between them the hymn stays domestic. The eleventh: the gods made you the first *āyu* for man, lord of Nahuṣa's house, and made Iḷā the instructress of Manu. The twelfth: guard our patrons and our own bodies, watching unblinking in your *vrata*. The thirteenth is quietly the tenderest thing in the hymn — kindled four-eyed for the man who has no quiver, you take to heart even the poor man's *mantra*. The fifteenth: you guard the man who has given the *dakṣiṇā* like well-stitched armour on every side, and the man who keeps good food in his house and makes ease there is the likeness of heaven.

Then the sixteenth asks for something none of the preceding fifteen prepared. *Imām agne śaraṇiṃ mīmṛṣo naḥ, imam adhvānaṃ yam agāma dūrāt* — forgive us this going-wrong, this road we have travelled far along. Only after that does it return the titles: kinsman, father, forethought, and *ṛṣikṛt martyānām*, maker of ṛṣis among mortals. The seventeenth asks him to come as he came for Manu, for Aṅgiras, for Yayāti, and seat the divine folk on the *barhis*. The eighteenth ends without a demand: grow by this *brahman*, which we made according to our power and according to our knowledge — a formula that concedes both may be small — and unite us with a *sumati* that brings *vāja*.
31.practice:
The hymn's own word for what a household wants from Agni is *pramati*, and it is not one of the usual requests. Not wealth, not protection, not victory — forethought. Something that looks ahead on your behalf. Verses 9, 10, 14 and 16 each name it, and each time the word sits beside *pitā*, father. Verse 14 is exact about the range: *ādhrasya cit pramatir ucyase pitā*, you are called the forethought even of the weak. This is what a parent is, described from the inside — the one whose thinking about tomorrow you are inside of, whether or not you know it.

Verse 13 belongs beside it. Agni is kindled *aniṣaṅgāya*, for the man without a quiver, the one who cannot defend himself, and *kīreś cin mantraṃ manasā vanoṣi tam* — you take to heart even the poor man's *mantra*. A tradition that elaborates its rites to enormous expense keeps, in its own oldest layer, the statement that the unarmed and the poor are heard. That verse is the standing answer to anyone who is sure that Vedic religion was only for those who could afford it.

The sixteenth verse is where this hymn earns its place in a manual. *Śaraṇim* — a straying, a going-wrong — and the road already travelled a long way down. It is not a request to be spared consequences, and there is no bargaining. Just: forgive this, and then, immediately, the titles of relation — kinsman, father, forethought. The order matters. The confession is followed not by penance but by the naming of the relationship that survives it.

Verse 5's *vaṣaṭkṛti* is the technical detail worth holding: Agni knows the offering *together with* the utterance that accompanies it. The word said as the ghee is poured is part of the offering, not decoration on it — which is why the utterance is fixed, and why anyone who has learned even one *homa* has learned the syllable before learning anything else.

And the last verse sets the honest limit. We made this *brahman* *śaktī vā yat te cakṛma vidā vā* — by whatever power we had, or whatever knowledge. Both are named, and both are admitted to be finite.
31.disagreements:
Verse 3 splits on whether Mātariśvan is a person. Griffith takes the dative as a name: "To Mātariśvan first thou, Agni, wast disclosed, and to Vivasvan." Sāyaṇa reads it as position rather than person — first *in* or *on* the wind — citing the sequence *agnir vāyur ādityaḥ* in which Agni precedes Vāyu, and Wilson follows him with "pre-eminent over the wind".

Verse 16's last words are the largest divergence in the hymn. The padapāṭha gives *bhṛmir asi ṛṣikṛt martyānām*, and the grammar analyses *ṛṣi-kṛt* as maker of ṛṣis. Griffith moves toward that — "who speedest nigh and who inspirest mortals". Wilson, following Sāyaṇa, reverses the direction entirely: *ṛṣikṛt* becomes becoming present through desire for the oblation, so Agni "makes himself visible to mortals" rather than making ṛṣis of them.

Sāyaṇa supplies most of the hymn's proper names. *Dvimātā* in verse 2 is either the two fire-sticks or the maker of the two, heaven and earth — he offers both and chooses neither. Purūravas in verse 4 is the son of Budha, who first produced fire by attrition and employed it in three fires. Nahuṣa in verse 11 is the son of Āyu, and Iḷā is *dharmopadeśakartrī*, she who instructs in duty. On verse 15's *jīvayāja* he gives three glosses at once — a sacrifice with a living offering, that by which life is supported, and the honouring of living priests with *dakṣiṇā*.

32.title: Indra Slays Vṛtra — the Waters Freed, a King Made
32.synthesis:
*Indrasya nu vīryāṇi pra vocam* — now I will proclaim the *vīryas* of Indra. The hymn announces itself as a telling, and then tells one thing, once, from four or five angles, and arrives somewhere the first verse gave no warning of.

The first verse compresses the whole: he slew the *ahi*, he bored out the waters after it, he split open the bellies of the mountains. The second sets the scene and supplies the weapon — he slew the *ahi* lying on the mountain, and Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned the roaring bolt for him; then the waters, lowing like cattle, went straight down to the sea. The third gives the drinking that precedes the deed: bull-like he chose soma and drank of the pressing at the *trikadrukas*, and Maghavan took up the missile and struck the first-born of the *ahis*. The fourth names the consequence that is not usually noticed: when you undid the *māyās* of the *māyins*, then, generating Sūrya and Dyaus and Uṣas, you found no rival at all. The sun, the sky and the dawn come into being in that verse. This is not only a rescue; it is a cosmogony.

Verses five to ten are the corpse. The bolt struck, and like tree-trunks felled by the axe the *ahi* lies pressed against the earth (v5). He challenged Indra like a bad drunk who is no warrior, and did not survive the meeting of weapons; broken, the *indraśatru* was crushed (v6). *Apād ahasto apṛtanyad indram* — footless and handless, he made war on Indra, who struck the bolt down on his nape; an ox wanting to be the equal of a bull, Vṛtra lay flung apart (v7). The waters, rising in spirit, go over him where he lies like a broken reed; the *ahi* has come to lie at the feet of the very waters he had encompassed (v8). His mother's vigour ebbed and Indra cast the weapon down on her; the mother above, the son below, and Dānu lies like a cow beside her calf (v9). And in the tenth his body has no name left: laid in the middle of channels that never stand still, the waters carry off Vṛtra's hidden body, and the *indraśatru* lies down into long darkness. Six verses on a thing that is already dead, and each takes something further away from it — its posture, its limbs, its mother, finally its name.

Then the reckoning of what was gained. The waters had stood shut in, wives of the Dāsa, guarded by the *ahi*, like cows held by the Paṇi; and having slain Vṛtra, he opened the closed hole (v11). The twelfth counts the winnings: you won the cows, hero, you won the soma, you released the seven rivers to run. The thirteenth: nothing helped him, not lightning, not thunder, not the mist and hail he scattered — when Indra and the *ahi* fought, Maghavan won for all time to come.

And then the fourteenth, which is why this hymn is not a boast. *Aher yātāraṃ kam apaśya indra hṛdi yat te jaghnuṣo bhīr agacchat* — what avenger of the *ahi* did you see, Indra, that fear came into your heart when you had killed him, and you crossed ninety-nine streams like a frightened hawk? The victor runs. Nothing in the preceding thirteen verses hints at it, no explanation follows, and the fear is placed in the heart at the moment after the killing, not before it.

The fifteenth then makes him king, and the terms are civil rather than martial. Indra is king of what moves and what stands, of the tame and the horned, *sa id u rājā kṣayati carṣaṇīnām* — as king he rules over the peoples, and he holds them all as the felly holds the spokes. A wheel does not compress its spokes. It keeps them apart at a fixed distance and turns because of them.
32.practice:
This is the hymn the tradition means when it says *vṛtrahan*. Indra's standing epithet, the one carried into every later stotra and every list of names, is fixed by these fifteen verses. Of the Ṛgveda's 1,028 sūktas the Anukramaṇī gives 218 to Indra alone and names him in 274 — more than any other deity, more than Agni's 186 — and this is the sūkta that says why.

What it is about is the release of what was being held. Waters stood shut behind a closure; something living lay across the opening; the opening was forced and they ran. Every level on which that has been read is present in the text itself and none is imposed: rains withheld by cloud and let down onto fields; rivers unfrozen; cattle shut in a raider's pen; and the fourth verse's claim that Sūrya, Dyaus and Uṣas came into being at the same stroke, which no naturalistic reading exhausts. The fifth verse is the sign that *vṛtra* is a description as much as a name: Indra slays *vṛtram vṛtrataram*, Vṛtra who is more Vṛtra than the rest — a comparative formed on the name itself, which only works if the word means something. Whatever else the being is, it is the obstruction, and the obstruction has a superlative form.

Two verses are the ones to keep for a life rather than for a cosmology.

Verse 14: fear entering the heart of the one who has just won, and the winner running from nothing anyone can name. The tradition did not edit this out, and it stands three lines before the coronation. A reader who has ever finished the thing they were most afraid of and then, that night, felt worse rather than better, has a verse in the Ṛgveda for it.

Verse 15: the image of rule the hymn finally settles on is a wheel. *Arān na nemiḥ pari tā babhūva* — as the felly is around the spokes, so he encompasses them all. Not a fist closing, not a yoke. The rim holds every spoke at its own distance and cannot turn without them. It is a description of authority that a household, a teacher or a ruler could be measured against, and the Ṛgveda puts it in the last line of its greatest battle hymn.
32.disagreements:
The whole hymn divides on one question, and it is the most consequential divergence in maṇḍala 1. Sāyaṇa reads it naturalistically: Vṛtra, also called Ahi, is a condensed accumulation of vapour shut up by a cloud, and Indra with his bolt divides the mass so the rain can descend and moisten the fields; *ahi* and *vṛtra*, he says flatly, are synonyms of *megha*, cloud. Wilson follows him into the English — "he clove the cloud; he cast the waters down (to earth)". Griffith keeps the story a story: "He slew the Dragon, then disclosed the waters." Every verse reads differently under the two, and both are inside the tradition's range.

*Indraśatru*, at verses 6 and 10, occurs twice in the whole Ṛgveda and both times here. The compound admits two constructions — Indra's foe, or the one whose slayer is Indra — and both translators take the first.

Verse 6's *rujānāḥ pipiṣe* is unsettled. Sāyaṇa has Vṛtra grinding the rivers or breaking down their banks as he falls, which Wilson prints; Griffith has him crushing "the shattered forts in falling".

On verse 3's *trikadruka* Sāyaṇa names three rites, *jyotis*, *gauḥ* and *āyus*; Griffith reads three beakers. On verse 9 he derives Dānu either from √do, to cut, or from Dānu the wife of Kaśyapa. On verse 14 he offers the only explanation of Indra's fear that anyone offers: uncertainty whether he should destroy Vṛtra or not.
32.note: ahan ×5 and the ahi/vṛtra distribution counted from the padapāṭha; indra-śatruḥ verified as occurring only at 1.32.6 and 1.32.10 across all ten padapāṭha files; Indra ascription counts from all ten Anukramaṇī files

33.title: Indra Fights the Riteless — 'Be No Paṇi to Us'
33.synthesis:
Where [[1.32]] told one story, this hymn lists many, and what holds them together is not an enemy but a category. The people Indra fights here are the *ayajvānaḥ* and the *avratāḥ* — those who do not sacrifice and those who keep no *vrata*.

It opens as a journey. *Ā ita ayāma upa gavyanta indram* — come, let us go up to Indra, wanting cattle; he will increase the good *pramati* that guides us; surely the unmarred one will turn toward us the far mark of this wealth in cows. The second verse gives the going a body: I fly to the wealth-giver, unopposed, as a falcon to his own cherished nest, honouring Indra with the highest songs.

Then the third, which is the hymn's most human line. He has slung his quivers on, with his whole host; the lord drives off the cattle of whom he pleases; heaping up much that is good — *mā paṇir bhūr asmad adhi pravṛddha*, do not be a Paṇi to us, O grown-great. A *paṇi* is a trader, a driver of hard bargains, and one hymn earlier the same word named those who held the cows shut in ([[1.32]].11). The worshipper is asking the god not to charge too much.

From the fourth verse the enemy is defined by what he does not do. You slew the wealthy Dasyu with your club, going alone though you had helpers; from the ridge of your bow they scattered in every direction, and the *ayajvānaḥ*, the ancient ones, went to their ruin (v4). They turned their heads and fled, the non-sacrificers contending with the sacrificers, when you blew the *avratān*, the vowless, out of heaven and earth (v5). They fought the army of the blameless one; the *navagva* peoples set themselves in array; and like bullocks matched against bulls, cast out and knowing it, they ran down the steep ways from Indra (v6). The seventh finishes them and shows how little their mood mattered: you fought them weeping and laughing alike, at the far edge of the *rajas*, and burnt the Dasyu down from heaven — and you welcomed the praise of the man who pressed and sang.

The eighth is a strange, glittering verse: making a covering over the earth, adorned with gold and with jewels, they did not get past Indra even hurrying, and he set his watchers around them with Sūrya. The ninth states the method and it is not a weapon: since you hold both worlds within your greatness, you blew away the Dasyu *amanyamānān abhi manyamānair brahmabhiḥ* — the unminding, by means of *brahman*s that mind. The tenth: they who reached no end of heaven or earth and could not surround the wealth-giver with their *māyās* — Indra made the bolt his yokefellow and with light milked the cows out of the darkness.

The eleventh returns to water: the waters ran according to their *svadhā*, their own nature, while he grew in the midst of the navigable streams; then Indra, with a mind gathered to one point, struck him with the strongest blow. The twelfth pierces the strongholds of Ilībiśa and splits the horned Śuṣṇa. The thirteenth breaks open forts and flings the bolt at Vṛtra, and — *pra svāṃ matim atirat śāśadānaḥ* — carried his own intention through.

Then the hymn stops fighting and starts naming people. *Āvaḥ kutsam*, you helped Kutsa, in whom you delighted; you helped Daśadyu fighting; the dust from the hooves reached heaven, and Śvitrā's son stood up to master men (v14). And you helped Śama among Tugra's folk in the winning of the field, Maghavan — long they had stood there before it was done (v15). *Āvaḥ*, you helped, opens the last two verses and appears three times in them, after standing once in verse 7. The hymn about a war ends as a list of individuals who were given a hand.
33.practice:
The line to take from this hymn is the one addressed to the god as though he were at a market stall. *Mā paṇir bhūr asmat* — do not be a Paṇi to us. Do not drive a hard bargain. The worshipper has just described Indra armed and taking whatever cattle he pleases, and the request that follows is not for mercy but for fair dealing. A tradition often described from outside as transactional turns out to be, in its own words, worried about the transaction being unfair — and worried on the god's side of it, not the man's.

The second thing is harder and should be met rather than avoided. This hymn divides the world into those who sacrifice and those who do not, and asks that the second group be destroyed. *Ayajvānaḥ*, *avratāḥ* — the non-offerers, the vowless — appear in verses 4, 5 and 9, and they are the enemy as such. Nothing is said about their beliefs. The line drawn is between people who keep an observance and people who keep none. Whatever a modern reader makes of that, it is worth seeing clearly that the Ṛgveda's earliest sense of an outsider is ritual rather than doctrinal, and that the Sanskrit for it names an omission, not an error.

Then verse 9, which reaches this project's own question. Indra blows away the enemy *amanyamānān abhi manyamānair brahmabhiḥ* — the ones who do not mind, by means of prayers that do mind. The words are built on √man, to think. What the hymn attributes the victory to is not the loudness of the recitation but whether there is a mind inside it. That is the sharpest statement in this range of hymns about what makes an utterance work, and it is made in passing, in the middle of a battle.

And the ending is worth the reading. After twelve verses of destruction the hymn's last two verses are *āvaḥ*, you helped — Kutsa, Daśadyu, Śvitrā's son, Śama among Tugra's people. Named men, helped in particular fights, some of whom stood a long time before it was finished. Whatever the cosmic scale of verses 4 to 13, the hymn chooses to close on individuals.
33.disagreements:
Verse 9 is where Sāyaṇa says something no translation carries, and it is the most interesting note in the hymn. He glosses *amanyamānān abhi manyamānair brahmabhiḥ* as meaning that those *yajamānas* who merely repeat the mantras without understanding their meaning are nevertheless protected by, or reap the benefit of, those mantras. The verse is read as a concession to the uncomprehending reciter rather than as a claim about comprehension. Wilson prints the concession — "with the prayers which are repeated on behalf of those who do not comprehend them" — while Griffith reads it socially instead: "those who worship not with those who worship".

Several proper names are disputed between the two. Wilson's *sanakāḥ* in verse 4 is a group of people, "the Sanakas, the neglecters of sacrifice"; Griffith's is an adjective, "the ancient riteless ones". Wilson's *navagvāḥ* in verse 6 are "men of holy lives", following Sāyaṇa's *kṣitayaḥ navagvāḥ*, men whose practices were commendable, possibly the Aṅgirasas who offered for nine months; Griffith keeps Navagvas as a proper name.

Sāyaṇa identifies the Dasyu of verse 4 with Vṛtra and glosses *arya* in verse 3 as *svāmin*, master, taking it as Indra himself. He also explains *mā paṇir bhūḥ* directly: Indra is asked not to demand too high a price from his worshippers.
33.note: āvaḥ counted in the padapāṭha at vv 7, 14 (twice) and 15; ayajvānaḥ vv 4,5 and avratān v5; brahma-bhiḥ v9

34.title: The Aśvins Thrice — Three Journeys, Three Medicines
34.synthesis:
This hymn has one word and it says it thirty-six times. Out of 234 words in twelve verses, thirty-six are built on the stem for three — *triḥ* alone twenty-one times, and *trayaḥ*, *tisraḥ*, *trī*, *tredhā*, *tridhātu*, *trivṛt* filling out the rest. Every verse but the tenth carries at least one. This is not decoration. The Aśvins are twins, and everything they are given here is threefold; the hymn is working out what a pair does with a number that will not divide in two.

The first verse asks for the pattern and gives the reason at once: be aware of us three times today; wide is your going and your giving; your holding is like a garment in frost, and you are to be drawn near by the thoughtful. The second describes the vehicle — three are the fellies of your honey-bearing chariot, three the props set on it to hold, and thrice by night you drive and thrice by day. The third puts the three into the rite: thrice in one day, O removers of blame, sprinkle our *yajña* with sweetness, and thrice swell strength-bearing food for us, at evening and at dawn.

The fourth turns it toward the house: thrice come to our dwelling, thrice to the man who keeps the vow, thrice teach threefold to the one who deserves help; thrice bring what gladdens; thrice swell our nourishment. The fifth is the densest — six occurrences in one verse. Thrice bring *rayi*; thrice at the divine service; thrice favour our *dhī*s; thrice good fortune, thrice glories — and the daughter of Sūrya has mounted your three-standing chariot.

The sixth is the one the tradition kept. *Trir no aśvinā divyāni bheṣajā trir pārthivāni trir u dattam adbhyaḥ* — thrice give us the heavenly remedies, thrice the earthly, thrice those from the waters; give favour and *śaṃ-yoḥ*, wellbeing and safety, to my son, and bring threefold ease, O lords of splendour. The medicines are sorted by where they come from: sky, earth, water. The seventh keeps the pattern and widens it — thrice worshipful day by day, you have laid the threefold about the earth, and you come from three distances as breath comes to bodies.

The eighth pushes the number outward into the world: thrice with the rivers of seven mothers; three are the troughs, the oblation made threefold; above the three earths you move, guarding the vault set fast through days and nights. Then the ninth turns and asks. *Kva trī cakrā trivṛto rathasya, kva trayo vandhuro ye sanīḷāḥ* — where are the three wheels of your threefold chariot, where the three seats fixed together, and when is the yoking of the strong ass by which you come? After eight verses of confident threes, the hymn does not know where the chariot is.

The tenth verse is the only one without the number, and it is the one where the guests actually arrive: come, Nāsatyas, the oblation is poured, drink the sweetness with mouths that know sweetness — and before dawn Savitṛ sends your bright ghee-laden chariot toward *ṛta*. Where the counting stops, the coming happens. The eleventh brings company and asks for the four things this hymn wants: come with the thrice-eleven gods, lengthen our life, wipe off our flaws, hold off hatred, and be *sacābhuvā*, those who are alongside. The twelfth closes with the chariot again — bring us, in the threefold car, wealth that is near at hand and rich in heroes; I call you, who hear, for help.
34.practice:
The Aśvins are the physicians, and verse 6 is the tradition's oldest statement of what a remedy is. *Divyāni bheṣajā*, *pārthivāni*, and those *adbhyaḥ*, from the waters: heavenly, earthly, and of the waters. Medicine is classified by origin, and all three sources are asked for at once. Anyone who has been given both a *cūrṇa* and an instruction about which water to take it with, and told when in the day to take it, is inside a very old habit of thought.

The same verse contains the word that made this hymn matter to Āyurveda: *tridhātu*, the three constituents. Read that way, verse 6 asks for the threefold to be brought into balance in a son's body — and that is exactly what the classical medicine means by *tridoṣa*. Whether the Ṛgveda means the three humours here is disputed, and the disagreement is recorded below; but the word is in the verse, the deities addressed are the healers, and the request is on behalf of a child's health. This is where the line begins, whatever its later shape.

*Śaṃ-yoḥ* in the same verse is worth keeping in the ear. Two syllables that mean, roughly, wellbeing and freedom from harm — and they survive as a fixed pair in later benediction. When a blessing is given in two words rather than a sentence, it is usually these.

The Aśvins receive 52 sūktas in their own right across the Ṛgveda and are named in 68 — third among the deities after Indra and Agni, and well ahead of Sarasvatī's 15. That is a large share for a pair who are asked, over and over, for health, long life and safe travel rather than for victory or for wealth. And note what the eleventh verse asks: *pra āyus tāriṣṭam*, lengthen our life; *nir rapāṃsi mṛkṣatam*, wipe off our flaws. The oldest request made of the physicians of the gods is not for a cure. It is for more time and for the removal of what is wrong.

One more thing about the number. The hymn's threes are not mystical arithmetic; they are the shape of the day — evening and morning and midday, named in verse 3. The three pressings of the rite, and the three *sandhyās* a Hindu still keeps, are the same division of time.
34.disagreements:
Verse 6 is where the readings matter most. Sāyaṇa allows that *tridhātu*, three elements, may denote the three humours — wind, bile and phlegm — which is the reading that later medicine took up, and he identifies Śamyu as a son of Bṛhaspati nourished by the Aśvins, so Wilson has "give to my son the prosperity of Śamyu" and "preserve the well-being of the three humours (of the body)". Griffith reads neither: *śaṃ-yoḥ* becomes "favour and health and strength", and *tridhātu* becomes "triple protection". The padapāṭha splits the words as *śam-yoḥ*, two elements, which supports Griffith on that half.

Verse 1's closing simile divides them completely. Wilson: "your union is like that of the shining (day) and dewy (night)". Griffith: "To you, as to a cloak in winter, we cleave close." One reads a cosmic pairing, the other a man pulling a garment tighter.

Sāyaṇa supplies the story behind verse 2 — the Aśvins went to the marriage of Vena with Soma and loaded their chariot — which Griffith reduces to "travels after Soma's loved one". On verse 9 he glosses *trivṛt ratha* geometrically, a chariot with three angles, and confirms that the Aśvins' draught animals are two asses. On verse 7 he identifies "the three" as three altars, for ghee, for animal offerings and for soma. On verse 11 the thrice-eleven are the 33: eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, twelve Ādityas, Prajāpati and Vaṣaṭkāra.

35.title: Savitṛ Gold-Handed — and 'Where Is Sūrya Now?'
35.synthesis:
The first verse calls four times and each call has its own verb. *Hvayāmi agniṃ prathamaṃ svastaye* — I call Agni first, for wellbeing; I call Mitra and Varuṇa here, for help; I call Rātrī, *jagato niveśanīm*, who settles the moving world; I call the god Savitṛ, for aid. Four *hvayāmi*s in one verse, and the fourth is the one the rest of the hymn belongs to.

The second verse picks up the word left behind in the first. Rātrī was she who settles; Savitṛ comes *niveśayan amṛtaṃ martyaṃ ca*, settling both immortal and mortal, turning here through the black *rajas* in a golden chariot, looking at the worlds. The same root, one verse apart, given first to Rātrī and then to him. What the night does for the moving world, he does for gods and men alike. This is not the god of waking that a first-time reader expects.

The third watches him travel: he goes by the downward way and the upward way, with two bright bays; he comes from the far distance driving away all *duritas*, all hard passages. The fourth mounts him: covered with pearls, all-formed, gold-pinned, lofty, *citrabhānu*, of dazzling light — and he takes on power against the black regions. The fifth sees what the chariot does for the people: the dusky white-footed horses have looked out over men, drawing the gold-fronted car, and always the clans and all the worlds stand *savitur daivyasya upasthe*, in the lap of divine Savitṛ.

The sixth stops describing and poses a riddle. Three are the heavens; two are the laps of Savitṛ; one, the hero-conquering, is in Yama's world. The immortal things rest on him as on the axle-pin of a chariot. And then: *iha bravītu ya u tac ciketat* — let the one who has understood that declare it here. The hymn does not claim to have understood it.

The seventh asks the second question, and it is stranger. The *suparṇa*, well-winged, has looked out over the mid-spaces, the deep-stirring *asura*, the good leader — *kva idānīṃ sūryaḥ kaś ciketa* — where is Sūrya now? who has understood? to which heaven has his ray stretched? The sun has been lost track of, and the hymn says so.

The eighth restores what can be counted: he has looked over the eight peaks of the earth, the three waste stretches, the seven rivers; the gold-eyed god has come, setting down desirable treasures for the giver. The ninth is the fullest picture of what he does: the gold-handed, far-moving, goes between heaven and earth, drives away sickness, sets Sūrya on his way, and reaches across the sky through the black *rajas* — the same black *rajas* of verse 2, closing a frame.

The tenth asks him to come, and names what he keeps off: gold-handed, *asura*, good leader, gracious, wealthy — drive away the *rakṣas* and the *yātudhānas*, and the god has taken his stand, *pratidoṣam gṛṇānaḥ*, praised toward evening. The eleventh closes on his roads: your paths, Savitṛ, are ancient, dustless, well made in the mid-space; come by those easy paths, guard us today, and speak for us.

*Hiraṇya* — gold — falls six times across verses 2, 4, 5, 8, 9 and 10: golden chariot, golden pin, golden fore-part, gold-eyed, gold-handed twice. Nothing else in the hymn is repeated at that rate. And in the middle of all that gold sit two flat admissions that nobody knows where the third heaven is or where the sun has gone.
35.practice:
This is the deity of the verse a Hindu says more often than any other. The Gāyatrī — *tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi* — is [[3.62]].10, and the Anukramaṇī assigns verses 10–12 of that sūkta to Savitṛ. The mantra given at the upanayana and repeated at every *sandhyā* is addressed to the god this hymn is about. Anyone who has said it daily for years and never met Savitṛ elsewhere can meet him here, in eleven verses, and find that he is not the sun. Verse 9 has him *veti sūryam*, setting Sūrya in motion, and verse 7 asks where Sūrya has got to. He is the impeller — the one who starts things moving — and the Gāyatrī asks for exactly that: not for light but for the impelling of our *dhīs*.

He is also rarer in the collection than his liturgical weight suggests. Eight sūktas belong to Savitṛ alone across all ten maṇḍalas, and he is named in fourteen. The one verse in the Ṛgveda that outlives all the rest belongs to a god with eight hymns.

Verse 10 fixes the hour. *Pratidoṣam gṛṇānaḥ* — praised toward evening. The impeller is not only a morning deity; the hymn has him invoked as the light goes, driving off what comes with the dark. That is the second *sandhyā*, named in the text.

And the first verse is worth noticing for who else is in it. Agni, Mitra and Varuṇa, Rātrī, Savitṛ — four calls in one verse, and the Anukramaṇī records all four as its deities. Rātrī is named as a deity in only two places in the whole Ṛgveda: here, and [[10.127]]. She gets one line, and what it says is that she is *jagato niveśanī*, the one who brings the moving world to rest — which is the definition of night that anybody's body already knows.

The last thing to carry is the register of verses 6 and 7. *Iha bravītu ya u tac ciketat* — let him who has understood declare it here. *Kva idānīṃ sūryaḥ* — where is the sun now? These are not rhetorical. A hymn that has just described a god's golden chariot in detail turns and says it does not know two large things. The tradition kept both the description and the not-knowing, in the same eleven verses, without treating them as a contradiction.
35.disagreements:
Verse 2 is where the two translators say opposite things, and the padapāṭha settles it. Wilson has Savitṛ "arousing mortal and immortal"; Griffith has him "laying to rest the immortal and the mortal". The form is *ni-veśayan*, and the first verse has just called Rātrī *jagato niveśanīm* — the same root, in a phrase Wilson himself renders "who brings rest to the world". Griffith is consistent where Wilson is not.

Verse 7 divides on *asura*. Sāyaṇa derives it from *asu*, vital breath, and *ra*, giving — hence life-bestowing — and Wilson prints "life-bestowing"; Griffith leaves it as "Asura", so his Savitṛ carries a word later Sanskrit reserves for the enemies of the gods. Sāyaṇa also glosses *suparṇa* not as a bird but as a synonym of *raśmi*, a ray, and Wilson follows: "Suparṇa, (the solar ray)". Griffith keeps a winged being: "He, strong of wing, hath lightened up the regions."

On verse 9 Sāyaṇa states the relation between the two solar deities carefully: though Savitṛ and Sūrya are the same as regards divinity, they are two different forms, and therefore one may go to the other. That is his answer to the puzzle the hymn creates by having Savitṛ send Sūrya on his way.

Verse 6 defeats both. Wilson has one sphere leading men to the dwelling of Yama; Griffith has "in Yama's world is one, the home of heroes". Neither claims to know what the three heavens are, and the verse itself asks for someone who does.
