36.title: Agni for Kaṇva: Stand Erect, and Guard, and Burn
36.synthesis:
Twenty verses in *bṛhatī*, one of only eleven sūktas in the whole Ṛgveda set in that metre alone — a long, uneven line followed by short ones, which suits a hymn that keeps gathering itself and then striking.

The opening third is about choosing. With well-made words we seek Agni, the *yahva* of many god-seeking clans, whom others praise too (v1) — the hymn concedes at once that its addressee is shared. Men have set him down as the increaser of *sahas*; be well-minded today, our helper in the contests (v2). *Pra tvā dūtaṃ vṛṇīmahe hotāraṃ viśvavedasam* — we choose you as messenger, as *hotā*, all-knowing; your rays travel wide and your beams touch the sky (v3). The gods themselves kindle him — Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman kindle the ancient messenger — and the mortal who has given wins all wealth through him (v4). Then the office in full: *mandro hotā gṛhapatir agne dūto viśām asi*, you are the gladdening *hotā*, the lord of the house, the messenger of the clans, and in you all the fixed *vratas* the gods made come together (v5). In you every offering is poured; be gracious today and afterwards (v6). The reverent sit near him, self-ruling, and men kindle him with their *hotrās*, having got past their failures (v7).

The eighth turns aside to a deed: slaying Vṛtra they crossed the two worlds and made the waters a wide dwelling; the bull stood by Kaṇva, brilliant, invoked, and the horse neighed in the fight for cattle. The ninth gives the hearth its instructions — sit down, you are great; blaze, best inviter of gods; send out the ruddy smoke, *miyedhya*, worth looking at.

Then the hymn signs itself. The gods set you here for Manu, and Kaṇva Medhyātithi set you as wealth-winner, and Vṛṣan, and Upastuta (v10); the Agni whom Medhyātithi Kaṇva kindled *ṛtād adhi*, out of *ṛta* — his nourishments shine, and these *ṛcs* and we ourselves magnify him (v11). The twelfth asks him to fill up our riches, since he has kinship among the gods, and to be gracious, for he is great.

From the thirteenth the verbs come in stacks. *Ūrdhva ū ṣu ṇa ūtaye tiṣṭha devo na savitā* — stand up erect for our help, like the god Savitṛ; erect, winner of *vāja*, we call you with unguents and with *vāghats* (v13). Erect, guard us from *aṃhas*, narrowness; burn down with your beacon every devourer; make us erect for moving and for living (v14). *Ūrdhva* four times across those two verses, of Agni and of us alike. Then *pāhi*, guard, three times in one verse: guard us from the *rakṣas*, from the injurer who gives nothing, from the one who would harm and the one who would kill (v15). And strike apart the ungenerous like a club, you whose teeth are heat; let no one who sharpens himself against us through the nights master us (v16).

The last four verses return to names. Agni won heroic power, and good fortune for Kaṇva; he helped the friends, and Medhyātithi, and Upastuta at the winning (v17). With Agni we call from far off Turvaśa, Yadu, Ugradeva; may Agni bring Navavāstva, Bṛhadratha, Turvīti (v18). Manu set you down as light for the endless people, and you have shone for Kaṇva, *ṛtajāta*, born from *ṛta*, anointed, revered by the peoples (v19). And the last verse leaves the household behind entirely: the flames of Agni are fierce, forceful, terrible, *na pratītaye*, not to be approached — burn the sorcerous, burn every devourer, always. A hymn that spent five verses making Agni the gladdening lord of the house ends by saying that nobody can go near him.
36.practice:
*Ūrdhva* is the word to take from this hymn, because of what it does in verse 14. In verse 13 it belongs to Agni — stand up erect, like Savitṛ. In verse 14 it is asked for the household: *kṛdhi na ūrdhvāñ carathāya jīvase*, make us erect, for moving and for living. The same posture requested for Agni and then for the men. Anyone who has watched a lamp being lit and seen the flame straighten has the image; the hymn's request is that people should stand the way the flame does. It is also the plainest thing in the Ṛgveda about why Agni is worshipped upright and why the *yūpa* is set standing.

The second thing is the signature. Kaṇva is named five times — verses 8, 10, 11, 17 and 19 — and Medhyātithi twice, along with Vṛṣan, Upastuta and, in verse 18, six more names of men. The Anukramaṇī gives Ghaura Kaṇva eight consecutive sūktas here, 1.36 to 1.43. This is not an anonymous liturgy; it is a family's fire, named as such, and the hymn says out loud that the same Agni is kindled by others too (v1). A tradition that transmits by lineage is describing itself.

Verse 11 has the phrase that a reader should not walk past: *ṛtād adhi*, kindled out of *ṛta*, and verse 19's *ṛtajātaḥ*, born from *ṛta*. Agni on this household's hearth is described as having its origin in the order of things, not in the sticks that were rubbed. That is the claim that makes a domestic hearth a place where the cosmos can be addressed.

And the closing verse is a caution the tradition keeps everywhere. *Bhīmāsaḥ na pratītaye* — terrible, not to be approached. The same fire that is *gṛhapati*, the lord of the house, in verse 5. Both are true and the hymn puts them twenty verses apart deliberately. It is why Agni is fed at a distance with a ladle, why children are taught how near to stand, and why *agni* is never handled casually in any observance that survives.
36.disagreements:
Verse 13's *ūrdhva* is where Sāyaṇa reaches for the ritual object: erect Agni, he says, is the *yūpa*, the sacrificial post. Neither translator carries that into the English — both keep "stand up erect" — but it explains why the word is repeated four times in two verses.

Verse 8 divides on who did the slaying. The padapāṭha has only *ghnantaḥ vṛtram*, a plural participle with no stated subject, in a hymn to Agni. Wilson supplies one in brackets — "the destroying (deities along with you) have slain Vṛtra" — while Griffith leaves it unassigned: "Vrtra they smote and slew". The deed of [[1.32]] turns up here without an agent.

Verse 7's *hotrābhiḥ* draws Sāyaṇa's longest note in the sūkta, a full list of the seven officiants of the soma rite — the instituting *yajamāna*, the *hotā* who recites the ṛcs, the *udgātā* who chants, the *potā*, the *neṣṭā*, the *brahmā* who oversees, and the one who guards the door, with the *adhvaryu* replacing the *yajamāna*. Wilson prints "(seven) ministrant priests" on that authority; Griffith has simply "with their sacrificial gifts".

On verse 18 Sāyaṇa identifies Turvaśa, Yadu, Ugradeva, Navavāstva, Bṛhadratha and Turvīti as *rājarṣis*, royal sages, with Turvaśa and Yadu the sons of Yayāti. Griffith keeps them as bare names and does not explain who they are.
36.note: ūrdhva ×4 in vv 13-14 and pāhi ×4 in vv 14-15 counted from the padapāṭha; Kaṇva named in vv 8,10,11,17,19; bṛhatī-only sūkta count (11) taken from all ten Anukramaṇī files

37.title: The Maruts Come Loud — 'Who Among You Is Greatest?'
37.synthesis:
This hymn is addressed to a plural and never once slips into a singular. *Vaḥ*, to you, and *eṣām*, of these, fall twelve times across fifteen short gāyatrī verses, and no member of the group is ever named. The Maruts arrive as a *śardhas*, a troop, and the hymn's real question — asked outright in the sixth verse and never answered — is whether such a thing has a chief.

It opens as an instruction to singers. *Krīḷaṃ vaḥ śardho mārutam* — sing forth, O Kaṇvas, to your Marut troop, playful, unrivalled, shining on the chariot. Playing is the first thing said about them. The second gives their birth: they came into being together, self-shining, with the dappled deer, with spears, with *vāśīs*, with gleaming ornaments. Nobody made them; they were born already equipped.

The third verse is the hymn at its best. *Ihaiva śṛṇva eṣāṃ kaśā hasteṣu yad vadān* — I hear it right here, the whips in their hands as they speak; on the march they make something dazzling for themselves. The sound arrives before the troop does, and the poet says he can hear it from where he is standing.

The fourth turns back to the singers: sing the god-given *brahman* to your troop, exultant, of fierce splendour, forceful. The fifth is compressed and difficult: praise the *aghnya* among the cattle — the playful Marut troop that grew strong on the *rasa*, the juice, in the jaw. Then the sixth stops and asks. *Kaḥ vo varṣiṣṭha ā naro divaś ca gmaś ca dhūtayaḥ* — which of you is the greatest, O men, O shakers of heaven and earth, when you shake them as one shakes a hem? The question is left standing. No answer is given in this verse or in the nine that follow, and that silence is the theology: the Maruts are a group whose power belongs to the group.

Three verses then show what the shaking does. Before your fierce coming a man braces what he has (v7); at your racings the earth trembles like a worn-out lord of the peoples (v8); firm is their birth, and they have the vigour to come out from their mother — twice over (v9). The tenth turns them into singers themselves: these sons, singing, have widened the boundaries in their courses, so that the lowing cattle go knee-deep. The eleventh sets them driving the long, broad, inexhaustible child of the mist ahead of them along their ways.

The twelfth speaks to them by name for the only time: *maruto yad dha vo balam*, Maruts, such as your strength is — you have shaken men, you have shaken the mountains. The verb is repeated with two different objects, and the parallel is the point: the same force that moves a mountain moves a man.

The thirteenth returns to sound and asks the third of the hymn's questions. *Yad dha yānti maruto saṃ ha bruvate adhvan ā, śṛṇoti kaś cid eṣām* — when the Maruts go, they talk together on the road; does anyone hear them? In verse 3 the poet said he heard the whips from right here. Ten verses later he is no longer sure anyone hears.

The last two verses are hospitality and end the hymn quietly. Come quickly with the swift ones; there are offerings for you among the Kaṇvas; take your pleasure there (v14). And: it is ready for your gladdening, and we are theirs — *viśvaṃ cid āyur jīvase*, for a whole lifetime, to live. After fourteen verses of a troop that shakes the earth, the last word the household asks for is a long ordinary life.
37.practice:
The Maruts are the tradition's oldest picture of a power that is plural by nature. Thirty-one sūktas belong to them alone across the collection and they are named in forty-two — eleven of the thirty-one in maṇḍala 1 and ten in maṇḍala 5. In every one of them they are *they*. The sixth verse of this hymn asks which of them is greatest and gets no reply, and that is not an oversight: a troop whose strength is in arriving together does not have a first among them. Anyone who has stood in a procession, a *bhajana* group, or a village *gaṇa* where the effect depends on everyone moving at once knows the thing being described.

The second thing is that this hymn is made of sound, and it says so. The whips heard from here (v3); the *devattaṃ brahma*, the god-given formulation, sung out (v4); the shaking (vv 6–8); the Maruts as *sūnavaḥ giraḥ*, sons who sing (v10); and finally, in verse 13, the doubt — they talk together on the road, and does anybody hear them? A hymn that is itself a noise made to attract a noise ends by wondering whether the sound carries. That is an honest thing for a reciter to sit with.

The word *brahman* in verse 4 is worth pausing on because of where it goes later. Here it is *devatta*, god-given: the formulation is not the poet's invention but something handed to him, which he then has to sing. That is the oldest sense in the vocabulary — a shaped, potent utterance — long before it becomes the name of the absolute. The chain runs from this verse to the priest called *brahmā* who oversees the rite, and only much later to the *Brahman* of the Upaniṣads. A reciter who wonders why the same word means all three has the beginning of the answer here.

And the closing verse is the one to carry. All the offerings are prepared, the troop has been praised for its violence for fourteen verses, and what is asked in return is *viśvaṃ cid āyur jīvase* — a whole span of life, to live it. Not victory, not wealth. The whole of one's years.
37.disagreements:
Verse 12 has the translators saying opposite things about the same verb. Wilson: "Maruts, as you have vigour, invigorate mankind; give animation to the clouds." Griffith: "so have ye cast men down on earth, So have ye made the mountains fall." The padapāṭha gives *janān acucyavītana girīn acucyavītana*, the same causative twice, and Griffith's shaking-down matches the sense the same root carries in verses 7 and 8.

Verse 13 divides just as sharply. Wilson has the Maruts filling the road with clamour so that "every one hears their (noise)"; Griffith reads a genuine question — "Doth any hear them as they speak?" The padapāṭha's *śṛṇoti kaś cid eṣām* will bear either.

Verse 5's *aghnya* is the same word that divides them at [[1.30]].19, and they divide the same way: Griffith reads a bull, "Praise ye the Bull among the cows"; Wilson, following Sāyaṇa, reads the Maruts as "born amongst kine" and unresisted. Sāyaṇa's ground is the tradition that the Maruts were born of Pṛśni's milk, and he glosses *jambhe rasasya* as their vigour, derived from the milk, increasing in the mouth or in the belly.

Sāyaṇa's remaining notes are lexical: *anarvan* in verse 1 means without a rival, since the Maruts' chariot is drawn by deer and needs no *arvan*, no horse; *vāśī* in verse 2 is not an axe but a voice, the war-cry that terrifies an enemy army; and the *mānuṣa* of verse 7 is the master of a house, planting a strong post to steady the dwelling.
37.note: vaḥ/eṣām/yeṣām counted at 11 occurrences across the padapāṭha of 15 verses, with no singular member ever named; aghnyam v5 cross-checked against 1.30.19; Marut ascription counts from all ten Anukramaṇī files

38.title: Maruts Asked Where They Are; Then the Rain
38.synthesis:
Seven questions in three verses, and no answer to any of them. That is how this hymn begins, and the maruts are not argued into replying — they simply arrive, in the middle, as weather.

*Kat ha nūnam* — what now, when now? The first verse asks when the maruts will take the worshipper up in their two hands, *pitā putram na*, as a father takes a son. They are addressed as *kadhapriya*, fond of the call, and as those *vṛktabarhiṣaḥ*, for whom the *barhis* has already been cut and strewn. The grass is ready; the guests are not here. The second verse presses: where now, and what is your errand — in heaven, is it, and not on earth? Where do your cattle take their pleasure? The third asks three times over — *kva vaḥ sumnā navyāṃsi*, where are your newest kindnesses, where the good passages, where all the good fortunes? By the end of the third verse *kva* has been said five times and *kat* twice.

Then the questions turn dangerous. The fourth verse sets a condition that ought to be impossible: were you, sons of Pṛśni, to be mortal, then your praiser would be the immortal one. Both verbs stand in the optative, and the sentence is left hanging — a poet reminding gods that the arrangement between them could in principle run the other way. The fifth asks that the singer never become unwelcome to them, like a wild animal turned off its pasture, and never walk *pathā yamasya*, on Yama's road. The sixth calls on Nirṛti, dissolution herself, hard to beat back, not to strike them down, and asks that she fall away *tṛṣṇayā saha*, together with thirst.

The seventh verse answers everything by changing the subject. *Satyam* — truly. The *rudriya*, the maruts who belong to Rudra, fierce and full of *ama*, force, lay their mist even on the waterless waste, and they do it *avātām*, without wind. Nothing is proved. The rain is simply there. The eighth verse gives the sound of it: the lightning bellows like a cow lowing, and follows the way a mother follows her calf, once their flood has been loosed. In the ninth they make darkness in broad daylight with the water-carrying *parjanya* and drown the earth. In the tenth, at the *svana*, the roar, every dwelling on earth shakes and the people inside them shake with it.

The eleventh and twelfth verses steady the storm rather than praise it. Come along the embanked rivers, on strong hooves, untiring in your going. Let your felloes be firm, your chariots and horses steady, your reins well made. Six verses of asking where they had gone, four of overwhelming arrival, and now the request is that the whole thing hold together.

The last three verses turn away from the maruts and instruct the poet instead. Call out with sustained song to Brahmaṇaspati and to Agni, who is lovely to look at as Mitra is. Measure the *śloka* in your mouth; stretch it the way *parjanya* stretches; sing the *gāyatra*, the *ukthya*. Then praise the *mārutaṃ gaṇam*, the marut troop, fierce, worth praising, hymn-bearing — and let them grow strong here among us. A hymn that opened by asking where the gods had gone ends by telling the reciter that making the sound is his own share of the work.
38.practice:
The maruts come as a *gaṇa*, a troop, and they are almost never singular. Counted from the Anukramaṇī, 46 sūktas across the collection name them and 31 are theirs alone — behind only Indra, Agni, Soma, the Viśvedevāḥ and the Aśvins. This one sits inside a run of three consecutive marut hymns by the same ṛṣi, [[1.37]] through [[1.39]], which is how the collection tends to treat them: not one appearance but a crowd of appearances.

What they are asked for is rain, and the seventh verse specifies rain *dhanva cit*, even on the desert, and *avātā*, with no wind driving it. Anyone who has waited out a late monsoon knows the difference between the wind that promises and the water that comes. The hymn is honest about the waiting: its first six verses are a man asking where the rain has gone, and one of them names Nirṛti and Yama's road, because a failed season is not an inconvenience.

The most usable thing here is the last three verses, and they concern recitation rather than weather. *Mimīhi ślokam āsye* — measure out the verse in your mouth. Not compose it, not feel it: measure it, the way one measures a quantity, and measure it in the mouth. Then *gāya gāyatram ukthyam*, sing the *gāyatra* — the metre this entire sūkta is in. The Ṛgveda is here describing the discipline that in fact carried it, syllable-exact oral transmission, and setting it beside the god's rain as work of the same order. It tells you to spread your voice *parjanyaḥ iva*, as the rain-cloud spreads. That comparison is the hymn's own estimate of what recitation is for.

*Vṛktabarhiṣaḥ* in the first verse names the maruts as those for whom the grass has been cut. The same formation returns two hymns later at [[1.40]].7, there describing the worshipper. Cutting and strewing the *barhis* is a preparation made before anyone has arrived and with no guarantee that anyone will. That is the posture this hymn opens in, and the questions follow from it.
38.disagreements:
Verse 4 is where the readings separate most sharply, and the morphology leans toward one of them. Wilson, following Sāyaṇa, takes it as a wish: "that you, sons of Pṛśni, may become mortals, and your panegyrist become immortal." Griffith takes it as a counterfactual: "If, O ye Maruts, ye the Sons whom Prsni bore, were mortal, and Immortal he who sings your praise." Both *syātana* and *syāt* are optative, which supports Griffith's conditional. Sāyaṇa glosses Pṛśni as *dhenu*, a cow.

Verse 13 divides them three ways. Wilson invokes three deities — Brahmaṇaspati, Agni and Mitra. Griffith collapses it to one, "Agni the Lord of Prayer, Him who is fair as Mitra is." The padapāṭha has *brahmaṇaḥ patim* and *agnim* as separate accusatives, then *mitram na darśatam*, Mitra with the particle of comparison. Two are being called; the third is a simile.

Sāyaṇa glosses *rudriyāsaḥ* in verse 7 as those who belong to Rudra, or are protected by him, and reads verse 3's *sumnā, suvitā, saubhagā* concretely as offspring, cattle, jewels, gold, horses and elephants. On verse 6 Wilson names Nirṛti outright, where Griffith depersonalises her into "destructive plague on plague, hard to be conquered".

39.title: Maruts Aimed, Undivided, at the Ṛṣi's Enemy
39.synthesis:
This hymn opens the way [[1.38]] did, with questions, and it ends by asking the maruts to shoot. Between those two points a poet stops asking where the storm is going and tells it where to go.

*Pra yat itthā parāvataḥ* — when from that far distance you hurl your measure like a flame: by whose *kratu*, whose effective purpose, by whose design, to whom do you go, to whom indeed, O shakers? Four interrogatives crowd the first verse — *kasya, kasya, kam, kam* — and every one is about destination. The second verse answers none of them and asks instead that the weapons be sound: *sthirā vaḥ santu āyudhā*, firm be your arms for driving off, firm for holding fast. Yours be the *taviṣī*, the mass of strength, that deserves praise — and not a deceitful mortal's. The line repeats, almost word for word, the request that closed the preceding hymn at [[1.38]].12, where it was the chariot's felloes that had to be firm. The same ṛṣi, two hymns running, asking that the equipment hold.

The third verse watches them work. When you strike down what is fixed and roll away what is heavy, you go straight through the trees of the earth and the clefts of the mountains. The fourth states the ground of the whole request: no enemy of yours has ever been found in heaven or on earth, *riśādasaḥ* — you who wear down hostility. Let your strength, held in this bond, be yours to defy with even now, sons of Rudra. The fifth is the storm at full height: they set the mountains shaking, they tear the *vanaspatis* apart, they drive on like men gone wild on drink, gods with their whole clan behind them.

The sixth verse harnesses them and hears them coming. The dappled *pṛṣatī* mares are yoked, a ruddy one runs as *praṣṭi* alongside — and then the line that makes the verse: *pṛthivī cit aśrot*, even the earth listened, and men were afraid. Something enormous is approaching, and the poet has just spent five verses inviting it.

The seventh turns it toward himself and names the name. *Ā vaḥ makṣu* — quickly we choose your help, for our offspring, sons of Rudra; come now as you came before, *itthā*, to Kaṇva when he was afraid. The questions of the first verse have been answered by the poet, not by the gods: you go to whoever calls, and I am calling. The eighth asks that whatever monstrous thing bears down on them — sent by the maruts themselves or by a man — be torn away with strength, with *ojas*, with their own protections.

The ninth and tenth close on a single word said four times. *Asāmi* — not by halves. Wholly, you who deserve worship, you have kept Kaṇva; come to us with helps that are not halved, as lightning comes to the rain. Whole is the *ojas* you bear, generous ones; whole the *śavas*, shakers. And then the last line, which is not gentle: at the man who hates the ṛṣi, at his fury, loose hostility like an arrow. The hymn that began by asking where the storm was headed finishes by giving it a target.
39.practice:
The address the maruts are given here is *rudriya* and *rudrāsaḥ* — Rudra's own, sons of Rudra — and their weather is not gentle. Counted from the Anukramaṇī, 46 sūktas name them and 31 are theirs alone. What they carry in this hymn is *ojas* and *śavas* and *taviṣī*: three separate words for force, none of them interchangeable with mercy. A reader who wants the Vedic gods to be uniformly benign will have to account for verse 10.

The word to take away is *asāmi*, said four times in the closing pair of verses. It is a negative — *a-sāmi*, not half — and it is asked of the protection, not of the god's power. The distinction matters. The poet is not requesting more help; he is requesting that the help not be partial. Half-help is the specific thing feared, and it is a fear anyone recognises: the rain that starts and stops, the recovery that stalls, the support that is offered and then withdrawn. The Ṛgveda has a word for the difference and spends its last two verses on it.

Verse 7 shows the tradition's oldest argument for being heard, and it is worth noticing because it is still the argument. *Yathā purā itthā kaṇvāya bibhyuṣe* — come now as you came before, to Kaṇva when he was frightened. Precedent, not merit. The claim is not that the petitioner deserves help but that this god has helped this line before, and the ṛṣi puts his own name in the verse so the precedent has an address. The following hymns of the group keep doing it: Kaṇva or Praskaṇva is named in [[1.44]], [[1.45]], [[1.46]], [[1.47]], [[1.48]] and [[1.49]]. Naming your teacher's lineage when you ask for something is not a later custom laid over the Veda; it is in the Veda.

Verse 2 is a caution about the same power. Let your strength be the kind that merits praise, *mā martyasya māyinaḥ* — and not a deceitful mortal's. Strength is not self-justifying even when it belongs to a god, and the poet says so before he asks to have it aimed.
39.disagreements:
Verse 1 is obscure and the two translators handle the obscurity in opposite directions. Wilson, with Sāyaṇa, supplies a full frame — "when you direct your awful vigour downwards from afar, as light descends from heaven, by whose worship, by whose praise are you attracted?" Griffith stays closer to the surface: "When thus, like flame, from far away, Maruts, ye cast your measure forth."

Verse 6 turns on one word. Wilson has "the firmament listens for your coming"; the padapāṭha reads *pṛthivī cit aśrot*, and Griffith renders it correctly, "Even the Earth herself listened as ye came near." Sāyaṇa's note here is technical rather than theological: *praṣṭi* is the position of the third horse harnessed beside a pair, and *rohita* the ruddy one that draws.

Verse 8 divides them completely. Wilson makes it a request to withhold — "withhold from him food and strength and your assistance." Griffith makes it a request to attack: "Tear ye him from us with your power and with your might." Verse 10 divides them the same way: Wilson has the maruts loose their own anger like an arrow, Griffith has them send an enemy against the enemy. Sāyaṇa glosses *pracetas* simply as those possessed of superior *cetas*, intellect.

40.title: Brahmaṇaspati Speaks the Mantra the Gods Live In
40.synthesis:
Eight verses on speech, and in the middle of them a claim about mantra that the whole later tradition rests on.

*Ut tiṣṭha brahmaṇaḥ pate* — rise up, Brahmaṇaspati. The first verse has men who are *devayantaḥ*, godward-turning, approaching him; it asks the maruts, *sudānavaḥ*, generous givers, to come near, and Indra to be present alongside. The second addresses him by a title that belongs equally to Agni — *sahasaḥ putra*, son of strength — and gives the human situation plainly: a mortal calls on you *dhane hite*, when the stake has been laid down and something is about to be won or lost. May the man who has praised you get *suvīrya* and good horses out of it.

The third verse sends two figures forward together. *Pra etu brahmaṇaspatiḥ, pra devī etu sūnṛtā* — let Brahmaṇaspati go forth, let the goddess Sūnṛtā go forth. Sūnṛtā is generous truth spoken aloud, and she walks beside the lord of the sacred formulation as his natural companion. Then: may the gods lead our *yajña* to the man who is heroic and *paṅktirādhas*, whose giving comes in the fivefold measure. The fourth turns to the priest's fee: whoever gives the *vāghat*, the one who chants, wealth worth having, obtains *akṣiti śravas*, renown that does not wear out — and for such a man the offering is made to Iḷā, rich in heroes, quick to prevail, *anehas*, faultless.

The fifth verse is the centre of gravity, and it is the reason to keep the hymn. *Pra nūnam brahmaṇaspatir mantram vadati ukthyam* — now Brahmaṇaspati speaks forth the *mantra* that is worth reciting — *yasmin indro varuṇo mitro aryamā devā okāṃsi cakrire*: in which Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, the gods, have made their dwellings. The verb is a perfect: they made them and they are still there. The mantra is not a message sent to the gods. It is the house they live in.

The sixth verse follows directly from that, and it is the first-person consequence. Let us speak that mantra in the *vidathas*, the assemblies — *śambhu*, bringing wellbeing, and *anehas*, without flaw, the same word given to Iḷā two verses earlier. And if you leaders take pleasure in this *vāc*, this speech, then everything good will reach you. Not: then we will receive. Then it will reach *you*. The exchange runs in both directions and the hymn does not hide which direction it is describing.

The seventh verse asks who can come near such a man: *kaḥ devayantam aśnavat janam, kaḥ vṛktabarhiṣam* — who can touch the godward man, who the one whose *barhis* is trimmed? He goes forward with his household, and he fills his dwelling from within with what is precious. The eighth ends in force rather than speech. He heaps up *kṣatra*, ruling power; with kings he strikes; even inside fear he keeps a good place to live; and of the wielder of the *vajra* there is no one who checks him and no one who overcomes him, in the great fight or the small.

Brahmaṇaspati stands at the head of the first, third and fifth verses, once every other verse, and each time the verse that follows him is about what speech can do.
40.practice:
Verse 5 is why this short hymn matters. *Yasmin indro varuṇo mitro aryamā devā okāṃsi cakrire* — the gods have made their dwellings in the mantra. Not: the mantra reaches them. Not: the mantra pleases them. They live in it, and the verb says they moved in and stayed. Every practice of *japa* the tradition later develops takes that as its premise: repeating a mantra is not sending a message to a deity elsewhere but entering the place where the deity is. The Ṛgveda states the premise in eight verses of *bṛhatī* long before anyone systematised it.

Brahmaṇaspati is the lord of the *brahman*, the formulated word — and he is rarer than his importance suggests. Counted from the Anukramaṇī, nine sūktas name him, and only four are wholly his: [[1.18]], this one, [[2.25]] and [[2.26]]. Under the name Bṛhaspati the total rises to nineteen. Small numbers for the god whose whole domain is the thing the Veda is made of.

Two things in the hymn are worth carrying into an ordinary week. The first is Sūnṛtā in verse 3, sent forward beside Brahmaṇaspati as though the two were a pair — generous true speech walking alongside the formulated word. The tradition treats the sacred utterance and everyday truthful speech as belonging to one household, not two. The second is verse 6's *anehas*, faultless: the mantra we are to speak in the assemblies is asked to be flawless, and the same adjective was given to Iḷā two verses before. Flawlessness is not a decoration on recitation here; it is what makes it the thing it is.

Verse 8 sets *kṣatra* — ruling power — beside the speech of the preceding verses without joining them by argument. Brahmaṇaspati amasses lordly might, and strikes alongside kings. What exactly is being claimed about the relation of the priestly word to royal power is not spelled out in this hymn, and reading the later theory of *brahman* and *kṣatra* back into eight verses would be putting weight on ground that will not hold it.
40.disagreements:
Verse 3's Sūnṛtā is read as a person by both translators but glossed differently. Sāyaṇa identifies her with *vāk*, speech itself; Wilson renders "the goddess, speaker of truth"; Griffith keeps the name untranslated, "may Sunrta the Goddess come." *Paṅktirādhas* in the same verse is "abounding with respectably-presented offerings" for Wilson and "the five-fold gift" for Griffith.

Verse 7 shows Wilson supplying a subject that is not in the text. He renders it "Who, except Brahmaṇaspati, may approach the man who is devoted to the gods" — the parenthesis is his and Sāyaṇa's, turning a rhetorical question into a statement about the god. Griffith leaves it open: "Who shall approach the pious?"

Verse 8 is the same problem enlarged. Wilson makes Brahmaṇaspati the subject throughout, armed with the *vajra*; Sāyaṇa's own note observes that the thunderbolt identifies Indra, which leaves the verse's subject genuinely unsettled. Griffith declines to name anyone: "He amplifies his lordly might, with kings he slays."

Sāyaṇa records that Brahmaṇaspati was earlier a form of Agni and is here associated with the maruts, and glosses *sahasaḥ putra* as the abundant protector of strength rather than its offspring.

41.title: Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman — a Road Without Thorns
41.synthesis:
Nine short verses about being kept safe, and then, at the very end, a refusal that changes the sense of everything before it.

The first verse states the whole claim and then the hymn spends eight verses working out what it costs. *Yam rakṣanti pracetasaḥ varuṇo mitro aryamā* — the man whom Varuṇa, Mitra and Aryaman, who see far, guard: that man is never brought down. The second says how it feels from inside: whomever they carry as if in both arms, whomever they keep from *riṣ*, injury — every such man thrives, *ariṣṭaḥ*, unhurt. The third turns to what the three do rather than what they are. They are called *rājānaḥ*, kings, and kings break things: they smash the strongholds and the hostilities, and they lead the *duritas*, the hard passages, *tiraḥ* — away past, out of the road.

The fourth verse is the one to remember. *Sugaḥ panthā anṛkṣaraḥ* — the road is easy going and free of thorns, Ādityas, *ṛtam yate*, for the one who is travelling toward *ṛta*, the order of things. And here there is no *avakhāda*, nothing to gnaw at you. The claim is precise and it is not a claim of universal protection: the road is smooth for a man going in one particular direction. The fifth extends it — the *yajña* you lead by the straight road arrives at your own *dhīti*, your regard — and the sixth says what such a man ends with: *ratna*, treasure; *vasu*, goods; all of it, and offspring of his own, and never thrown down.

Then the seventh verse breaks the run of statements with a question the poet asks his own friends. *Kathā rādhāma sakhāyaḥ stomam* — how, companions, shall we bring off the praise of Mitra and Aryaman, the great abundance of Varuṇa? Six verses of confident description, and the seventh admits the singers are not sure they are equal to the task.

The eighth is where the hymn does something unusual, and it does it in one line. *Mā vaḥ ghnantam mā śapantam prati voce* — I will not point out to you the man who strikes, nor the man who curses. These are gods who demolish strongholds and lead the hostile away; the poet has just spent six verses saying so; and now, holding that instrument, he declines to use it. He will not name his enemy. Instead, *sumnaiḥ it vaḥ ā vivāse*, with kindnesses alone I invite you in.

The ninth closes with an image from the gaming board. Let a man not be fond of ill-speaking, but fear — as one fears the player who holds the four dice, right up until they are set down. Verses of *gāyatrī* do not have room to explain themselves, and this one does not. What it puts side by side is a bad tongue and a throw not yet made: you do not know what is coming, and the man who has not yet released his handful is exactly the man you should be careful around. The hymn about a road without thorns ends by pointing at the thorns a person puts there himself.
41.practice:
The Ādityas are addressed as a group here, and the group is small in the collection: counted from the Anukramaṇī, eleven sūktas name *ādityāḥ* collectively and only six are wholly theirs — this one, [[2.27]], [[7.51]], [[7.52]], [[8.67]] and [[10.185]]. Yet the three named in the first verse, Varuṇa, Mitra and Aryaman, are anything but marginal. Aryaman in particular has survived where a hymn count would not predict it: he is the one invoked over a marriage, and his name is a common noun for the fitting order among people — what is owed between host and guest, kin and kin.

The fourth verse gives the phrase to carry. *Sugaḥ panthā anṛkṣaraḥ… ṛtam yate* — for the one going toward *ṛta*, the road is easy and thornless. Two things about how it is put. First, the smooth road is not a reward handed over at the end; it is a description of the journey itself, offered to whoever is already travelling in that direction. Second, *ṛta* is in the accusative and the traveller is a participle — someone actually going. The verse promises nothing to an admirer of order, only to one moving toward it. That is a distinction worth keeping when *ṛta* is spoken of, which is often, as an idea rather than a destination.

The eighth verse is the hymn's moral centre, and it is easy to miss because it is stated as a negative. A worshipper with a real grievance, addressing gods who are said in this very hymn to destroy the strongholds of the hostile, refuses to name the man who struck him or cursed him. *Sumnaiḥ it vaḥ ā vivāse* — with kindnesses only do I bring you near. This is a limit placed on prayer from inside prayer. The gods are not to be used as an instrument for settling accounts, and the ninth verse extends the point to the tongue: do not develop an appetite for saying bad things.

The dice held in the closing verse — four of them, Sāyaṇa says, and cowries at that — are the same equipment that will be at the centre of the gambler's lament in the tenth maṇḍala. Here they are only a comparison, and they carry the one thing this hymn keeps saying: what is coming has not been thrown yet.
41.disagreements:
Verse 4 divides the translators over who is walking. Wilson makes the road the gods' own approach: "Ādityas, to you repairing to the sacrifice, the path is easy and free from thorns." Griffith makes it the worshipper's: "Thornless, Adityas, is the path, easy for him who seeks the Law." The padapāṭha has *ṛtam* in the accusative with *yate*, a dative participle of √i, to go — which puts a traveller on the road, and supports Griffith here.

Verse 7 splits over *psaraḥ*. Wilson has "the great glory" of Varuṇa; Griffith keeps the concrete sense, "Glorious food of Varuna." Verse 3's *nayanti duritā tiraḥ* is "put aside their evil deeds" for Wilson — moral failings — and "lead him safely o'er distress" for Griffith, which reads *durita* as hard going rather than wrongdoing. Both senses are live in the word.

The closing verse is the most contested. Sāyaṇa reads it as a gambler holding four dice, and adds that the dice are cowrie shells, *kapardaka*. Wilson follows him and turns the fear into the gamester's own — "as a gamester fears his adversary holding the four, until they are thrown." Griffith declines to name a gambler at all and leaves the figure open: "fear the One who holds all four Within his hand, until they fall." Sāyaṇa also identifies the three of the first verse as sons of Aditi by Kaśyapa.

42.title: Pūṣan Asked to Clear the Road Ahead
42.synthesis:
There is no cosmology in this hymn. A man is about to travel, the country between here and there has robbers in it, and he asks Pūṣan to go first.

*Sam pūṣan adhvanaḥ tira* — carry us across the stretches of road; put aside *aṃhas*, the narrow, closing distress. Then a name that is not explained: *vimuco napāt*, child of the unyoking. And the request the whole hymn turns on: *pra naḥ puraḥ*, go ahead of us, out in front. The second verse names what is out there. If some evil *vṛka*, some wolf, some ill-disposed creature marks us out — beat him off the path. The third pushes him further: away with that *paripanthin*, the one who lurks about the road, the thief, the crooked-minded; drive him far from the track. The fourth stops asking politely. With your foot, tread down the burning weapon of that double-dealing *aghaśaṃsa*, the man of evil utterance, whoever he may be. Four verses, and the danger has moved from a general narrowness to a specific man with a specific weapon.

The fifth changes register. *Ā tat te dasra mantumaḥ pūṣan avo vṛṇīmahe* — we choose that help of yours, wonder-worker, you who hold counsel: the very help with which you urged the *pitṛs* onward. The road being asked about is suddenly a longer one than the road to market, and the hymn does not say more. The sixth calls him *viśvasaubhaga*, holder of every good fortune, and *hiraṇyavāśīmattama*, best wielder of the golden blade, and asks him to make wealth easy to come by.

Then the refrain begins, and the last three of those verses each end on the same half-line: *pūṣan iha kratum vidaḥ* — Pūṣan, know here the *kratu*, the effective purpose. In the seventh, lead us past those who pursue; make the goings good, make the paths good. In the eighth, bring us where the grass is good, *suyavasam*, and let no new fever meet us on the way — the two things a traveller with animals actually thinks about. In the ninth the requests come in a single burst of imperatives: *śagdhi pūrdhi pra yaṃsi ca śiśīhi prāsi udaram* — be able, fill, hold out, sharpen us, fill the belly. Five commands in one line, ending with the belly. This is not a metaphor.

The tenth verse steps back and states the relationship. *Na pūṣaṇam methāmasi* — we do not slight Pūṣan, we do not quarrel with him. With *sūktas* we sing him; from the *dasma*, the one who works wonders, we ask for goods. After nine verses of asking a god to do specific unglamorous jobs — chase off a thief, find grass, stop a fever, fill a stomach — the last verse takes care to say that the asking has not been complaint. That is the tone of the whole thing: a working relationship with a god who is expected to be useful, stated without embarrassment on either side.
42.practice:
Pūṣan is the god of the road, and this hymn is the plainest evidence of what that meant. Counted from the Anukramaṇī, sixteen sūktas name him and eight are wholly his, with a striking cluster in the sixth maṇḍala where six consecutive hymns, [[6.53]] through [[6.58]], are his or shared with Indra. He is a small god by hymn count and a constantly used one, which is the profile of a deity people actually called on rather than one they theorised about.

The road words run through five of the ten verses — *adhvan* in the first and eighth, *pathas* in the second, *sruti* in the third, *sugā* and *supathā* together in the seventh. And the request that opens the hymn is spatial and specific: *pra naḥ puraḥ*, go in front of us. Not accompany, not watch over — go first. Anyone who has sent someone ahead on an unfamiliar road knows the difference.

Two things here bear directly on how Pūṣan survived. The first is verse 5, which recalls the help by which he urged the *pitṛs* on. Pūṣan's roads are not only the ones with grass beside them, and the hymn leaves the implication where it found it, without elaborating. The second is that his name did not stay in the Ṛgveda. He is addressed at the close of the Īśa Upaniṣad — *pūṣann ekarṣe yama sūrya prājāpatya* — where a dying man asks him to draw aside the golden disc so that the truth beneath can be seen. The god who is asked in this hymn to move an obstruction off a road is asked there to move an obstruction off the sight. The continuity of function across a very long stretch of tradition is exact.

The refrain of verses 7 to 9 is the phrase to hold: *pūṣan iha kratum vidaḥ*. *Kratu* is not knowledge and not strength but the resolve that makes an act effective — the same word given to Agni in [[1.1]].5 as *kavikratu*. What is asked of Pūṣan three times over is not that he be powerful, which is assumed, but that he apply himself *iha*, here, to this journey. Most requests worth making are of that shape.
42.disagreements:
Verse 1's *vimuco napāt* is where both translators import something the words do not carry. The padapāṭha has *vi-mucaḥ napāt*, from √muc, to release or unyoke. Sāyaṇa's tradition gives "son of the cloud", which Wilson prints, and Griffith has "cloud-born God"; neither takes the compound at face value as the child of the unharnessing — the moment at the end of a journey when the animals are let out of the yoke. Sāyaṇa separately derives Pūṣan from √puṣ, to nourish, and makes him one of the twelve Ādityas presiding over the earth and over travel.

Verse 2 divides them on what the enemy does. Wilson, following Sāyaṇa, has an adversary who "points out to us the way we ought not to go" — a false direction. Griffith has a literal animal: "Drive, Pusan, from our road the wolf, the wicked inauspicious wolf, Who lies in Wait to injure us."

The refrain is read two ways. Sāyaṇa explains *iha kratum vidaḥ* as "know here how to fulfil your function of giving us protection", and Wilson follows with "know how to protect us on this journey." Griffith takes *kratu* as capacity rather than office: "O Pusan, find thou power for this." Verse 8's *navajvāraḥ* is "extreme heat" for Wilson and "early heat" for Griffith.

43.title: What to Say to Rudra — Medicine, Then Soma
43.synthesis:
The hymn begins by admitting it does not know how to begin. *Kat rudrāya pracetase mīḷhuṣṭamāya tavyase vocema śaṃtamam hṛde* — what shall we say to Rudra, who sees far, who gives most generously, who is strongest, that will be *śaṃtama*, most benign, to his heart? Every other epithet in the line is superlative; so is the word for what the words must be. This is a god you approach by first asking what is safe to say.

The next two verses answer with six clauses of *yathā*, three in each, and every one of them is a purpose rather than a compliment. So that Aditi may make *rudriya* — Rudra's own thing, which the tradition understands as his medicine — for our cattle, for our men, for our cow, for our offspring. So that Mitra and Varuṇa may take note, so that Rudra may take note, so that the Viśvedevāḥ, all in agreement, may. The whole grammatical weight of the opening question falls into these clauses: tell us what to say, so that the medicine comes.

The fourth verse names him with three titles and asks for one thing. *Gāthapatim medhapatim rudram jalāṣabheṣajam* — lord of the song, lord of the offering, whose remedy is cooling. A god of the chant and of the rite, and in the same breath a god who holds medicine that soothes; the Ṛgveda sees no distance between those offices. What is asked of him is *śaṃyoḥ sumnam*, the favour of wellbeing and safety. The fifth describes him with two comparisons and no request at all: he shines like Sūrya at his brightest, he glows like gold, best of the gods, *vasu*.

The sixth is the verse that shows what the hymn is for. *Śaṃ naḥ karati arvate* — may he make it well for the horse; for the ram, for the ewe, for the men, for the women, for the cow. Six datives, and the list is simply the contents of a household, animals and people together, in no hierarchy. Whatever else Rudra is, in this verse he is asked to look after everything alive on the property, and the word for what he is asked to do is *śam*, the same root as the *śaṃtama* of the first verse and the *śaṃyoḥ* of the fourth. Three times across six verses the hymn reaches for that one syllable, and it is the syllable it began by asking permission to use.

At the seventh verse the address changes to Soma and does not change back. *Asme soma śriyam adhi ni dhehi* — set upon us the splendour of a hundred men, great *śravas*, abundant in manly force. The eighth asks that neither those who hem in the soma nor hostile powers lead us astray, and calls him *indu*: give us our share in *vāja*. The ninth ends on something larger and stranger than anything in the six Rudra verses. Those offspring of yours, immortal one, in the furthest seat — *ṛtasya mūrdhā nābhā*, the head of *ṛta*, its navel — Soma, know them; know those who are attending on you. A hymn that opened by asking what could safely be said closes with a god who is himself the point at which the order of things is centred, and asks only that he recognise his own.
43.practice:
Rudra is nearly absent from the Ṛgveda and central to everything after it, and this hymn is one of the places where you can see the discrepancy. Counted from the Anukramaṇī, six sūktas name him at all, and just three are wholly his — [[1.114]], [[2.33]] and [[7.46]]. The first six verses here, plus one verse in [[5.42]] and one in [[7.59]], are the remainder. Three hymns out of 1,028, for the god who becomes Śiva.

What he is asked for is medicine. *Jalāṣabheṣaja* in verse 4 names him as holding a remedy that cools, and Sāyaṇa quotes for it the line every Hindu who has heard the Rudram knows — *yā te rudra śivā tanūḥ*, that form of yours, Rudra, which is auspicious. The healing Rudra of the Yajurveda's Śatarudrīya, invoked as physician and as the auspicious one, is not a later softening of a fierce Vedic god. He is here, in the Ṛgveda, in the earliest hymn addressed to him.

The word to carry is *śam*. It appears three times across the six Rudra verses — *śaṃtamam* in the first, *śaṃyoḥ* in the fourth, *śaṃ naḥ karati* in the sixth — and it is the ancestor of a great deal of what a Hindu says out loud. *Śāntiḥ* at the close of a recitation, *śaṃ ca me mayaś ca me* in the Camaka, the *śiva* of Śiva and the *śaṃ* of Śaṃkara: all of it is this root, and this hymn shows what the root means in use. It is not peace as an inner state. It is the absence of harm to a specific list of creatures.

That list is verse 6, and it deserves to be read slowly: horse, ram, ewe, men, women, cow. There is no ranking, and the humans are neither first nor last. The wellbeing asked for is the wellbeing of a household that includes its animals, and the god who provides it is the one whose other name the tradition will spend three thousand years being careful about.

The closing verses hand the hymn to Soma without transition. What they add is verse 9's *ṛtasya mūrdhā nābhā* — head and navel of *ṛta* — one of the collection's most compressed statements of where the order of things is anchored.
43.disagreements:
The most consequential divergence is over three syllables in verse 4. Sāyaṇa reads *śaṃyoḥ* as a proper name, Śaṃyu, whom he identifies as the son of Bṛhaspati, and Wilson follows him — "we ask the felicity of Śaṃyu, from Rudra" — and carries the person into verse 5 as well, "who is so brilliant as Śaṃyu?" Griffith takes it as the standard benediction: "we pray for joy and health and strength." The word is a genuine crux; the grammatical apparatus lemmatises it as *śaṃyu*, which keeps Sāyaṇa's reading live, while verse 6's plain *śaṃ* keeps the other one live too. Both should be kept.

Verse 8 is a simpler error. The padapāṭha has *indo*, the vocative of *indu*, a name of Soma. Wilson prints "cherish us, Indra"; Griffith has "Indu, give us a share of strength," which the text supports.

Sāyaṇa glosses *rudriya* in verse 2 as *rudrasambandhi bheṣajam*, medicines belonging to Rudra, and takes Aditi there as the earth. He derives the name Rudra from causing to weep — he who makes all weep at the end of time — while noting that in this sūkta he presides over healing plants and is a beneficent deity. The tension is Sāyaṇa's own and he does not resolve it.

44.title: Agni at Daybreak — with Uṣas and the Aśvins
44.synthesis:
This is an Agni hymn in which Uṣas will not stay out of the frame. Ten forms built on her name run through eight of the fourteen verses, and the reason is structural: Agni is kindled before there is any light, and everything this hymn asks of him happens at the moment the sky changes.

The first verse asks him, *jātavedas*, knower of all that is born, to convey to the giver the *citra rādhas*, the shining bounty, that belongs to the dawn, and to bring today the gods who are *uṣarbudhaḥ* — awake at dawn. The second names his office: welcome messenger, *havyavāhana*, bearer of the offering, and *rathī adhvarāṇām*, charioteer of the rites — and asks him, *sajūḥ* with the Aśvins and with Uṣas, to set on us manly strength and high renown. He is not acting alone; he is acting in company, and the company is a daybreak.

The third verse chooses him afresh: today we select the messenger, *dhūmaketu*, whose banner is smoke, whose light is straight, glory of the rites at the *vyuṣṭis*, the shinings-out. The fourth calls him best, youngest, guest, well-offered-to, dear to the man who gives, and praises him at the *vyuṣṭis* again — so that he may go and fetch the gods. The fifth drops the ritual vocabulary and simply praises: I will glorify you, deathless nourisher of everything, *trātṛ*, preserver, immortal, worthy of the offering, best of sacrificers. The sixth asks him to speak well of the singer, *madhujihva*, honey-tongued, and to lengthen Praskaṇva's *āyus* so that he may live — and then to do honour to the *daivyam janam*, the divine folk.

The seventh returns to Agni himself: the clans kindle you, *hotā*, all-knowing — bring the far-seeing gods here quickly. The eighth is the fullest picture of the moment: Savitṛ, Uṣas, the Aśvins, Bhaga, Agni himself at the shining-out of the night, and the Kaṇvas with their soma pressed, kindling him. The ninth repeats the first almost word for word — lord of the rites, messenger of the clans, bring today the gods who wake at dawn, who look on the light, to drink soma. Two verses at either end of the hymn's middle saying the same thing, and between them everything the god is.

The tenth turns from the day to all the days: you have shone after the former dawns, *vibhāvasu*, visible to all; you are the helper in the settlements, *purohita* among men at the sacrifices. The eleventh sets him in place as Manu did — instrument of the *yajña*, *hotā*, *ṛtvij*, far-seeing, swift messenger, undying. The twelfth gives him a sound: when as *purohita* of the gods you carry their errand, your flames blaze and roar like the waves of a river in flood.

The last two verses call the guests. *Śrudhi śrutkarṇa* — hear, you whose ears hear: let Mitra and Aryaman, who move at dawn, sit down with the offering-bearing gods on the *barhis*. And let the maruts, generous, *agnijihvāḥ* — having Agni for their tongue — growers of *ṛta*, hear the soma; let Varuṇa whose *vrata* holds firm drink it, together with the Aśvins and Uṣas. The hymn ends where it started, at first light, with the whole company assembled.
44.practice:
The arrangement around this hymn is the thing to notice, and it is verifiable from the Anukramaṇī rather than inferred. Praskaṇva Kāṇva's run of sūktas goes this hymn and [[1.45]] to Agni, [[1.46]] and [[1.47]] to the Aśvins, [[1.48]] and [[1.49]] to Uṣas, [[1.50]] to Sūrya. That is the order of an actual daybreak: Agni kindled while it is still dark, the twin riders who go before the light, the dawn, and then the sun. Whether the ṛṣi or a later arranger set it in that order, the sequence is there in the text and a reader moving through it is walking through a single morning.

Which makes this the hymn of the first act, and explains the vocabulary. *Uṣarbudh*, awake at dawn, is said of the gods twice, in the first verse and the ninth. Rising before light and kindling a fire is the oldest continuously practised thing in the tradition; the *agnihotra* offered at the junctures, and the *sandhyā* that a householder performs facing east, both begin at the hour this hymn is describing, and both begin with fire. The hymn asks Agni to bring the gods *adya*, today — twice — which is what makes it a hymn and not a description.

Two phrases repay attention. *Agnijihvāḥ* in the last verse describes the maruts as having Agni for a tongue. That is the entire logic of offering into fire, compressed: the gods do not come and eat, they taste through him. And *pratiran āyuḥ jīvase* in verse 6 — extending the ṛṣi's lifespan so that he may live — is the oldest form of a prayer the tradition never stopped making, said over a child at *āyuṣya* rites and over the old.

The tenth verse names Agni *purohita* in the sacrifices and helper *grāmeṣu*, in the settlements. The same title opened the collection at [[1.1]].1. Here it comes with the plain domestic word beside it: the god at the head of the rite is also the one who helps where people live.
44.disagreements:
Verse 10 is where Griffith departs furthest from the text. He renders it "Thou art our help in battle-strife, the Friend of Indra, the great high priest in sacrifice." The padapāṭha has *grāmeṣu avitā*, helper in the settlements, and *mānuṣaḥ*, belonging to men — no battle and no Indra. Wilson keeps closer: "you are the protector in villages, you are the associate of man." Sāyaṇa glosses *purohita* here concretely as the domestic priest, and elsewhere as Agni placed to the east.

Verse 1 divides them on a single case. Wilson makes the wealth come *from* the dawn — "bring from the dawn to the donor wealth of many sorts." Griffith makes Agni himself the dawn's gift: "Immortal Jatavedas, thou many-hued fulgent gift of Dawn."

Verse 6's *daivyam janam* is read by Sāyaṇa as the ṛṣi Praskaṇva himself — a human being called divine — and Wilson follows with "do honour to the divine man." Griffith takes it as a class of gods: "show honour to the Heavenly Host." The same phrase returns twice in the following hymn, where the question recurs.

Sāyaṇa reads *rathīr adhvarāṇām* in verse 2 as *rathasthānīya*, standing in the place of a chariot, rather than as the charioteer, and glosses *svadhvara* in verse 8 as the *āhavanīya* fire.
44.note: 10 uṣas-forms across 8 of 14 verses, dūta x5, and the v1/v9 uṣarbudh frame verified from padapāṭha; Praskaṇva sequence counted from anukramaṇī

45.title: Agni Told to Bring the Thirty-Three
45.synthesis:
Ten verses of *anuṣṭubh*, and the argument running under all of them is not about Agni's power. It is about whether a particular man will be heard.

The first verse gives Agni his commission: worship here the Vasus, the Rudras and the Ādityas, and that folk born of Manu who perform the rite well and sprinkle *ghṛta*. Three classes of gods and one class of men, given to Agni in a single instruction. The second says why it will work — the gods are *śruṣṭīvān*, ready to hear, and discerning, toward the man who gives — and then names the number: bring the three-and-thirty, lord of the ruddy horses, you who take pleasure in song.

The third verse is the hinge, and it is a list of names. *Priyamedhavat atrivat… virūpavat aṅgirasvat* — as for Priyamedha, as for Atri, as for Virūpa, as for Aṅgiras: so, *jātavedas*, whose observance is great, hear Praskaṇva's call. Four ṛṣis of former time, and the claim is not that Praskaṇva is worthy but that this fire has heard men of this line before. The fourth verse keeps the lineage in view — those great in praise, the Priyamedhas, have called on Agni for help, Agni ruling the rites with pure flame. The fifth brings it down to the living generation: you into whom the *ghṛta* is poured, giver of rewards, hear these songs, the ones by which the sons of Kaṇva call you for help.

*Śrudhi* — hear — is said in both the third verse and the fifth; the second called the gods ready to hear; and the seventh will call Agni *śrutkarṇa*, whose ears hear. Four times across the hymn the same root, and each time it is attached to a different party: the gods hear, Agni is asked to hear, Agni is one who hears by nature. The hymn is systematically working the question of whether a call arrives.

The sixth verse widens out: men in their settlements call on you, most wonderful in renown, *śociṣkeśa*, whose hair is flame, dear to many, to carry the offering. The seventh sets him in office — the inspired have placed you as *hotā* and *ṛtvij*, best finder of wealth, sharp of hearing, of widest reach, at the *diviṣṭis*. The eighth has them shaking him into motion: the inspired with their soma pressed have made you hasten toward the food, bearing the great light and the oblation, on behalf of the mortal who gives.

The ninth and tenth are the seating of the guests. Born of exertion, giver of rewards, set here today on the *barhis* the *daivyam janam*, the divine folk who travel at dawn, for the soma-drinking. And then: worship with joint calls, Agni, that divine folk now turned toward us; here is the soma, generous ones — drink it, *tiroahnya*, pressed a day ago and kept. The hymn ends with a cup that is not fresh, offered without apology, to guests who have been persuaded to come because they came to somebody's teacher's teacher.
45.practice:
The third verse is the whole tradition in one line. Praskaṇva asks to be heard *priyamedhavat atrivat virūpavat aṅgirasvat* — in the manner of Priyamedha, of Atri, of Virūpa, of Aṅgiras. The ground of the request is not his merit and not his need. It is that this fire has heard these names, and he stands in their succession. Reciting one's *pravara*, naming the ṛṣis of one's line before an act of worship, is a practice every Hindu who performs a *saṅkalpa* still carries out, and this verse is that practice at its source. The logic has not changed in three thousand years: you are heard because of who taught you.

The number in verse 2 is the other thing to take. *Trayastriṃśatam* — the three and thirty. That count outlives the Ṛgveda entirely; it is the standard enumeration of the gods in the Brāhmaṇas and the Upaniṣads, and the figure Yājñavalkya is famously pressed down from in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka. What this hymn does with it is unceremonious: bring them, all of them, here.

Two small practical details are worth seeing. Agni is addressed in verse 5 as *ghṛtāhavana*, the one into whom *ghṛta* is poured — still the commonest offering in any Hindu home, and still poured into fire rather than set before an image. And the soma of the last verse is *tiroahnya*, pressed on the far side of a day, kept overnight and offered now. A rite that admits its materials are a day old is a rite operating in real conditions, not an idealised one.

Between them, verses 3, 4 and 5 name Priyamedha and his descendants, Kaṇva and his sons, and Praskaṇva himself. Three generations of reciters inside three verses of a hymn about being heard. The Veda's own account of how it survived is embedded in the hymns and not appended to them; the two Aśvin hymns that follow, [[1.46]] and [[1.47]], run the same argument from precedent, and the Agni hymn before it, [[1.44]], names Praskaṇva in the same way.
45.disagreements:
Verse 1's *janam manujātam* is genuinely unsettled. Sāyaṇa reads it as a man born of Manu — a divine being standing alongside the enumerated classes of gods — and Wilson follows with "or any other living being sprung from Manu." Griffith attaches the phrase to the gods themselves: "the Rudras, the Adityas, all Who spring from Manu." The same problem returns in verses 9 and 10 with *daivyam janam*, which Sāyaṇa again takes as some divine or deified person; Wilson prints "or other deified being" and Griffith "the host of heaven."

On the three-and-thirty of verse 2, Sāyaṇa cites Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 2.18 for two distinct sets of thirty-three: the *somapās*, drinkers of soma, and a second set that are personified sacrifices — eleven *prayājas*, eleven *anuyājas*, eleven *upayājas*, offered with clarified butter rather than soma. He does not say which set the verse means.

Sāyaṇa identifies the four ṛṣis of verse 3 from Purāṇic genealogy: Atri and Aṅgiras among the Prajāpatis, Priyamedha equated with Priyavrata son of Svāyambhuva Manu, Virūpa a descendant of Vaivasvata Manu. On verse 9's *sahaskṛta* he notes an apparent reference to the production of fire by friction — strength-made, in the literal sense.

46.title: Come as a Boat, Aśvins — the Crossing at Dawn
46.synthesis:
Fifteen short verses that open with Uṣas, close near her again, and in between build one sustained image: the Aśvins as the means of getting across water in the dark.

*Eṣā uṣāḥ apūrvyā vi ucchati* — this Uṣas, unlike any before her, shines out, dear daughter of heaven; and high, Aśvins, I praise you. The hymn establishes the hour first and the gods second. The second verse names them wonder-working, *sindhumātarā*, whose mother is the flood, devisers of riches, finding goods *dhiyā*, by thought. The third has them already moving: your tall ones speed across the burning height when your chariot flies on wings. The fourth is the hardest verse in the hymn and does not yield a secure reading — a lover of the waters, a filler, a father, someone who watches over the rite, feeding with the offering. It is not clear who is meant, and the honest description of the verse is that it is obscure.

The fifth steadies again: regarders of our thoughts, Nāsatyas, minding what we say — drink the soma boldly. The sixth asks for the aid that has light in it, the one that will carry us past darkness; give us that nourishment. And the seventh puts the image into words that cannot be mistaken. *Ā naḥ nāvā matīnām yātam pārāya gantave* — come to us by the boat of our thoughts, to go to the far shore; yoke your chariot, Aśvins. The vessel is not theirs. It is made of the hymn.

The eighth extends the picture without softening it: your oar is wide as heaven itself; the chariot stands at the *tīrtha*, the ford, of the rivers; the soma drops have been harnessed *dhiyā*, by thought. The ninth ends in a question — from heaven the drops, Kaṇvas; the treasure at the place of the rivers; where do you mean to set your own form? *Kuha dhitsathaḥ*. The gods have been called, the vehicle is ready, and nobody yet knows where they will appear.

Then two verses answer, and they answer with daylight. *Abhūt u bhāḥ* — there was light; and Sūrya appeared like gold, and the dark one shone out with his tongue. *Abhūt u pāram etave panthāḥ* — there came to be, for going to the far shore, the straight road: *ṛtasya*, the road of *ṛta*, and the track of heaven was seen. Two verses beginning with the same two words, the second completing the first. Light came, and with the light the way became visible. Everything the hymn asked for in verses 6 to 9 is granted in these two lines, and granted as an event rather than a favour.

The last four verses settle. The singer attends on whatever help the Aśvins give, who carry across in the gladness of soma. Dwelling with Vivasvat, come to the soma and to the song as you came to Manu, you who bring wellbeing. Uṣas follows the splendour of your circuit, and by the nights you win what is in accord with *ṛta*. And the close, which asks for nothing elaborate: *ubhā pibatam aśvinā, ubhā naḥ śarma yacchatam* — both of you drink, both of you hold out shelter over us, with helps that nothing can break into.
46.practice:
The Aśvins are the pair who ride ahead of the dawn, and this hymn is the clearest demonstration of what that means in practice: it begins in the last of the dark and ends in full light. Counted from the Anukramaṇī, 69 sūktas name them and 52 are wholly theirs — a total exceeded only by Indra, Agni, Soma and the Viśvedevāḥ.

What makes the hymn unusual is that it thinks about crossing water for eleven verses. *Sindhu* appears three times, and with it a boat, an oar, a ford, and twice the word *pāra*, the far shore. Verse 7 is the one to memorise: *nāvā matīnām*, by the boat of our thoughts. The gods are asked to arrive by a vessel built out of the hymn being recited — which makes the recitation not a request for transport but the transport itself. Everything the later tradition says about crossing over, about the *tīrtha* as a place where a crossing is possible and about a teaching that ferries, is already operating here as a figure that has not yet become a cliché.

Verse 11 says where the road goes. *Pāram etave panthāḥ ṛtasya* — the road of *ṛta*, for going to the far side. Placed where it is, immediately after Sūrya rises, it makes a plain claim: the way across is not opened by effort but becomes visible when there is light. The two verses are built to be read together, and the second is the answer to a question asked two verses earlier about where the gods would show themselves.

The Aśvins' own standing office is medicine, and the tradition preserves them as *devānāṃ bhiṣajau*, physicians of the gods, an address noted at [[1.3]]. This hymn adds the other half of their portfolio and shows why the two belong together: they are the ones who bring a person through a bad passage. The last verse asks not for wealth but for *śarma*, shelter, from both of them at once, and the word for their protections is *avidriya* — not to be broken into. The companion hymn [[1.47]] takes up the same pair in a different key, and [[1.48]] follows the light they have brought in all the way up.
46.disagreements:
Verse 4 defeats both translators and should be said to. Wilson, with Sāyaṇa, makes it about the sun evaporating and returning the waters, supplying most of the sentence in parentheses; Griffith produces "He, liberal, lover of the flood, Lord of the House, the vigilant, Chiefs! with oblations feeds you full," which agrees with Wilson on almost nothing. The padapāṭha gives *jāraḥ apām*, *papuriḥ*, *pitā kuṭasya*, *carṣaṇiḥ* — words whose individual senses are clear and whose subject is not.

Verse 11 divides them on the genitive. Wilson makes it the sun's road: "a fit path was made for the sun to go beyond the boundary of night." Griffith reads "the path of sacrifice was made to travel to the farther goal." The padapāṭha has *panthā ṛtasya* — the road of *ṛta* — which neither reproduces, Wilson dropping it and Griffith substituting the rite for the order.

Sāyaṇa identifies the *sindhumātarā* of verse 2 as the sun and moon, born of the sea, and reads verse 6's *tamas* as poverty rather than literal darkness. On verse 9 he is candid that the reading rests on an assumption not in the text — that the Kaṇvas are being told to put the questions to the Aśvins on the poet's behalf. Wilson prints that assumption; Griffith leaves the verse abrupt.

47.title: Aśvins on the Three-Seated Car, Growers of Ṛta
47.synthesis:
Ten verses, and three of them end the same way: the Aśvins are called *ṛtāvṛdhā*, growers of *ṛta*, and told to drink. The epithet and the invitation are welded together, and the hymn will not let them come apart.

*Ayam vām madhumattamaḥ sutaḥ somaḥ ṛtāvṛdhā* — here for you two is the sweetest pressed soma, growers of *ṛta*; drink it, this *tiroahnya*, kept from the day before, and place treasures on the man who gives. The second verse brings the vehicle: come with the three-seated, threefold, well-figured chariot; the Kaṇvas are making the *brahman*, the formulation, for you at the rite — hear their call well. The third repeats the first almost exactly, and repeats the epithet: drink the sweetest soma, growers of *ṛta*, and come today to the giver, bearing goods on the chariot. The fourth sets the scene at the seat: on the thrice-heaped *barhis*, all-knowing ones, drench the *yajña* with honey; the Kaṇvas, their soma pressed, turned toward the light of day, call on you.

The fifth verse makes the case that the rest of the hymn keeps making. *Yābhiḥ kaṇvam abhiṣṭibhiḥ pra āvatam* — with the helps by which you protected Kaṇva, protect us; lords of splendour, drink the soma, growers of *ṛta*. That is the third and last appearance of the epithet, and it comes attached to the argument from precedent: what you did before, do again. The sixth extends the precedent to a king: you brought abundance to Sudās on the wealth-bearing chariot, so bring us the riches many long for, *samudrāt uta vā divaḥ* — from the sea or from heaven, whichever is nearer to hand.

The seventh admits that nobody knows where they are. Whether you are *parāvati*, far off, or near Turvaśa, come from there on the smooth-rolling chariot, *sākam sūryasya raśmibhiḥ* — together with the rays of Sūrya. The eighth asks their horses, called the ornament of the rite, to carry them here to the pressings, mixing food for the man who acts well and gives well, and asks the two of them to sit down on the *barhis*. The ninth names the chariot again and gives it its finest description: come by the car that is *sūryatvacā*, sun-skinned, in which you have always carried wealth to the giver, to drink the honey of the soma.

The tenth closes on the same argument once more. With *ukthas* and with *arkas* we call the two rich in goods down to us for help; for always, in the beloved seat of the Kaṇvas, you have drunk the soma. *Śaśvat* — always — appears in the ninth verse and again in the tenth. The hymn does not claim the Aśvins ought to come. It claims they have come, repeatedly, to this family, in this place, and it puts the sweetness of the drink and the office of upholding *ṛta* on either side of that claim so neither can be considered without the other.
47.practice:
*Ṛtāvṛdh*, the epithet said three times here, is worth stopping on because of who else carries it. In [[1.2]].8 it is given to Mitra and Varuṇa — *ṛtena mitrāvaruṇāv ṛtāvṛdhāv ṛtaspṛśā* — where it is the centre of one of the collection's most concentrated statements about cosmic order. Here the same word is given three times to the Aśvins, a pair of riders whose usual business is rescue and healing. It also lands on the maruts at [[1.44]].14. The epithet names an office, not a temperament: whoever makes *ṛta* increase holds it, and the Ṛgveda is willing to say that of the physicians as readily as of the two who keep the day and night in their courses.

What is asked of them, three times over, is that they drink. Not that they think about order, or maintain it — that they accept hospitality. The hymn's theology is entirely conducted through the offering of a cup.

The chariot is the other thing here, and it does what the boat does in [[1.46]] — it is the means by which the distance is closed. It is *trivandhura* and *trivṛt*, three-seated and threefold, and *sūryatvac*, sun-skinned. The third seat has occupied the tradition for a long time: two riders, three places. Sāyaṇa records that older commentators read the compound as three posts and a triangular frame, and offers his own reading of three fastenings of timber and a car that passes unobstructed through the three worlds. Neither claim is settled, and it is worth knowing the tradition itself is unsure.

The argument the hymn actually runs on is precedent, and it is stated four times: as you helped Kaṇva, as you brought to Sudās, as you have *always* brought, as you have *always* drunk in the Kaṇvas' seat. The Aśvins are asked to be consistent. That is a modest thing to ask of a god and a demanding one, and it is the request that the household-scale religion of the Veda is mostly made of.
47.disagreements:
Verse 2 shows Sāyaṇa recording a change of mind. He notes that *trivandhureṇa trivṛtā rathena* was earlier explained as a car with three posts and a triangular shape, and prefers in this context "having three undulating fastenings of timber, and passing unobstructedly through the three worlds." Wilson prints the older reading, "three-columned triangular car"; Griffith gives "your triple car three-seated, beautiful of form."

Verse 7 divides them over a name. The padapāṭha has *turvaśe*, and Griffith keeps it as a proper noun — "whether ye be far away or close to Turvasa." Wilson reads it as a common expression and renders the whole as "whether you abide far off or close at hand," dissolving the name into a contrast of distances.

Sāyaṇa's note on Sudās in verse 6 is a piece of honest confusion preserved rather than resolved: he records two figures of that name from the Purāṇic genealogies, one in the solar line and one in the lunar, son of Divodāsa, without choosing. On verse 9 he glosses *sūryatvacā* as sun-skinned in the sense of being surrounded by the sun or resembling it in brightness, which Wilson prints as "sun-clad" and Griffith renders as a canopy.
