48.title: Uṣas, in Whom the Breath and Life of All Rests
48.synthesis:
Her name is in fourteen of the sixteen verses. Verse 6 leaves it out, and so does verse 10 — and verse 10 is the one that says the breath of everything alive is in her. The hymn can afford to drop the name at the moment it makes its largest claim, because by then there is nothing else it could be about.

*Saha vāmena naḥ uṣo vi uccha* — shine out on us together with what is lovely, daughter of heaven; shine out with high *dyumna*, splendour, you who shine wide; with *rayi*, goddess, you who give. The second verse has a run of feminine plurals with no noun attached to them — rich in horses, rich in cattle, finders of every good, they have often sped forth to make light — and then turns personal: Uṣas, rouse up the *sūnṛtās*, the true and generous words, toward me; impel the bounty of the liberal. The third puts her in two tenses at once. *Uvāsa uṣāḥ ucchāt ca nu* — she has dawned, and she shall dawn now: a perfect and a future in one line, which is the hymn's way of saying that this morning is not a separate event. She quickens the chariots, and those who fix their thought on her as she draws near are like men after wealth upon the sea.

The fourth verse is where the poet steps in. Those patrons who, at your comings, yoke their minds to giving — of these, Kaṇva, most Kaṇva of them, sings the names aloud. The fifth is the finest verse in the hymn and the most disquieting. *Ā ghā yoṣeva sūnarī uṣā yāti prabhuñjatī, jarayantī vṛjanam* — Uṣas comes like a good woman of the house, enjoying, taking her pleasure in everything — and aging the settlement. The two participles sit side by side in one line, and the second is from √jṛ, to wear out. She rouses whatever has feet, and she makes the birds fly up; and she is spending the lives she wakes.

The sixth sends people to work. She looses the gathering and those who have business to do; she does not miss a step; and at her shining-out the birds that have flown will not settle again. The seventh has her yoke from a great distance, from beyond the rising of Sūrya, and come with a hundred chariots toward men. In the eighth the whole moving world bends down to be looked at by her; she makes the light, and the wealthy daughter of heaven shines hostility and failure away.

The ninth asks her to shine here with a bright ray, bringing much good fortune, shining out at the morning rites. The tenth is the claim the hymn exists for: *viśvasya hi prāṇanaṃ jīvanaṃ tve* — for in you is the breathing and the living of everything, when you shine out. Come with the great chariot; hear our call. Nothing in the fifteen other verses contradicts this and nothing softens the fifth verse either. She is where life comes from, and she is what wears it down.

The eleventh asks her to win the *vāja* that is remarkable among men, and to bring the well-doers by it to the rites. The twelfth asks her to bring the gods down from the mid-air for the soma, and to give cattle, horses, strength worth praising. The thirteenth: may she whose bright rays are seen all round give riches easy to come by. The fourteenth reaches back — the ancient ṛṣis called on you for help and protection, so answer our praises with bounty and with clear flame. The fifteenth: since you have opened today the two doors of heaven with your light, hold out over us a wide shelter with no wolves in it. And the sixteenth says *sam* four times — join us with great wealth, with nourishment, with splendour, with strength.
48.practice:
Counted from the Anukramaṇī, twenty sūktas in the whole Ṛgveda are wholly given to Uṣas. [[1.113]] at twenty verses is the longest; this one at sixteen is next. She also holds something no other goddess does: a run of seven consecutive hymns in a family book, [[7.75]] through [[7.81]]. Twenty hymns out of 1,028 is not many, and they are among the most admired things in the collection — which is a fact about what the tradition valued, not about how often it spoke.

The reason to face east is verse 10. *Viśvasya prāṇanaṃ jīvanaṃ tve* — in you is the breathing and the living of everything. The *sandhyā* performed at the junctures, the *arghya* offered toward the coming light, the whole habit of getting up before dawn that this culture has never quite abandoned: the justification is stated here and it is not sentimental. It is a claim that the light arriving and the breath continuing are one event.

Verse 5 is what keeps the hymn from being a greeting card, and it should not be softened. She comes *prabhuñjatī* and *jarayantī* — enjoying, and aging. Every dawn that wakes you has also taken a day. The Ṛgveda puts both words in one line and asks for her arrival anyway, in the next verse and the next. That is a particular kind of maturity about time, and it is available to anyone standing outside at five in the morning: the thing you are glad to see is the thing that is counting you down.

Verse 14 supplies the other half. *Ye cit hi tvām ṛṣayaḥ pūrve* — the ancient ṛṣis called on you too. This is the same argument made in the second verse of the collection's first hymn, that the ancients and those alive now praise the same god ([[1.1]].2). Applied to Uṣas it becomes literal in a way it cannot be for anyone else: the dawn a ṛṣi watched and the dawn outside the window are not similar events, they are the same recurring one. Verse 3 says so directly — *uvāsa uṣāḥ ucchāt ca nu*, she has dawned, and she will dawn now.

And verse 15 asks for something small after all that: a wide shelter, *avṛka*, with no wolves in it. The four-verse [[1.49]], by the same ṛṣi, asks for less still.
48.disagreements:
Verse 5 is the hymn's crux and the translators go opposite ways. Wilson, with Sāyaṇa, keeps the harder sense — Uṣas "conducting all transient creatures to decay." Griffith turns the same participle benign: "Like a good matron Usas comes carefully tending everything." The grammatical apparatus reads *jarayantī* as a present participle of √jṛ, to grow old or wear away, which supports Wilson; Griffith appears to have read it toward *jar*, to sing or to woo.

Verse 2 has a run of feminine plural epithets with no noun to attach to. Sāyaṇa supplies one — *uṣodevatāḥ*, the many divinities of dawn — and Wilson prints "the divinities of morning" in parentheses. Griffith attaches them to the gifts instead: "They, bringing steeds and kine, boon-givers of all wealth."

Sāyaṇa is at his most concrete on verse 6. The *arthinaḥ* whom Uṣas releases are, he says, the petitioners who rise at daybreak and go to the houses of their respective benefactors. On verse 8 he reads *sridhaḥ* as "the driers-up", suggesting the clouds that take up the night's dew, where Griffith simply has "enmities." On verse 3's *samudre na śravasyavaḥ* Wilson follows Sāyaṇa in supplying ships sent to sea; Griffith leaves it as "glory-seekers on the flood."

49.title: Uṣas Called Down to the Soma-Presser's House
49.synthesis:
Four verses, and the first thing they do is make the dawn a guest at a particular address. After the sixteen verses of [[1.48]], the same ṛṣi turns to the same goddess and asks for something much smaller and more exact.

*Uṣo bhadrebhiḥ ā gahi* — Uṣas, come by auspicious ways, *divaḥ cit rocanāt adhi*, from up above the shining region of heaven itself. And then the destination, which is not the sky and not the world: *upa tvā sominaḥ gṛham* — let the ruddy-formed ones bring you to the house of the man who has pressed the soma. The verse travels from the luminous height of heaven to a doorway in three lines. That descent is the entire form of the hymn.

The second verse gives her the vehicle and gives the householder his standing. That chariot you have mounted, beautiful in form, easy-running — by it, *duhitaḥ divaḥ*, daughter of heaven, favour today the man of good renown. Both halves of the line matter. She is addressed by the great title, the one the long hymn opens and turns on; and what is asked of her under it is not that she bless the world but that she turn, on this particular morning, toward one household that has done the work and is known for having done it.

The third verse opens outward again, and it is the widest thing in these four. *Vayaḥ cit te patatriṇo dvipat catuṣpat arjuni* — the birds, the winged ones, biped and four-footed, O bright one: *uṣaḥ pra āran ṛtūn anu*, they have started up, Uṣas, in accord with the *ṛtus*, the fixed times — *divaḥ antebhyaḥ pari*, from the ends of heaven all around. Everything with wings and everything with legs is awake, and the verse says why: not because they were roused but because it is the appointed hour and they keep it. Two words carry that — *ṛtūn anu* — and they are the reason this small hymn matters.

The fourth closes the circle the first verse opened. *Vyucchantī hi raśmibhiḥ viśvam ābhāsi rocanam* — shining out with your rays you illuminate the whole shining realm. The word *rocana* stood in the first verse as the place she was asked to come down from; here it is what she lights up. She has arrived, and what was above her is now what she shines on. And the last line brings the hymn back to its own house: *tām tvām uṣo vasuyavaḥ gīrbhiḥ kaṇvāḥ ahūṣata* — you, such as you are, the Kaṇvas, wanting goods, have called with their songs.

*Divaḥ* has now been said in three consecutive verses — the shining place she comes from, the parentage she is addressed by, the far edges the birds rise from — and the fourth lets the word go, because by then she is here.

Four verses, and each has one job: come here, come to this man, see that everything is already awake and on time, and know who called you. Nothing is elaborated and nothing is missing.
49.practice:
This hymn is the short companion of [[1.48]] — same ṛṣi, same goddess, sixteen verses of *bṛhatī* followed by four of *anuṣṭubh* — and it is worth noticing that the collection preserved both. Twenty sūktas in the Ṛgveda are wholly Uṣas's; this is among the briefest of them, with only [[10.172]] equally short at four verses and [[7.80]] shorter at three. The small hymn is not a fragment of the large one. It does something the long hymn does not: it brings the dawn indoors, to *sominaḥ gṛham*, the house of a man who has pressed soma. Vedic worship happens in a household, and here is the household saying so.

The two words to carry out are in the third verse: *ṛtūn anu*. The birds and the animals have risen *in accord with the ṛtus* — the appointed times. *Ṛtu* is the word a Hindu still says aloud in the *saṅkalpa* when the occasion of a rite is declared, naming the season before naming anything else, and it is the word inside *ṛtvij*, the title given to Agni in the first verse of the collection ([[1.1]].1) — *ṛtu* + √yaj, one who offers at the right time. What this verse observes is that the birds already do it. They have no formula and no priest, and they keep the hour exactly. The Vedic concern with timeliness is not an invention of ritualists; the hymn points at the sky at daybreak and says the rest of creation is already doing this.

That gives the hymn its quiet argument. Uṣas is asked to come to one house, on one morning, because she is the one by whom the times are kept — and the household that rises to meet her is doing what everything with wings and legs is doing anyway, only deliberately. A person who gets up before light and faces east is not performing an unusual act. They are rejoining something already in progress.
49.disagreements:
Verse 1's *aruṇapsavaḥ* is where the two translators diverge and neither stays with the word. It means those of ruddy form, and specifies no animal. Sāyaṇa supplies cows — *aruṇyo gāva uṣasām*, the purple kine that are the vehicles of the morning — which Wilson prints as "the purple kine"; Griffith has "red steeds." The text names a colour and a shape and leaves the species open.

Verse 3 shows a different kind of loss. The padapāṭha has *ṛtūn anu*, and the grammatical apparatus confirms *ṛtu* in the accusative plural with the postposition. Wilson does not render it at all — "upon your coming, bipeds and quadrupeds are in motion" — and the sense of appointed recurrence disappears. Griffith keeps it, though he transfers it to the goddess: "Bright Usas, when thy times return." The same verse's vocative *arjuni* is "white-complexioned" for Wilson and simply "Bright" for Griffith.

Verse 2's *suśravasam janam* divides them along a familiar line. Wilson makes it the ritual actor — "the pious offerer of the oblation" — while Griffith reads social standing, "men of noble fame." The compound itself says only "of good renown", and the disagreement is really about whether renown in this collection is earned at the altar or in the world.
